body_text: United Airlines bans AI agents from booking flights on behalf of travelers - CBS News Latest U.S. Iran War Trump Interview Midterms World Politics Entertainment HealthWatch MoneyWatch Crime Space Sports Brand Studio The Free Press Local News Atlanta Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas Live CBS News 24/7 Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas 48 Hours 60 Minutes Shows 48 Hours 60 Minutes CBS Evening News CBS Mornings CBS Morning News CBS Reports CBS Saturday Morning The Daily Report The Dish Face the Nation Sunday Morning The Takeout Things That Matter The Uplift CBS News Investigates CBS News Confirmed Podcasts Newsletters Download Our App CBS News Team Executive Team Brand Studio Paramount+ Join Our Talent Community RSS Feeds MoneyWatch | Managing Your Money CBS News Price Tracker Watch CBS News MoneyWatch United Airlines bans AI agents from booking flights on behalf of travelers By Megan Cerullo Megan Cerullo Reporter, MoneyWatch Megan Cerullo is a New York-based reporter for CBS MoneyWatch covering small business, workplace, health care, consumer spending and personal finance topics. She regularly appears on CBS News 24/7 to discuss her reporting. Read Full Bio Megan Cerullo November 11, 2026 / 2:37 PM EST / MoneyWatch Add CBS News on Google United Airlines said on Wednesday that it is banning artificial intelligence agents from making flight reservations on behalf of travelers, citing  security risks  and the possibility that such actions could violate federal rules. Many consumers are turning to AI agents such as Meta's Muse and OpenAI's dots to complete tasks ranging from researching products and tracking down deals to making purchases. To make an airline booking, an AI agent requires access to a customer's personal information, including credentials like payment information. United has a problem with that, saying that "sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles." The carrier also said that using an AI agent to, for example, check in for a flight could violate federal regulations, including rules requiring travelers to verify in person that their luggage does not contain banned substances. "As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access — directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators — to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants," said the airline, which is updating its booking and ticketing policies to reflect the new rule. United's new policy suggests the company wants to retain control over the customer booking process, said Henry Harteveldt, an aviation analyst at Atmosphere Research Group.  "United is saying they don't want to add yet another, and potentially even more powerful, intermediary than they already face in terms of Google search, price-comparison metasearch sites and online travel agencies," he told CBS News. "Flight searches cost airlines money, and undoubtedly United wants to avoid the expense associated with the surge of AI bot flight searches." Other airlines are taking a different tack to the emergence of AI agents. For example, Southwest has made its flight inventory viewable to ChatGPT users, who can access the airline's website through the AI app.  United fares will continue to be bookable through flight aggregators such as Kayak, Hopper and Google Flights, Harteveldt said, adding that "consumers shouldn't find it any more difficult to find good fares on the airline." "But by blocking the AI bots, United won't make it any easier to find its fares, either," he said.  Edited by Alain Sherter Kris Van Cleave contributed to this report. You use it to test your software without calling AWS, on your own machine, on a development server, or in continuous integration (CI). You don’t need an AWS account. Your requests go to the emulator, not to AWS. So you work with emulated resources instead of AWS resources. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. The emulator is a local program that serves an AWS API endpoint. It has no graphical interface. After you start the emulator, you set environment variables to point the AWS CLI or an AWS SDK at its endpoint. Then you run your code as usual. In embedded mode, you pass the emulator’s HTTP client to your SDK instead. AWS Emulator is for building and testing. Don’t use it for production workloads or to test security. See Security in AWS Emulator . Documentation: AWS Emulator User Guide Quick start With an AI coding agent Install the aws-emulator skill, then ask your agent to set up the emulator. This needs the AWS CLI version 2.35.0 or later. See Getting started with an AI coding agent . aws agent-toolkit add-skill --skill-name aws-emulator --region us-east-1 Server mode (CLI and any SDK) Linux: install the RPM or Debian package and run aws-emulator . See Getting started on Linux . Windows / macOS: run the emulator in a container built from a short Dockerfile. See Getting started with Docker . Point your SDK at a running emulator by setting environment variables. See Pointing your AWS SDK at AWS Emulator . Embedded mode (Rust tests) Add the emulator as a dev-dependency and run it in-process, one isolated instance per test. There is no endpoint URL, certificate, or environment variable to set. Your test wires the emulator's HTTP client straight into the SDK client. See Getting started with embedded mode , and Building from source below for its build cost. Known issues To see how closely each service matches AWS, check the fidelity scores published with each release on the releases page . To check whether your own project is expected to work, see Checking whether your project works with AWS Emulator . Individual gaps are tracked in the repository's issues/ directory. APIs and behaviors that don't work yet are under issues/things-that-do-not-work/ , and ones that have since been fixed move to issues/things-that-now-work/ . Building from source You need this if you are modifying the emulator, running it from a checkout, or using embedded mode. Embedded mode compiles the emulator into your test binary, so the prerequisites and build-cost guidance below apply to it too. Most other users install a prebuilt package instead (see Quick start ). Building from source is supported on Linux (x86_64 and aarch64) ; on Windows and macOS, use the Docker path above. Prerequisites A Rust toolchain with Cargo (install via rustup ). A C compiler, such as GCC or clang. Some dependencies build C code. At least 100 GB of free disk for target/ . The workspace has one crate per AWS service, so a debug build of everything is large, and it grows as services are added. A multi-core machine. A cold full build compiles every service crate, so the first build takes a while; fewer cores take proportionally longer. After that, rebuilding after a change to one service is much faster. Build and run cargo build -p aws-emulator-router cargo run -p aws-emulator-router The emulator serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297 (self-signed certificate). Embedded mode build cost Embedded mode compiles the emulator into your test binary, so your project's first cargo test builds the emulator's service crates alongside your own code. Budget a first build and target/ on the same order as building from source above, then fast incremental builds. Recommendation: reuse one CARGO_TARGET_DIR across projects, cache target/ (or use sccache) in CI, and pin the emulator to a release commit so it isn't rebuilt on every change. Repository layout . ├── Cargo.toml # workspace: one member per service, plus the core crates ├── services/ │ └── service-<name>/ # ONE CRATE PER SERVICE │ ├── smithy-model/ # <name>.json — the Smithy model that drives the wire protocol │ ├── build.rs # generates the service declaration from the model │ ├── src/ │ │ ├── service.rs # request routing and refusal overrides │ │ ├── state.rs # this service's in-memory state │ │ └── ops/ # one file per operation │ └── tests/ ├── core/ │ ├── router/ # the emulator binary: mounts every service on one endpoint │ └── embedded/ # the in-process (embedded mode) facade ├── vendor/ # framework crates — do not edit (replaced on update) └── issues/ # tracked fidelity issues Telemetry AWS Emulator is configured to collect and report usage data to AWS, to gain insight into how AWS Emulator is used. Telemetry is on by default. AWS Emulator collects telemetry data with strict data minimization in mind, preventing identification or attribution to specific users, accounts, or organizations. Its records never include what’s in your requests or responses, your code, your credentials, or personal data. We don’t share telemetry with third parties. For details on what is collected and how the data is handled, see Telemetry in AWS Emulator . To turn telemetry off, use one of the following options. Use a command-line option Start the emulator with the --telemetry option (short form -t ) set to off . This setting applies only to that emulator process. aws-emulator --telemetry off In a container, add --telemetry off after the image name in the docker run command. Use an environment variable Set EMULATOR_TELEMETRY to off before you start the emulator. This setting applies to every emulator that you start from that shell. EMULATOR_TELEMETRY accepts on , true , or 1 to turn telemetry on, and off , false , or 0 to turn it off. Values aren’t case sensitive. Any other value turns telemetry off, and the startup notice shows a warning. export EMULATOR_TELEMETRY=off aws-emulator Use a configuration file To turn telemetry off for every run on a machine, add these lines to the emulator settings file, config.toml . The file is ~/.aws/emulator/config.toml on Linux and macOS, and %USERPROFILE%\.aws\emulator\config.toml on Windows. To use a different file, set the EMULATOR_CONFIG environment variable to its path. [ telemetry ] enabled = false Use the embedded configuration API In embedded mode, turn off telemetry in the options that you pass when you create the emulator. use aws_emulator_embedded :: { AwsEmulatorEmbedded , EmbeddedOptions , Telemetry } ; fn main ( ) { let emulator = AwsEmulatorEmbedded :: new ( EmbeddedOptions :: default ( ) . telemetry ( Telemetry :: Off ) ) ; let _http_client = emulator . http_client ( ) ; } You might build a tool that includes the emulator, such as a test framework that other people run. If you do, tell your users about telemetry and give them a way to turn it off. You can also ship your tool with telemetry off. Reporting issues and contributing Report bugs and fidelity gaps in GitHub Issues . The most useful report names the service, the operation, your SDK and version, the request you sent, and how the response differed from real AWS. This repository does not take PRs. title: Tim Peters has died
body_text: In Memoriam: Tim Peters 1952–2026 - Core Development - Discussions on Python.org = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-ai_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-reactions_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="poll_desktop" /> Discussions on Python.org In Memoriam: Tim Peters 1952–2026 Core Development guido (Guido van Rossum) November 11, 2026, 5:36am 1 I am immensely sad to announce that Tim Peters has died earlier this year on July 15. It’s hard to overestimate Tim’s influence on Python. He’s probably best known for writing the Zen of Python ( PEP 20 ), but to me he was a mentor and language co-designer long before that. Tim found Python not long after its initial release. His first deed was to convince me that Python should support mixed arithmetic between int and float , because most users would expect them to work that way. And he never stopped contributing. Tim quickly became a major phenomenon on the Python mailing list (including later incarnations and spinoffs), where he earned the nickname “Timbot” by his innumerable, careful and patient answers to user questions. These he filled with mild humor (always marked by <wink> or <0.5 wink> ) and often referred to as “channeling Guido”. At the same time Tim participated in numerous in-depth design discussions, saving me or others from embarrassing design mistakes or solving deep problems, guided by his vast mathematical knowledge and compiler-building experience. In fact, Tim really set the tone for early core development, never outright dismissing people and explaining in detail why things could or couldn’t work. In 2002, Tim gave us Timsort : a new sorting algorithm he designed for Python lists, which was later adopted by Java and Android. Python-would-not-be-what-it-is-today-without-Tim-ly y’rs, –Guido 169 Likes guido (Guido van Rossum) November 11, 2026, 5:41am 2 Feel free to respond with your own Tim anecdotes. I could not cover everything he did. 5 Likes Rosuav (Chris Angelico) November 11, 2026, 6:04am 3 Very sad news. I have had the privilege and pleasure of discussing MANY topics with Tim, and his input into technical discussions has always been something I value very highly. He never treated you like an idiot, never dismissed your concerns out of hand, always answered and explained. I exchanged emails with him many times, but geography meant that sadly, we never met in person. 14 Likes hugovk (Hugo van Kemenade) November 11, 2026, 6:13am 4 Guido van Rossum: In fact, Tim really set the tone for early core development, never outright dismissing people and explaining in detail why things could or couldn’t work. From the start to the end. His last post concluded: Which is all a long-winded say of saying the real world is more complicated than our clean abstractions hope for . 40 Likes mcdonc (Chris McDonough) November 11, 2026, 6:41am 5 I wrote this some time ago about Tim: “”" I worked with Tim and the rest of Python Labs for a couple of years in the early 2000s. Tim was a hugely positive influence on me throughout my Python career. Before I had ever spoken to Tim, he was already legendary. He had worked for Cray Research writing compilers for supercomputers, and for Dragon Systems, writing speech-to-text software at a time when such a task was considered largely impossible. He took up Python on a lark in its very early days, becoming something like Python’s second real user after Guido. Guido came to rely on Tim heavily. Tim will demur about this, but as far as I can tell, Tim and Guido were largely partners in the design evolution of very early Python, and before most important features made it in to Python, you could be sure that they had been examined from every angle, shaken, stirred, and thunk about very hard by both of them. Tim often played the role of gatekeeper and polisher. You have Tim to thank at least partially if you were a refugee from Java or Microsoft languages, which made excuses for their sprawling verbosity, complexity, and poor readability. Python, at the time, made none of those and had none of that (it now does). Tim was crucial in ensuring it stayed that way during his most active years. He will claim differently, but, by my observation, it is no accident that Python ballooned in complexity after his exit as day-to-day core developer. Perhaps this was more due to the resignation of Guido as BDFL and the new Steering Council model, which was also coincident, but not having Tim around didn’t help either. It was pure joy to read Tim’s Usenet and mail list posts, which were full of humor and good nature and measured positivity and not a little winking darkness. They somehow resonated with me on my journey from becoming a new programmer to a not-so-new programmer and they lit a path to becoming one on which you could be dramatically competent without becoming cryptic and insufferable. He was intensely knowledgeable, and unfailingly precise when arguing for or against some design change. But he was always gentle and patient and matter-of-fact, preferring to use humor and warmth rather than bile and authority as the currency in which he dealt. Tim penned “the Zen of Python” (“beautiful is better than ugly…”) which can be seen via “import this” to this day. You can see a bit of his wonderful humor and style in the prelude to his introduction of the poem . His enthusiasm was infectious, and in the days when he was most involved, most everyone could be witnessed spouting Tim-isms (winks and “'lys” and whatnot). When I did get the chance to work with Tim, he was just as influential. He had absolutely no pretensions. If I hadn’t already known him to be a computer savant, I would have assumed he was a biker or mechanic due to his long grey locks, full mustache and and working-class fashion sense. I would later find out that he had indeed worked at Harley-Davidson. I think he’s originally from Wisconsin, but an East- or West-Coaster not fluent in Midwest tongues could be excused for believing his disarming accent is Chicagoan. He seemed just like a regular-looking neighborhood punch-the-clock guy, not unlike all the mechanics and deliverymen and cooks and dishwashers and event staff I’d worked around as a kid and in my 20s. Except he was pretty much the smartest guy in every room he entered. Tim’s demeanor and lack of pretense inspired me to think that despite my own lack of education and pedigree, with enough effort and grace, that I might become a half-competent programmer. And eventualy I did. But before meeting Tim, it was not a given. I was alienated by the pretensions of my community peers, and I was often reminded that they were not necessary only by Tim. He was somewhat private. He could often be found with a pen and paper outside the building just standing alone, staring blankly off into space, presumably thinking about some mind-boggling algorithmic topic with which he had just been charged by our CTO, or perhaps mentally designing some aspect of a pet project, scribbling something every few minutes. He applied himself to our code, which included a custom database written in C and Python. He diagnosed and fixed a data-destroying bug in that byzantine codebase for our largest customer. This saved the account, and likely gave us enough runway for another year or so. Everyone who worked there was in awe of his programming and debugging skills, and while we tried our best to let the poor man be, we often asked him questions, many of which were pedestrian and dull. I remember one of our teammates trying to engage him into a debugging session, claiming that some fault seemed to happen every six runs. He smiled winkingly and asked “have you grepped the source for six?” It was a minor jab but given the sincerity of the question, and the person from which it had come, it occurred to me at the time that it might not be the worst theory of debugging from which to start. Tim was a Director of the Python Software Foundation from 2001 to 2014, bringing Python across an uncanny valley from a time where it was “interesting but ignorable” to “the planet’s default language” along with a cast of other incredible people. If you use Python, it’s not in small part due to Tim. When I started my own open source projects, it was Tim whom I channeled during design discussions and sprints. I quite consciously used tricks I had learned from him to make the process fun and welcoming. Rather than become prickly about some technical conflict, I would try to use low-brow humor to defuse things and I would try very hard to learn everything I could about the topic before responding such that I could gain and rely on the respect of other contributors. I often failed, of course, because I’m not Tim, but I was at least a twentieth a Tim, and at the time, I think my co-contributors would have agreed that the projects I led were fun and worthwhile to work on. It is in this way that Tim’s influence is likely most obvious to people today, because I’m not the only one who channeled him; any Python project started between 1995 and 2010 has a bit of Tim culture in it. “”" In sadness, . C 28 Likes duncathan (Dunc Graham) November 11, 2026, 6:46am 6 As a young child, only about 15, I first learned timsort. Some dozen years later, I had the briefest opportunity to exchange words with Tim himself on this forum. What a treat to have had that chance, just in time. RIP 9 Likes encukou (Petr Viktorin) November 11, 2026, 8:32am 7 When I was finishing university, head full of textbook algorithms, I read Objects/listsort.txt and was overwhelmed by how much depth, rigor, common sense and humanity can fit in a technical note. That was when I picked a programming language. 24 Likes pitrou (Antoine Pitrou) November 11, 2026, 9:53am 8 Tim’s main legacy for me has been the Zen of Python, which - despite being less cited nowadays - has been so useful and influential as a framework for elegance and clarity, and has informed so many people in their daily practice (and I cannot find a better way to describe him than as an excellent practitioner ). He was already less active when I started contributing around 2007; in fact my most frequent interactions with him have been in the recent years while he grew a slightly more confrontational attitude in some discussions, including here on d.p.o. I believe [1] he was acting with the best of intentions and was still deeply caring for the community he had been such a pivotal member of; acting with the same objectives as others, but having trouble to understand that different means might be used towards the same ends. and I might be full of myself here ↩︎ 16 Likes malemburg (Marc-André Lemburg) November 11, 2026, 9:58am 9 This is so sad and such a big loss for Python. Tim has given us a lot and we owe him. He was one of the extremely smart people who drew me into PythonLand in the late 1990s. Coming out of university, I was amazed how approachable, down to earth and humurous really great folks can be. Rest in Peace, Tim, and thanks-for-being-one-of-those-great-people-ly, Marc 17 Likes pf_moore (Paul Moore) November 11, 2026, 10:51am 10 So sad. I never had the chance to meet Tim in person, but his posts were always a delight to read, full of knowledge, insight and humour. I learned more than I can express from him. He will be missed. 13 Likes hodgestar (Simon Cross) November 11, 2026, 10:55am 11 One of the great souls, and roughly treated here near the end. 14 Likes nas (Neil Schemenauer) November 11, 2026, 12:31pm 12 A +1 to what Chris wrote. Tim was always pragmatic, preferring simple solutions over complex ones. In the early days of syntax highlighting in text editors, like Emacs and Vim, I remember that Python’s triple-quoted strings were tricky to get right. They span multiple lines and opening and closing tokens are identical, so it’s easy to get out of sync. Doctests make things especially tricky. I was telling Tim about some techniques I was using in the Vim syntax file to make it work more reliably. I don’t recall the editor Tim used (some commercial program on Windows) but he explained how he did it in his editor. Open the syntax highlighting config window, for open string token, type three quotes, for close string, type three quotes, close config window. Job done. That tickled him. He primarily used Windows 95 or 98 at a time when many Python core devs used NT, Unix, or Linux. He said if you installed all of Microsoft’s updates, it was quite reliable. Maybe he preferred it because it worked for him and there was no reason to change. Or, he found it useful when supporting people, since Windows was the most common platform Python was used on. Tim was about the furthest thing from an elitist you could be. This Bible quote comes to mind for me: “Ye shall know them by their fruits.”. Tim gave us a lot of fruit. I poked around at Python 2.4, since that seems a good version to show off the things he worked on. His contributions were all over the codebase but I’ll point out a few that stand out to me. pymalloc was contributed by Vladimir Marangozov but it was Tim who polished it to diamond-like form. A memory allocator is one of those things where it is impossible to have something completely optimal; you always make tradeoffs. Tim’s special contribution in that unit is Py_ADDRESS_IN_RANGE . It is well commented, if you want to understand how it works. Technically, it relies on undefined behavior but Tim figured it should work in practice. It did so for many years. At some point I wanted to increase the pymalloc pool size, since typical RAM sizes had increased so much since 2000. Tim helped me optimize the address_in_range() check. TimSort is a good example of Tim’s approach to software problems. Someone must have “nerd sniped” him on the problem of sorting. He already had an encyclopedic knowledge of the classic algorithms, like you’d find in Knuth. He spent a few days reading the recent research papers on sorting. With that knowledge and throwing in a few twists of his own, he made TimSort. He was always thinking of the common case, the favorable case as well as the worst-case scenarios. TimSort does all three well (it exploits already sorted runs, and uses galloping during merging to copy long stretches efficiently). Speaking of Knuth, the dict object algorithms were heavily optimized by Tim. The C file contains lots of comments. He also wrote dictnotes , which is a good example of his technical writing. Another example is weakref.txt , which I think Tim wrote after fixing a particularly difficult GC bug revealed by ZODB (while working at Zope Corp). On the topic of GC, the initial version of the cyclic garbage collector was written by me, merged before the 2.0 release. It was Tim who polished it into robust and well-performing shape. Likewise, I wrote the initial version of “simple generators” but it was Tim who put them on solid foundation, both the PEP and the implementation. Tim was skilled with numerical algorithms and error analysis, and Python benefited from his expertise. The float object and math module got special attention from him. He also worked on the Karatsuba multiplication algorithms in longobject . In addition to the C code, Tim also wrote beautiful Python code. As an example, see the N-Queens and Knight’s tour solvers in test_generators.py . He wrote the initial version of doctest . Some more examples of his work: difflib , pickletools , tabnanny (she shows no mercy!). It’s clear that Tim enjoyed writing code and solving problems. It’s also the case that he spent many thousands of hours of his time doing things primarily to help his fellow humans, without expectation of financial gain or of glory. Thank you, friend, for that and thank you for setting such an example. 33 Likes vinitkme (Vinit Kumar) November 11, 2026, 12:58pm 13 Thanks for everything Tim. Zen of Python has always been and will be my programming " North Star" and I strive to use it in every language I work with. Your impact has been on many of us Python Programmers and our families lives. Thank you and rest in peace! 6 Likes Stefan2 (Stefan Pochmann) November 11, 2026, 1:09pm 14 I’ve been fearing this since I noticed his absence end of July, dreading the thought whenever I saw his name but still no new activity. I’ve had quite a few interactions with Tim, he was one of my main contact points to Python, and he was the one who added me to Misc/ACKS . Thank you for everything, Tim. 7 Likes Paddy3118 (Paddy3118) November 11, 2026, 1:30pm 16 GNU Tim. 2 Likes diegor (Diego Russo) November 11, 2026, 2:39pm 17 I wish I’d had the chance to meet Tim in person. We had just a few exchanges on social media, but I always enjoyed reading his messages. There was always something to learn from his experience, his perspective and his way of thinking. Reading the memories shared here by those who knew and worked with him makes me regret even more that I never had that opportunity. I remember when Timsort was created. I was at university, studying algorithms, and it was a big deal at the time. But it’s the Zen of Python that influenced me most personally. “Now is better than never.” That sentence has stayed with me since I started using Python in the early 2000s. Over the years, it has become one of my personal mottos, encouraging me to keep trying, strive to do better and step outside my comfort zone, both in life and at work. We’ll probably never know what the 20th aphorism of the Zen of Python would have been. But perhaps that’s OK. I like to think that Tim left us the freedom to fill that space with something meaningful to each of us. Thank you, Tim, for everything you gave to Python and for the impact your work and words had on people. Rest in peace. 11 Likes holdenweb (Steve Holden) November 11, 2026, 3:09pm 18 Tim and I originally thought we first met fairly shortly after we both moved to Virginia, and became friends over Chinese lunches and discussions with Guido about starting a new Python conference. As we got to know each other better we realised that we had seen each other once before, when I visited a fellow academic’s office in Manchester, England, and Tim was there representing Cray Research back in 1983. Small world. After PythonLabs dissolved on Guido’s departure for the West coast the lunches eventually became a regular date at our local PF Chang, where Tim would invariably end with their huge “Mountain of Chocolate” dessert. The resulting sugar rush was often amusing. Tim was well-known long before I arrived in the Python world, and remained so after I left it. His technical contributions to Python, now the most popular programming language in the world, are legion. Just as significant, if not more so, was the way he communicated the joy, both of being a programmer and a human being. He was deeply affected by the ban imposed on him for ideological reasons by the Python Steering Committee but did not let that affect his desire to help others, which was on display until the end. I respected Tim above anyone else in the Python world for his wisdom, his witty humour and his deep humanity. There won’t be another one like him. Goodbye, old friend. 21 Likes sdeibel (Stephan Deibel) November 11, 2026, 3:41pm 19 This is very sad. I worked with Tim for quite a few years in context of the PSF board and of course also knew him from IPC and PyCons, starting in the relatively early days. He stood out to me almost immediately because so obviously utterly brilliant and yet with such a kind, helpful, respectful, good-humored way about him. One of the best people I’ve known, he was an inspiration to me and I think clearly also to very many others. Thanks, Tim, you will be missed. 7 Likes mwichmann (Mats Wichmann) November 11, 2026, 3:42pm 20 I only met Tim once, along with Guido, in 2001. I was writing a Python training course, and the training company wanted to arrange for “the experts” to get a look at it, so on a week I was in Reston working on it, we sat down over a meal. It wasn’t a very good course (“if I knew then what I know now”, a quarter century later…), but they generously gave of their time to critique, including Tim’s trademark humor, and I so appreciated it. He will be missed! 6 Likes mdickinson (Mark Dickinson) November 11, 2026, 4:00pm 22 Tim was hugely influential on my own CPython core development journey. Initially that influence was through his voluminous writings, mailing list discussions and his code itself: when I joined the core dev team in 2008, Tim himself was absent from the scene in person, but very much present through his many many contributions. Later on, after his return to core development, I was privileged to interact more directly with Tim on many topics. His gentle erudition, his humour and his patience were endless. Rest in peace, Tim. You will be sorely missed. 13 Likes next page → Home Categories Guidelines Terms of Service Privacy Policy Powered by Discourse , best viewed with JavaScript enabled

Generative AI is experimental Voice Speed Voice Speed 0.75X 1X 1.5X 2X Read AI-generated summary We are introducing the Gemini Decisions API to help you make fast, probabilistic choices across text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. This tool computes confidence scores for multiple questions in a single pass, providing a cost-effective way to route queries, grade content, or check policy rules. You can start building today by accessing your API key in Google AI Studio and reviewing our documentation for Python, JavaScript, and REST guides. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Today, we’re introducing the Gemini Decisions API, a new endpoint for fast, closed-set decisions powered by our new Gemini Decision 1 model (gemini-decision-1), available through the Gemini API in Google AI Studio . The Decisions API gives you purpose-built primitives for bounded choices like tool selection, policy checks, model routing, and context grading. You can pass one multimodal input across text, images, audio, video, and PDFs (up to 256K tokens) along with up to 1,000 independent questions. Rather than generating answer text token by token, Gemini Decision 1 scores your candidate options in a single forward pass, returning probabilities and confidence scores in 150-250 ms end-to-end latency at $0.10 per 1M input tokens with zero output tokens billed. Strong performance and calibration On benchmarks spanning agent routing, reasoning, ranking, and multimodal understanding, Gemini Decision 1 leads across the suite, with the lowest calibration error. Gemini Decision 1 scores options without token-by-token decoding, keeping median latency 50-100 ms of model compute (150-250 ms end-to-end), across multimodal inputs and contexts up to 16K tokens, remaining nearly flat from 1 to 100 questions per request. With zero output tokens billed, Gemini Decision 1 with the Decisions API is nearly 5x cheaper across the shared benchmark suite than Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite with the Interactions API. Native multimodal evaluation across three decision types in one pass Built on Gemini’s native multimodal architecture, Gemini Decision 1 can process text, images, audio, video, and PDFs directly in a single forward pass. You can combine modalities in one shared input, such as pairing a call recording with account metadata or a scanned PDF claim with damage photos, and tune resolution on image and video inputs to control visual detail and token cost. You can evaluate multiple questions against that shared input in a single request, mixing yes/no checks, multiple choice, and rubric scores. Every answer includes a confidence score (from 0 to 1) so your code can route ambiguous cases to a fallback or human reviewer: noul (Yes/No): Estimates the probability that a yes/no condition holds, with optional true and false description criteria. choice (Multiple Choice): Selects from 2 to 255 choices, returning the winner and normalized probabilities for every candidate. score (Ordered Rubric): Grades inputs across an ordered rubric (starting at 0), returning a continuous weighted score and per-level probabilities. The input field uses the same Content block format as the Interactions API . Here is how to check a photo of a breakroom counter, together with a text note, against all three question types in one request: from google import genai client = genai.Client(http_options={"api_version": "v1beta"}) result = client.decisions.create( model="gemini-decision-1", input=[{ "type": "image", "uri": "https://storage.googleapis.com/generativeai-downloads/images/spill.jpg", "mime_type": "image/jpeg", }, { "type": "text", "text": "Breakroom counter check before the 9 AM client meeting.", }, ], questions={ "has_spill": { "type": "noul", "instructions": "Is there an uncleaned liquid spill on the counter?", }, "next_action": { "type": "choice", "instructions": "Which cleanup action fits the scene?", "criteria": { "wipe_with_cloth": "Small counter spill with a cloth or towel already nearby.", "dispatch_janitorial": "Large floor hazard, broken glass, or active leak.", "ready_for_meeting": "Counter is clean and ready.", }, }, "severity": { "type": "score", "instructions": "Rate the severity of the counter mess.", "criteria": [ "Clean and ready.", "Minor localized spill.", "Major spill or safety hazard.", ], }, }, ) How teams are building with the Decisions API Teams across Google are already using the Decisions API as a low-latency control plane, shipping features simply by defining options rather than training custom classifiers or waiting on generative calls: Dynamic model routing in Gemini Notebook: Gemini Notebook uses the Decisions API as a real-time router to instantly direct incoming queries to the optimal model tier and thinking level for each request. The Decisions API classifies intent in milliseconds to serve everyday queries with up to 40% lower latency while reserving deep reasoning models for complex tasks. Rapid design iteration in Stitch: The new rapid canvas experiment in Stitch uses the Decisions API to generate playable wireframes of a product flow in seconds and to apply edits made by voice or tap almost instantly. When the flow feels right, one click hands the screens off to the full Stitch experience for deeper design polish. Emoji selection in CC: CC from Google Labs uses the Decisions API to pick the right emoji reaction from a palette of more than 200 options in a fraction of a second, so reactions appear instantly without adding latency. Safety layer for MCP tools in Search : Google Search uses the Decision API to detect adversarial behavior and content against adversarial evals with high efficacy within the latency envelope. Stitch Rapid uses the Decisions API to design an entire product flow in seconds (1x speed). Start building today Gemini Decision 1 is priced at $0.10 per 1M input tokens and $0 for output tokens, with an API no-cost tier you can use in Google AI Studio for prototyping. Your shared input is billed once per request no matter how many questions you evaluate (each question adds only its own instruction and criteria tokens). There are no output-token charges, variable thinking-token bills, or separate audio transcription and OCR costs. You can start building today by grabbing an API key in Google AI Studio , trying our Doorstep Parcels , Speed Sketch , and Find the Zoo Keeper demo apps, and following the Python, JavaScript, and REST guides in the Decisions API documentation . Ecosystem integrations are rolling out across OpenRouter , LangChain , Vercel , LiteLLM , Pydantic AI , Pipecat , LiveKit , and OpenCode alongside the google-genai SDKs, with support coming soon to Gemini in Google Cloud. title: A false smoke alarm almost drowned Jane Street's only NYC datacenter
body_text: How a false smoke alarm almost drowned Jane Streetâs only NYC datacenter | Michael Bacarella Michael Bacarella _ Posts of varying effort on technology, cybersecurity, transhumanism, rationalism, self-improvement, DIY, and other stereotypical technologist stuff. How a false smoke alarm almost drowned Jane Street's only NYC datacenter jane street war stories datacenter Published on 10 Nov 2026 by mbacarella A war story from Jane Street's systems team: a false smoke alarm, a datacenter with no cooling, and a sprint to pull every power cord before the sprinklers went off AI disclosure: this story was written entirely by human hands, with AI doing proof-reading and light edits. Some tasteful imperfections kept to heighten Wabi-Sabi effect. Everyoneâs heard of how awesome Jane Street is. Fewer people have heard about the times something stupid nearly put it out of business and it was saved by grit and dumb luck. I was on the systems team for some of those. Jane Street didnât do titles, and we on the systems team werenât above getting our hands dirty. You could think of us as the firmâs blue-collar OCaml programmers: when something broke, we were the ones running through the corridors to fix it. Call this story a Star Trek: Lower Decks view of Jane Street. For the longest time Jane Street insisted on having its machine room close to its trading floor. When it was 10 people it was cute. When it was 150 people it was starting to feelâ¦ odd. Part of the reason for this was intellectual property concern: they didnât want to risk having their servers stolen by spies who would learn their precious trading strategies. Another reason was technology risk: they wanted to make sure out-of-control automated trading systems could always be shut down by running across the hall and pulling power cables. Yes, tools existed to mitigate both of these fears. But Jane Street moved irritatingly slowly on this stuff, and they still wanted the last-resort option of yanking power cords. Their risk culture didnât exclusively come from reading heady thinkpieces. A lot of it was instilled by a partner whoâd served on a nuclear submarine, and it showed, mostly in a good way! On a sub, you donât trust the automation unless thereâs a big red-painted, mechanically connected lever you can pull to turn it off. As the company grew this humble machine room was built out into a respectably sizable datacenter, complete with an online UPS, Computer Room Air Conditioner (CRAC) units, refrigerator-sized network switches, a subterranean diesel backup generator and about 10 rows of server cabinets, 10 cabinets deep. Oh, and it was all crammed into the middle of a skyscraper called 1 New York Plaza , which was otherwise just a normal office building. When I first landed my job at Jane Street I was commuting to the southern tip of Manhattan all of the way from Queens, an hour or more each way. Iâd gone to a magnet high school in the city, so Iâd been doing commutes like that since I was a teenager, and I was tired of it. Now that I was making big Wall Street money I decided Iâd get an apartment. A real estate agent kept trying to show me what they called âpanty droppersâ, but I was only interested in one thing: proximity to the office. I ended up in a 200 square foot studio that was a 9 minute commute on foot from my apartment door to my desk on the trading floor. I would weirdly boast about it to the rest of the systems team, but it also meant everyone at the office knew I was a stoneâs throw away in case there was an emergency. And that day came soon enough. One evening after work, just as I was about to climb into the elevator at my apartment building, my phone rang. It was our Hong Kong office, and when Hong Kong had a New York problem, mine was (now) the number they called. The smoke alarm in our NYC datacenter had gone off. We had contractors working on a prep room next to the datacenter. While cutting into stuff, some dust was kicked up and it set off the smoke alarm. This is bad, but not for the reason you might think. Office buildings have sprinklers in them for fire suppression. You may have seen it go off in movies where someone just holds a lit cigarette up to the sprinkler on the ceiling and it floods the entire room. In reality theyâre not quite that dumb, but itâs close. Firstly, the sprinklers over a machine room like ours usually arenât kept full of water all of the time. This saves you from having to deal with any leaks that might develop overhead over the years. Secondly, the sprinkler heads donât have smoke sensors. Instead, a different system detects the smoke, and thatâs when the pipes fill with pressurized water, but they donât spray yet. What triggers the spray is heat: each sprinkler head has its own heat-sensitive plug, which opens once the air around it becomes hot enough. The logic is that the smoke alarm must be real, whatever fire triggered it hasnât been brought under control since itâs gotten very hot, and the sprinklers should douse it with water. Of course, the ceiling of our datacenter was full of sprinklers set up exactly this way. Weâre still fine because even though contractors might have set the smoke detector off by kicking up dust, thereâs no actual fire producing heat, so the sprinklers wouldnât spray, right? Well, no. One final piece of this contraption is that if the smoke alarm detects smoke, it would be absolutely terrible to keep circulating air through the room since that would help feed any fires, so the smoke alarm is wired to shut down the CRAC units(!) Can you see the problem now? Rooms full of computer racks have high cooling demands. If you shut down the cooling, the temperature starts climbing. If you have a bunch of sprinklers that have just become pressurized because of a smoke alarm, you now have a serious, potentially business-ending problem on your hands. And so my mission was made clear: as fast as I possibly could, get back to Jane Street, get into the machine room, and pull the power cord on every device in that room before the temperature climbed past 150 F and the sprinklers destroyed everything. I ran down the (ironically named) Water Street in the Financial District faster than probably anyone has ever run down it, mashed the elevator button in the lobby of 1 NYP, waited very impatiently for the elevator to climb the 33 floors, slammed my keycard against the reader, booked through the main office door, took a hard right turn to the machine room door, slammed my keycard against that, stepped into what felt like a sauna and went row by row, cabinet by cabinet, yanking power cables out with both hands. Then I watched the temperature monitor. 141 F. 142. 143. 143.5. 143.6. Finally it stopped. A quiet Iâd never heard before set in on the machine room. The machine room had been kept across the hall so that someone could always run in and pull the power cords. I doubt anyone had pictured doing it to save the servers from the goddamn sprinklers. Since the major NYC markets were closed for the day, the downtime from this fiasco was minimal, and we were up and running the next morning. There were a couple of meetings after that. You might picture Gordon Gekko coldly deciding whose career was over, but meetings at Jane Street were never like that. They were matter-of-fact, level-headed and honestly kind of fun, closer to engineering students in a college dorm arguing over what went wrong. The outcome of all that level-headed discussion: the sprinklers would stay, we would tighten up procedures and surveillance, and we would continue hosting servers in our office building right next to our trading floor. That is, until Hurricane Sandy smacked us upside the head, but thatâs a story for another day. As for me, when the next morning came around I knew what had to be done. Our Hong Kong team had only caught the problem by luck: someone happened to see on a display that server after server was popping up a climbing temperature condition. No one server was configured to alert just because it was a little hot, since that happens from time to time. But an across the board increase in temperature on many servers means thereâs a generalized cooling failure. What we needed was a system monitor built for this exact purpose, one we could trust to be ultimately, unfailingly reliable at the task of asking each Linux server for its temperature and computing a simple mean. Bash wouldnât cut it for this. Nor would Perl. No, a job of this magnitude called for the most reliable and type-safe programming language imaginable. So I fired up emacs and wrote it in good old OCaml: every minute, ask every server in each location directly for the temperature from its onboard sensors, take the average, and if itâs elevated, blast an alert out to everyone on the systems team to check for datacenter overheat. Yes, we could have also alerted if the CRAC units shut down or if a dedicated temperature sensor in the room was high, but the telemetry for this stuff was nowhere near as reliable, and unknown unknowns can still ruin you, so the most durable thing sometimes really is to ask your fleet of Linux boxes for their temperature and freak out if the average is just a little too high. Our team didnât interact much with the partner with the nuclear sub experience, but Iâd like to think he would have approved. Got a better tale of woe? Let me know at X , Bluesky , Hacker News or Lobsters . related posts Why Google didn't use Git OCaml Compiler Implemented in C++: It's Not Just FasterâIt Also Increases Trust Will superintelligent AGI even care about OCaml? all tags agi ai android arms race brew c++ campervan chilling effects china cowculator ctypes culturewar datacenter deepseek dune endofc gce git google hippies jane street laptop linux macbook mirage monorepo ocaml parler professionals scott secondbrain shell solar spyware ssc tls transhumanism unikernel vanlife veganism war stories zettelkasten zsh theme inspired by bitbrain

title: 93% of paint splatters are valid Perl programs (2019)
body_text: 93% of Paint Splatters are Valid Perl Programs | Colin McMillen Colin McMillen 93% of Paint Splatters are Valid Perl Programs Posted 2019-04-01. TLDR: read the paper and view the gallery of pretty Perl programs . In this paper, we aim to answer a long-standing open problem in the programming languages community: is it possible to smear paint on the wall without creating valid Perl? We answer this question in the affirmative: it is possible to smear paint on the wall without creating a valid Perl program. We employ an empirical approach, using optical character recognition (OCR) software, which finds that merely 93% of paint splatters parse as valid Perl. We analyze the properties of paint-splatter Perl programs, and present seven examples of paint splatters which are not valid Perl programs. Accepted for publication at SIGBOVIK 2019, held April 1st 2019 in Pittsburgh. Winner of a Unwitting Participation Ribbon, “an unwelcome brand weâve affixed to each paper determined after careful scrutiny to have included a genuine artifact, thereby furthering the admirable causes of open science and fruitful procrastination.” Read it on Google Docs or download a PDF . Or grab the entire SIGBOVIK 2019 proceedings ; I’m on page 174. Supplementary Materials Here’s all the paint splatters on a single page, along with the valid Perl source code corresponding to each. “Not valid” is written in red for those images which did not parse as valid Perl programs. If different OCR settings recognized multiple valid Perl programs, I chose the one that seemed the most “interesting”, according to my own aesthetic sense. Here’s a tarball of 100 paint-splatter images that were used as the main dataset for this paper. (source code not available yet because i am bad at GitHub) Errata There are a few paint splatter Perl programs that I didn’t recognize as “interesting” until after the SIGBOVIK submission deadline. For example, this splatter is recognized by OCR as the string lerzfijglpFiji-j , which evaluates to the number 0 in Perl: The image below is recognized as the string -*? , which also evaluates to the number 0 in Perl: Another surprising program is shown below; OCR recognizes this image as the string ;i;c;;#\\?z{;?;;fn':.; , which evaluates to the string c in Perl: Finally, this image is recognized as the string ;E,'__' , which evaluates to the string E__ in Perl: © 2023 Colin McMillen . My AI agents found an unmapped Maya site?
body_text: My AI Agents (Re)discovered a Maya Site in 72 Hours ~ latest My AI Agents (Re)discovered a Maya Site in 72 Hours 5 min read (Last edit: 11 Nov) Update (11 November): it turns out the site had already been mapped in Estrada-Belli et al. 2025 . The agents missed it while going through the literature, so they rediscovered it rather than discovered it (it just wasn't in the register of Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History, INAH, yet). Still work to do then! The rest of the story still holds. By analyzing NASA lidar data, my AI agents found a Maya site in Mexico that wasn't in the official register. (It turned out archaeologists had mapped it already, more on that at the end.) It took less than 72 hours to go from a random thought while traveling to an official reply from the Mexican government. This is by far the best time ever to be alive. Lidar: bare ground, 2013 Satellite image today Drag the slider. The same hilltop today from a satellite (just trees) and in lidar (no trees). Colours show height. Satellite © Esri, Maxar, Earthstar Geographics. Disclaimer: I'm not an archaeologist. I'm going to tell this story as a diary, because the timeline is probably the best part. 18 October I was traveling in Peru, Gemini-ing about the history of the place, when I learned about Hiram Bingham , the American explorer who "discovered" Machu Picchu in 1911. "What luck!" I thought. He was actually looking for a different city, Vilcabamba , the last refuge of the Incas, when a local farmer in the valley below guided him to the ruins. "Imagine if Bingham had our tools," I thought. "What would he do?" Left: Bingham at his tent, 1912. Right: Machu Picchu, photographed by Bingham the same year. Public domain, Wikimedia Commons ( left , right ). I brainstormed a bit with a few agents (Gemini, ChatGPT, Claude and Grok), and they all said lidar . From above, a ruin in the jungle is just a bunch of trees (like Machu Picchu before it was cleared), so satellite photos don't help much. Lidar, instead, fires laser pulses through the gaps in the canopy and maps the ground underneath. [1] So the agents went looking for lidar data. Peru isn't well covered, and hiring a company to do a survey meant permits, costs and bureaucracy, so I gave up on that. Then I thought: why not the Maya ? Their region is much better covered by public lidar. That night, I asked the agents to analyze it and went to bed. 19 October I woke up and checked the agents' reports. 'DAMN!' They had found lots of villages and other regular shapes that looked like structures or houses. A few of the sites the agents flagged overnight. Keep an eye on the bottom-left one. So how did they do it? They turned the lidar strips (about 1,200 km² of jungle) into images, and 48 agents went through them one by one like very patient archaeologists, looking for pyramids, platforms, and plazas while filtering out natural hills, sinkholes, and roads. There was no special model or classifier involved: the agents literally looked at the pictures, following a precise guide. Me: That's awesome! Please check which of these villages haven't been discovered yet. Search both the literature and the archives. …a few hours later… Agent: One major village doesn't seem to have been registered. This is the hilltop from the top of this post. It sits on the edge of a cliff, under the jungle, and it has straight edges and sharp corners. Nature doesn't really do straight lines. Zooming in, there's a levelled plaza, an oval pyramid at least 8–12 m tall, a raised courtyard attached to it and a flat-bottomed hollow that might have been a water reservoir. The hilltop with the trees removed (top), and a zoom into its civic centre (bottom). And this is what it looks like in 3D. The site in 3D, from the lidar. Heights exaggerated ~1.5×. Me: OK, what should I do? Agent: You should contact INAH (Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History), write a report on your discovery, and check whether the site is in their register. Sometimes they have unpublished results. Me: OK, how do I contact INAH? How does the reporting process work? Agent: …instructions for the report… + email addresses Me: OK, please do the report. And I went to bed. 20 October I iterated on the report a bit, since a few things were off, and translated it into Spanish to improve the chances of getting a reply (at least, that's what Claude suggested). I don't speak Spanish, so I had to trust the agents on that one. The agents also checked the raw point cloud, to make sure the shapes were really on the ground and not created by the trees. Green dots are leaves, brown dots are the ground. Two slices through the raw lidar points. Under 10–17 m of forest, the ground (brown) traces the plaza, the pyramid and the courtyard. Then I sent the report to INAH. The top of my letter to INAH. The exact coordinates went in a confidential annex, not shown here. 21 October INAH replied: they checked their records and found no registered archaeological site at that location . INAH's reply. The highlighted part: "…no registered archaeological site was identified at the location given in your report." At that point I thought nobody had put it on a map before. I was wrong (see below). So what was it? This part is speculation, from a long chat with the agents. It looks like a small Maya civic centre from the Classic period (roughly AD 250–900), basically the "downtown" of a local elite. The plaza is where people gathered, for ceremonies and maybe even a market. The pyramid was probably a temple, and the raised courtyard next to it might have been where the local ruler lived. The hollow could have been an aguada , a rainwater reservoir: Maya towns needed them to get through the dry season. Or it's just a hole. The three platforms around were probably houses. I asked Gemini to imagine how it looked back then: How it might have looked around AD 700. Generated with Gemini from the lidar layout For similar studies, have a look at how NASA's G-LiHT instrument works ( Cook et al. 2013 ) and how lidar collected for environmental research can be reused for archaeology ( Golden et al. 2016 ). In 2024, archaeologists found a whole Maya city in Mexico this way ( Auld-Thomas et al. 2024 ), others mapped settlements across the Maya lowlands, including this very site ( Estrada-Belli et al. 2025 ), and another study found what may have been ancient Maya marketplaces ( Šprajc 2026 ). What's next The site is now in the hands of the people who should have it: Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) and the archaeologists who mapped it first. If anything comes out of it, I'll post an update. What I've learned You can just do things. I'm not an archaeologist, so I didn't know this was supposed to be hard. I just picked an old problem, tried the most obvious thing and threw some compute at it. Being a naive outsider might be a superpower now. And it turned out professional archaeologists had already mapped the same site. I guess that's a good sign: an outsider with agents ended up in a similar place to the experts. And I don't think this is really about archaeology. So far, most agentic AI stories have been about coding, math and physics, but it's much more general than that, and I hope this small example makes it a bit more obvious. We are on the brink of a revolution in all the sciences, and the only bottlenecks left will be curiosity and imagination (and compute). At this point, we should probably lidar the whole planet and let the agents discover the rest. If you don't know how lidar works, copy and paste this prompt into your favorite AI tool: "Build an HTML page that explains how lidar works, with beautiful visualizations." ↩ @pietromiotti

title: Can a Linear Program Do Weight-Space Programming?
body_text: Can a Linear Program Do Weight-Space Programming? nathan.rs Writing X Github LinkedIn ☾ Can a Linear Program Do Weight-Space Programming? Nathan Barry November 9, 2026 Introduction Thinking loops How Astra fixed the loops Choosing v is a linear program Results A steering vector does the same job Limitations and what’s next Citation Last week, MIT CSAIL published Sparks of Weight-Space Programming . Given the raw weights of a small network, GPT-6 Astra could tell which game it had been trained to play. Given only a game’s rules, it could write the weights of a small network from scratch and beat networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. No gradients, no training loop, just reasoning about what the weights compute. They coined this weight-space programming . In another experiment, they asked Astra to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math by editing its weights. Astra changed only 0.016% of the weights, and MATH-500 accuracy jumped from 7.9% to 48.1%. 1 Looking at Astra’s edit, I realized most of its search was solving a linear program by trial and error. It spent about 8 hours and 28 forward passes choosing which weights to change and by how much. A couple of LP solves, about a minute each, do the same job with 8× fewer changed weights. In this post I’ll walk through the edit, why it’s an LP, and what that says about the fix itself. Thinking loops # Small reasoning models have a common failure: they get stuck in thinking loops , repeating the same few lines over and over instead of finishing their reasoning. Qwen3.5-0.8B is especially prone to it, and its model card says so. On MATH-500, 93% of the base model’s answers ran into the 32,768-token limit without ever reaching an answer. The edit fixes the loops, so it helps anywhere the model loops. That includes instruction following: IFEval went from 21% to 62%. Qwen3.5-0.8B MATH-500 GSM8K IFEval Hit token limit Base 7.9 13.8 21.0 93.0% Astra’s edit 48.1 67.1 62.3 33.1% On Gemma 3 270M, which rarely loops, Astra couldn’t meaningfully improve its math ability. As the authors put it, editing the weights could remove an obstacle hiding an ability, but couldn’t add one the model lacked. How Astra fixed the loops # Transformers use residual connections: each layer’s output is added to its input rather than replacing it. Follow one token through the network and you get a single vector that every layer adds to, called the residual stream (1,024-dimensional in this model). When the model is looping, the residual stream shifts in a consistent direction. Astra’s fix was to edit two layers so that what they add points the opposite way. Finding the loop direction # Astra wrote four pairs of short texts, each a piece of productive reasoning and a looping version of the same reasoning. It ran all eight through the model and recorded each token’s residual stream vector at one layer. Averaging over the looping texts gives one vector, and averaging over the productive texts gives another. Their difference, normalized, is the loop direction $u$: the way the residual stream moves when the model loops. Editing the weights # Each MLP ends with a matrix $W$ (called down_proj ). At every token, it turns the MLP’s 3,584-dimensional hidden activation $h$ into a 1,024-dimensional output $Wh$, which gets added to the residual stream $x$: $$x \leftarrow x + Wh, \qquad Wh = \sum_j h_j \, w_j$$ So the MLP’s output is always a weighted sum of the same 3,584 vectors, the columns $w_j$ of $W$. $W$ fixes what those vectors are; the activations $h_j$ decide how much of each one gets added at each token. Each column points partly along $u$. That amount, $u^\top w_j$, is how much column $j$ pushes the model toward looping whenever $h_j$ is active. Astra’s edit subtracts a multiple $\alpha$ of it: $$w_j \to w_j - \alpha \, (u^\top w_j) \, u$$ At $\alpha = 1$ the component along $u$ is gone, so the column no longer pushes toward looping. Doing this to every column in layers 15 and 19 took accuracy from 9% to 33% on GSM8K and MATH training problems. At $\alpha = 6$ the component is flipped: a column that wrote $+a$ along $u$ now writes $-5a$, and pushes the model away from looping whenever it’s used. Every edited column changes by a multiple of the same vector $u$. So the whole edit is one direction $u$ plus one number per column, $v_j = -\alpha\,(u^\top w_j)$, which is zero for columns left alone. That’s a rank-1 change: $$\Delta W = u\,v^\top$$ At each token, it adds $(v \cdot h_t)\,u$ to the residual stream: some amount of $u$, set by how active the edited columns are. No other direction changes. That leaves $v$ to choose: which columns to edit, and how large $\alpha$ should be. Astra worked it out by trial and error, testing each edit on a fresh batch of those training problems: Edit on layers 15 and 19 Accuracy Base model ~9% Every column, α = 1 33% Every column, α = 2 43% Every column, α = 3 48% Random direction (control) 12.5% Top 64 columns, α = 6 55% Pushing harder than $\alpha = 1$ helped more, and a random direction did nothing. The final edit used $\alpha = 6$ on only the 64 columns per layer that wrote the most $u$ on looping text. Where the time went # The paper released Astra’s full logs: every tool call, every forward pass, every note it wrote to itself. Astra had a Python kernel with the weights loaded and a budget of 50 forward passes, each a batched run of the model on training problems or texts of its choosing. The edit was frozen after about 10 hours, and the last 17 passes re-tested it without changing anything. 2 Of those 10 hours, finding $u$ took 15 minutes. Finding $v$ took about 8 hours. Choosing v is a linear program # Astra was searching for a $v$ that strongly pushes looping tokens away from $u$ while barely touching productive ones. Since the push at token $t$ is $v \cdot h_t$, linear in $v$, both requirements are linear inequalities. I labeled tokens from the base model’s own traces: looping tokens ($R$), deep inside a loop, and productive tokens ($P$), well before any loop starts, 3 and recorded their activations $h_t$ at layers 15 and 19. Each one becomes a constraint, and the LP picks the $v$ with the smallest L1 norm $\sum_j |v_j|$: $$ \begin{aligned} \min_v \quad & \sum_j |v_j| \\ \text{s.t.} \quad & v \cdot h_t \le -\delta && t \in R \quad \text{(at least } \delta \text{ away from } u\text{)} \\ & |v \cdot h_t| \le \varepsilon && t \in P \quad \text{(at most } \varepsilon\text{)} \end{aligned} $$ In practice no $v$ satisfies every constraint, so each one gets a penalized slack variable. Minimizing L1 tends to make $v$ sparse. The L1 ball is a diamond, and when you grow it until it touches the feasible region, it usually touches at a corner, where most coordinates are exactly zero. So the LP picks the columns as well as the amounts. To get exactly 8 columns per layer, I kept the 8 with the largest effect and solved again with the rest fixed at zero. 4 That replaces Astra’s 8-hour search, including its choice of columns and $\alpha$, with a couple of LP solves. An off-the-shelf solver (HiGHS) took over 20 minutes each on these constraints, so I wrote a GPU solver (PDHG, the algorithm behind PDLP) that gets within 0.2% of its optimum in about a minute. 5 Results # I tested two LP edits. Both use Astra’s layers. One uses Astra’s direction $u$. The other uses a heuristic direction : label tokens in the model’s own traces as looping or productive with a simple repetition detector, then take the difference of their average residual streams. It’s the same recipe Astra used, minus the hand-written texts, so no LLM is involved. I tuned the LP’s settings on a separate 128-problem dev set; everything in the chart and table is on data never used for fitting or tuning. Changed weights GSM8K test MATH-500 IFEval Base model 0 14.1 7.0 22.9 Astra’s edit 130,188 68.2 50.9 61.9 LP, Astra’s direction 16,291 69.6 51.7 59.7 LP, heuristic direction 16,271 65.4 47.8 60.4 With Astra’s direction, the LP matches Astra’s edit on every benchmark, within noise, while changing 8× fewer weights. With the heuristic direction, it gets about 93% of the way there. A few other things showed up: The search mattered, and the LP replaces it. On the dev set, reusing Astra’s recipe (top 64 columns, $\alpha = 6$) on the heuristic direction without searching again scores 44.5. The LP scores 54.7. Different columns, same fix. The LP’s 8 columns share only 3 (layer 15) and 1 (layer 19) with Astra’s 64. Many sparse solutions work; what matters is the total push along $u.$ A random direction does nothing. On the dev set, a random $u$ of the same size scores 10.2, against 10.9 for the base model. A steering vector does the same job # An edit can only tell a looping token apart from a productive one through its activations, and a loop isn’t recognizable from them until it’s well under way. 6 So on the dev set, asking the LP to push only on loop-like tokens did no better than pushing on every token. The LP’s 8 columns in layer 15 are active on 89% of tokens, and the push they add barely varies from token to token, so the edit is close to a constant push along $u$. A constant push doesn’t need a weight edit. It can be added directly as a steering vector , a fixed vector added to the residual stream at every token. The table below adds the LP edit’s average push along $u$ to the unedited model at layers 15 and 19, at three strengths: Steering strength (× the LP edit’s average push) Dev set MATH-500 0.5× 51.6 1× 57.8 50.8 2× 31.2 For comparison, on the same runs: the LP edit scores 62.5 on the dev set and 53.2 on MATH-500, Astra’s edit 59.4 and 50.0, the base model 10.9 and 7.0. MATH-500 here is one sample per problem. At 1×, the steering vector recovers essentially the whole fix. The window is narrow: at 0.5× the loops come back, and at 2× they stop but the reasoning falls apart. The only difference is delivery. The LP edit is an ordinary checkpoint; the steering vector needs extra code at inference time. Limitations and what’s next # This is one model. The LP still relies on Astra for the layers, and the best results use Astra’s direction too. The heuristic direction gets most of the way without an LLM, but not all of it. Loops also turned out to be fixable with a constant push, so the LP’s per-token constraints didn’t end up mattering much. A behavior that should change some tokens and leave others alone would be a better test of them. Choosing the layers without an agent is the other open piece. Lastly, this was only tested on removing loops. Many other behaviors, like refusal or sycophancy, can be steered by adding or removing a single direction in the residual stream. 7 If a behavior can be steered with one direction, choosing how to build it into the weights should be the same LP, but that still needs testing. Code, edits, and the full write-up are on GitHub . Citation # Please cite this work as: Barry, Nathan. "Can a Linear Program Do Weight-Space Programming?" nathan.rs (Nov 2026). https://nathan.rs/posts/weight-space-lp. Or use the BibTex citation: @article{barry2026wslp, title = "Can a Linear Program Do Weight-Space Programming?", author = "Barry, Nathan", journal = "nathan.rs", year = "2026", month = "Nov", url = "https://nathan.rs/posts/weight-space-lp" } Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang and Omar Khattab, Sparks of Weight-Space Programming , MIT CSAIL, 2026. The logs are released under CC BY 4.0, and everything about Astra’s run in this post comes from them.  ↩︎ Astra’s full run took 158 turns and 20.3 hours, 4.7 of them an outage. 19 forward passes failed and weren’t counted against its budget. The full breakdown is in the write-up .  ↩︎ A token counts as repeated if the 16 tokens ending at it already appeared earlier in the answer. A loop starts at the first point after which at least 80% of the remaining tokens are repeats. Looping tokens are repeats at least 64 tokens into a loop. Productive tokens come at least 256 tokens before it, or anywhere in an answer that finished.  ↩︎ Each column is ranked by $|v_j|$ times the standard deviation of $h_j$, roughly how much it adds along $u$ at a typical token.  ↩︎ PDHG (primal-dual hybrid gradient) only needs matrix-vector products, so all the token constraints fit on the GPU at once, and it returns an exactly sparse $v$.  ↩︎ A linear probe on layer 15’s activations can tell looping tokens from productive ones once a loop is under way (AUC 0.93), but much less well at the point where it starts (0.73).  ↩︎ Or whether you can make it sound like her .  ↩︎ Last modified: November 9, 2026 nathan.rs - © 2025 Nathan Barry

Goldilockâs glitch End results Framebuffer unlock Compute unlock PCIe generation NVLink Future directions References Footnotes Summary Iâve discovered a voltage fault injection vulnerability on the GA100 die, allowing an operator to blow arbitrary fuses. Utilizing this vulnerability, Iâve converted my CMP 170HX 8GB card into what is effectively an A100-80G! Further, my unlocked cards actually perform ~1.2x faster than a retail A100 by having all functional SMs enabled (~120-126, die-lottery dependent), rather than the yield-safe 108 SMs NVIDIA chose for all production A100 cards. Finally, CMP-disabled features like NVLink, PCIe Gen4, NVJPG, NVDEC, MIG are all unlockable with this approach, though I havenât specifically tested NVJPG/NVDEC/MIG. Hereâs how my âA100-80Gâ appears and functions.
