body_text: Claude Whiteboards, Claude Sheets, and Claude Data | Claude by Anthropic Skip to main content Product Products Claude Claude Code Claude Cowork Claude Duet Claude Platform Claude Tag Specialized Claude Security Claude Science Capabilities Artifacts Design Connectors Plugins Skills Extensions Claude in Chrome Claude for Google Workspace Claude for Microsoft 365 Models Mythos (including Fable) Opus Sonnet Haiku Import to Claude Download apps Login (opens in new tab) Developers Build with Claude Code Claude Platform Managed Agents For developers Claude Academy Community Developer blog Developer docs Console Enterprise Enterprise Overview Claude Code for Enterprise Claude Platform Use Cases AI Agents Coding Commerce Departments Customer support Cybersecurity Legal Sales Industries Financial advisors Financial services Government Healthcare Higher education K-12 teachers Life sciences Nonprofits Browse marketplace Customers Contact sales Resources Insights Resources Articles Webinars Customer stories Marketplace Anthropic news Learn Claude Academy Courses Tutorials Use cases Connect Events Community Pricing Overview API Login Contact sales Try Claude Claude Resources Home Articles Guides Webinars Videos Home Articles Guides Webinars Videos Search Introducing Claude Whiteboards, Claude Sheets, and Claude Data Now you can brainstorm on whiteboards, build sheets, and share data directly in Claude. Category Product updates Product Claude apps Date November 10, 2026 Reading time 6 min Share Copy link Contents Claude Whiteboards Claude Sheets Claude Data Work in your other tools, too Getting started Today we’re launching Claude Whiteboards and Claude Sheets in beta, and Claude Dashboards (opens in new tab) becomes generally available as Claude Data. Whiteboards is a shared board where your team brainstorms with Claude, Sheets is a spreadsheet Claude builds and edits with you, and Claude Data adds data stories, certified queries, and live sharing. These are available on all paid plans. Working with Claude on a project often meant moving the output over to another tool or program, where Claude didn’t have live access to follow progress and changes. Now, your documents, boards, sheets, and dashboards can stay in Claude, with access for your team to continue editing together. When ready, you can bring the outputs directly into tools from our partners and continue working there. Claude Whiteboards Many people use Claude as a thought partner, but brainstorming with it has typically meant copy-pasting the results elsewhere so you can then start brainstorming or collaborating with your coworkers. Now, you can talk through a messy plan out loud with Claude, and Claude can turn it into a board with a timeline with owners and dates, so you and your team can collaborate in real time. In a retro meeting, for example, everyone can add their notes, and Claude can group them by theme and draft the action items for each person. You can focus on any part of the board by dragging a box around it and asking Claude questions. When you’re done brainstorming, Claude can turn the board into a doc or deck, or bring it into tools like Lucid, Miro, or Vani by Zoho, where you can continue working on it with your team. Claude Sheets Claude can now generate spreadsheets with tabs, formulas, formatting, and drop-downs, often from just a prompt like asking for a campaign tracker or a hiring budget. It can edit in the cells, outlining each new edit so you can track changes. You can share sheets with your team, so you and Claude can work on them together. For now, sheets have simple spreadsheet functionality, but we are working on adding more. When you need the full functionality of Excel, you can export your file to .xlsx or CSV, or use Claude for Excel (opens in new tab) . You can also continue working in partner tools including Airtable, Asana, monday.com, and Smartsheet. Claude Data Claude Dashboards (opens in new tab) launched in beta in October, enabling teams to ask quick questions of their company’s data in tools like Amazon Redshift, BigQuery, and ClickHouse. Starting today, it’s generally available as Claude Data. We changed the name because the way companies use their data is broader than dashboards, and the product now covers how they work more broadly. Certified queries and live sharing are in beta. Here are some ways teams can use Claude Data: Create certified definitions of metrics. Your data team can certify the queries everyone should use, so you don’t end up building or working on dashboards with conflicting data. Charts built on these metrics carry a "certified" badge showing they’re certified. Craft stories from data. You can work with Claude in Claude Data to draft data stories or narrated videos from your metrics, for you to review before sharing. Share current numbers with everyone. With live sharing, your colleagues can see up-to-date numbers when they open a shared dashboard, even if they don’t have access to the connectors that keep that data current. Viewers see the results of the queries you’ve approved, and can’t run others with your access. Match your look-and-feel. Design systems are now supported in Claude Data. Get faster loading with caching. Previously, every dashboard would reload on every load. Now, dashboards support caching, and refresh cadences can be set on a per-dashboard basis. Track changes over time. Claude Data now has tracked changes, so you can see who has made edits and roll back to a specific version if needed. Our partners for Claude Data include Amplitude, Mixpanel, Omni, PostHog, and Sigma. Work in your other tools, too Starting today, interactive connectors (opens in new tab) can open as full apps beside your conversation or in full screen, so you can work in tools like Adobe, Atlassian, Box, and Notion yourself, or ask Claude to make changes with you. Getting started Claude Whiteboards, Sheets, and Data work on web, desktop, and mobile. Claude Data needs a data connector, such as a warehouse or CRM. For admins: On Team plans, all three are on by default. On Enterprise plans, Claude Whiteboards and Sheets are off by default, and Claude Data turns on by default on November 19, 2026. You can change these anytime in Organization settings > Artifacts. Related articles Explore more product news and best practices for teams building with Claude. title: .name Grandfathered
body_text: Neil Fraser: News: .name Grandfathered Neil's News   2026   .name Grandfathered   Request for Reconsideration   .name Termination   Blockly AGC   2025   2024   2023   2022   2021   2020   2019   2018   2017   2016   2015   2014   2013   2012   2011   2010   2009   2008   2007   2006   2005   2004   2003   2002 .name Grandfathered 10 November 2026 We won! After a long and expensive battle, news just dropped that Verisign is retracting its plan to terminate 22,000 domain names and email redirects. Although they will be closing new registrations for 3rd-level .name domains, all existing domains (including this website) and email redirects will remain indefinitely. This was a team effort. It was inspiring how many talented people joined this fight. From Doytchin who kicked everything off, to Jim who flew to Bali to make the case to ICANN in person, to Patrik, Troy, Huyen, Keith, Judy, Erik, and Ryan who wrote formal reconsideration requests, to my lawyers Jan, Flip and Diégo who threw the book at ICANN, to Beverly, Stefan, Vaughan, Irv, Pablo, Larry, Lionel, Daniel, Ori, Markus, Kirk, Ed, Jeremy, Stephan, Matija, Jan, Simon, Mark, and Evan who filed letters of support. I'd also like to sincerely thank selected individuals within ICANN who had the courage to stand up against the bureaucracy. Without exception, everyone I spoke with was a remarkable person. < Previous | Next >   Legal yada yada: My views do not necessarily represent those of my employer or my goldfish. title: Protecting SSH Keys with macOS Secure Enclave
body_text: Protecting SSH Keys with macOS Secure Enclave (Native Approach) | Serge Gatezh Skip to main content $ Serge Gatezh Posts Projects Talks About Contact > Posts > Projects > Talks > About > Contact ~/posts/macos-secure-enclave-ssh-keys cat macos-secure-enclave-ssh-keys.md Protecting SSH Keys with macOS Secure Enclave (Native Approach) February 12, 2026 Updated November 11, 2026 by Serge Gatezh 8 min read 1534 words How to keep SSH keys in the macOS Secure Enclave, with Touch ID on every use and no third-party apps. Update, November 11, 2026: I’ve since switched to Secretive , which keeps keys in the Secure Enclave with a much better prompt. Part 2 is coming. I’ve also corrected one error, marked below. I’ve been paranoid about my SSH keys for a while now. They just sit there in ~/.ssh/ , protected by nothing but file permissions. Any malicious script that gets access to my filesystem could just copy them and get into all my servers. Also, there have been many stories out there online about fake interview assignments that asked to clone a repo and run it on your local machine. This is one of the reasons I switched completely to using devcontainers, but even that was not really enough for me (and it shouldn’t be enough for you or anybody else really). So I finally decided to do something about it. TL;DR I have decided to NOT go with the native macOS Secure Enclave approach (using only out-of-the-box tools) because it ended up plain ugly and I can’t live with that. However, it is a fully functional, working solution that I would definitely use otherwise. The Options After some research, I found several ways to protect SSH keys: Native macOS Secure Enclave â no third-party apps, built into the OS Secretive â third-party app that stores keys in Secure Enclave YubiKey â hardware security key with FIDO2 support 1Password / Bitwarden â store keys in an encrypted vault, use their SSH agent I already use 1Password, but I might switch to something else in the future. Bitwarden recently added SSH key support (even on the free tier!), but it’s still a software solution â the keys are encrypted at rest but decrypted in memory when used. What I really wanted was hardware-backed security. The private key should literally be impossible to extract, even if my Mac is fully compromised. That left me with YubiKey or Secure Enclave. I have a YubiKey 5C, but I wanted to try the native approach first â no extra hardware to carry around, no third-party apps to maintain. What is Secure Enclave SSH? Since macOS Sequoia (and Tahoe), macOS supports SSH keys backed by the Secure Enclave, a security subsystem on the Mac’s chip that is isolated from the main processor. The private key is created inside it and never leaves. When you SSH somewhere, your Mac asks the Secure Enclave to sign the authentication challenge. If you enable Touch ID, you have to approve each signing operation. The actual private key never exists in memory or on disk. The workflow is surprisingly similar to regular SSH keys: Aspect Regular SSH Key Secure Enclave Key Where private key lives ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 (a file) Secure Enclave What’s on disk Actual private key Just a reference (useless without this Mac) Setup on remote server Copy public key to authorized_keys Same Connecting Just works Touch ID prompt, then works Setting It Up Step 1: Create the Secure Enclave Key macOS provides the sc_auth command (Smart Card Authentication) to manage CryptoTokenKit identities. Despite the name, it works with Secure Enclave too. sc_auth create-ctk-identity -l "ssh-MacBook" -k p-256-ne -t bio Breaking this down: -l "ssh-MacBook" â a label for your reference (only visible locally) -k p-256-ne â NIST P-256 curve, n on- e xportable (the key can never leave Secure Enclave) -t bio â require bio metric (Touch ID) for every use You’ll be prompted for Touch ID to create the key. Problem 1: Touch ID Error When I first ran this command, I got a scary error: Error: Error Domain=NSOSStatusErrorDomain Code=-25293 "Failed to generate keypair" (errKCAuthFailed / errSecAuthFailed: / Authorization/Authentication failed.) UserInfo={..., NSUnderlyingError=... "Failed to get bio catacomb UUID for user 502." ...} Turns out my Touch ID enrollment got reset somehow. After re-enrolling my fingerprint in System Settings â Touch ID & Password , the command worked fine. You can verify the key was created: sc_auth list-ctk-identities Output: Key Type Public Key Hash Prot Label Common Name Valid To Valid p-256-ne A71277F0BC5825A7B3576D014F31282A866EF3BC bio ssh-MacBook ssh-MacBook 2027-01-26, 10:18 YES Step 2: Export the Key Handle Now we need to create a “key handle” file that SSH can use. This is NOT the private key â it’s just a reference that tells SSH “go ask the Secure Enclave to sign this.” ssh-keygen -w /usr/lib/ssh-keychain.dylib -K -N "" When prompted for PIN, just press Enter (it’s not used for biometric keys). Touch ID will pop up. This creates id_ecdsa_sk_rk and id_ecdsa_sk_rk.pub in your current directory. Move them to your SSH directory: mv id_ecdsa_sk_rk* ~/.ssh/ Step 3: Configure SSH to Use the Secure Enclave Provider Add this to your ~/.zshrc (or ~/.bashrc ): export SSH_SK_PROVIDER = /usr/lib/ssh-keychain.dylib Reload your shell: source ~/.zshrc Problem 2: Outdated Commands Everywhere If you search for “macOS Secure Enclave SSH” online, you’ll find a lot of guides telling you to run ssh-add -K . Don’t. It’s deprecated: WARNING: The -K and -A flags are deprecated and have been replaced by the --apple-use-keychain and --apple-load-keychain flags, respectively. And even the new flags don’t work for Secure Enclave keys â they’re for the traditional macOS Keychain, not CryptoTokenKit. The SSH_SK_PROVIDER environment variable is the correct approach. Step 4: Get Your Public Key cat ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa_sk_rk.pub Output: sk-ecdsa-sha2-nistp256@openssh.com AAAAInNrLWVjZHNhLXNoYTIt... ssh: That ssh: at the end is the comment. The key’s FIDO2 application ID is stored inside the key itself (the last field of the base64 part). ssh-keygen -K copies it into the comment, so the line shows it twice. You can replace the comment with anything when copying to authorized_keys ; the key stays the same: sk-ecdsa-sha2-nistp256@openssh.com AAAAInNrLWVjZHNhLXNoYTIt... macbook-secure-enclave Correction, November 11, 2026: An earlier version said the trailing ssh: was the FIDO2 application ID. It’s the comment; the application ID is stored inside the key. Thanks to computerfriend on Hacker News for pointing it out. Step 5: Copy to Your Server ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa_sk_rk.pub user@your-server Or manually paste the public key (with your comment) into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server. Step 6: Configure ~/.ssh/config Problem 3: SSH Doesn’t Find the Key After setting everything up, I tried to SSH… and it asked for my password. The verbose output ( ssh -vvv ) showed SSH was only trying my old RSA key: debug1: Offering public key: /Users/sergii/.ssh/id_rsa RSA SHA256:... The problem: SSH doesn’t automatically look for files named id_ecdsa_sk_rk . It only auto-discovers standard names like id_rsa , id_ed25519 , id_ecdsa . The fix is to explicitly add it to your ~/.ssh/config : Host * IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa_sk_rk IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_rsa IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 SSH tries identity files in order, so put the Secure Enclave key first if you want it to be the default. â ï¸ Note: If you’re using 1Password’s SSH agent ( IdentityAgent ), it might conflict with this setup. I had to comment it out while testing. Step 7: Test It ssh user@your-server You should get a Touch ID prompt, then connect. The Ugly Touch ID Prompt Touch ID prompt One thing I’m not thrilled about: the Touch ID dialog says “ctccardtoken needs to authenticate to continue” instead of something friendly like “SSH wants to use your key.” This is because the prompt comes from CryptoTokenKit â a low-level framework that Apple hasn’t polished for end-user SSH. If this bothers you, Secretive provides a much nicer UI while still using Secure Enclave under the hood. Why Touch ID for Everything? I initially thought about creating two keys â one with Touch ID for “important” servers, one without for convenience (like Git operations). But then I realized: without -t bio , malware could use my key silently. With -t bio , I always know when something is using my SSH key. A few extra taps per day is a small price for that visibility. So my recommendation if you’re planning to store your SSH keys this way: just use -t bio for everything. If it ever gets annoying, you can always create a second key later. The Catch: No Backups Secure Enclave keys are tied to your specific Mac. If your Mac dies, the keys die with it. That’s by design: the key can’t be exported, so it can’t be backed up either. Keep more than one key instead. Add your Secure Enclave key AND a backup key (from a YubiKey, or another Mac) to your servers’ authorized_keys . If one device is lost, you still have access via the other. Final Thoughts It seems to be a proper way to store your SSH keys securely, and it is way better than storing them on your hard drive. With the implementation above you get: â Private key literally cannot be stolen (it’s in hardware) â Every SSH operation requires Touch ID (I know when my key is used) â No third-party apps needed â Works with existing authorized_keys workflow However, I’ve been somewhat surprised by the ugliness of the UI. Not sure why Apple released such an unpolished thing. In each and every presentation they have a section on security (where their Apple logo becomes an Apple lock), so I was expecting an actual aesthetically appealing look for their security features. It is definitely not the case. My sense of beauty is not compatible with this ugliness, so I will be looking into other solutions to store my SSH keys in Secure Enclave such as Secretive . I also still need a backup option in case anything happens to my Mac. ls --related Docker Desktop Disk Full on macOS: The 1 TB Default and the Dev Containers Cache Sep 2026 MCP: What It Is and Why It Matters (by Addy Osmani) Jul 2025 ← Publishing Multi-Platform Docker Images to GitHub Container Registry Docker Desktop Disk Full on macOS: The 1 TB Default and the Dev Containers Cache → ./comments --list Please enable JavaScript to view the comments. title: AMD's Zen 6 Family: Feeding the Beast
body_text: AMD’s Zen 6 Family: Feeding the Beast - by George Cozma Chips and Cheese Subscribe Sign in AMD’s Zen 6 Family: Feeding the Beast George Cozma Nov 10, 2026 53 2 7 Share Hello you fine Internet folks, Today we’re looking at AMD’s next-generation Zen 6 CPU core family. We’ll explore the changes from Zen 5 and what the differences between Zen 6 and Zen 6c tell us about AMD’s approach to microarchitecture. Hope y’all enjoy! Overview From a bird's eye view, Zen 6 is the natural evolution of Zen5, with the expansion of many OoO structures and iterative improvements found throughout the core. Digging in deeper however tells a different story, with AMD heavily re-working several parts of the core, reminding me of the changes from Zen 1 to Zen 2. At a high level the changes AMD made to the integer schedules stand out, returning to a layout reminiscent of Zen 3 and Zen 4. Branch Prediction Zen 5 had the best direction predictor of any core we have measured and Zen 6 seemingly builds upon that same direction predictor. The biggest difference we do see is in what happens once the direction predictor gets overwhelmed. Both cores hit that wall in about the same place and past it, the predictor is left guessing at random data, so the time per branch mostly reflects how long the core takes to recover from a wrong guess. That plateau sits at roughly 3.5 to 4 ns of extra time per branch on Zen 5 and roughly 3 to 3.5 ns on Zen 6 so Zen 6 is paying less for each branch it gets wrong, which speaks to AMD reducing the latency of a branch mispredict compared to Zen 5. Zen 6 has also improved the ability of the core to do 2 branches per cycle with Zen 6 able to do 2 branches per cycle within the L1 instruction cache. When the footprint exceeds the L1i, then it falls to just a single branch per cycle for the rest of the BTB except for the 64B test which goes up to 4 cycles per branch for the L2 BTB. When comparing the BTB of Zen 6 to Zen 5, Zen 6 appears to have focused on improving the speed of the BTB compared to beefing up the capacity. The accuracy of Zen 6’s Branch Predictor Unit is very similar to Zen 5’s while also being faster which is a good thing considering that Zen 5 already had a very accurate Branch Predictor. Instruction Fetch Zen 6 carries forward the same dual decode cluster schema that Zen 5 introduced but, unlike Zen 5 where a single thread could only effectively use a single decode cluster, now with Zen 6 a single thread can use both decode clusters. Outside of the L1i, Zen 6 looks very similar to Zen 5’s behavior on the instruction side of things. Execution Engine The execution engine of Zen 6 is overall very similar to Zen 5, but there are some important differences to be mindful of. On the integer side, Zen 6 brings back Zen 4’s NOP pairing behavior, retiring up to 16 NOPs per cycle. Zen 6 also comes closer to theoretical peak throughput for simple integer instructions than Zen 5, sustaining 5.96 64-bit adds per cycle against Zen 5’s 5.25 with the same six ALUs. AMD has reduced the number of integer multiply units from three to two, with PDEP and PEXT throughput also falling from three instructions per cycle to two. According to AMD, Zen 5’s third integer multiply unit did not justify its area cost. On the vector side, the floating-point units are unchanged, with Zen 6 still handling two 512-bit FADDs, FMULs, or FMAs per cycle. The change is in VNNI, where Zen 6 doubles the number of units from two to four and our 512-bit VNNI test goes from 1.99 to 3.88 instructions per cycle, with Zen 6c matching it. VNNI instructions are useful for operations like calculating the inner loop of quantized inference as well as for video codecs using them for video filters as well. Moving over to the other notable change, Zen 5 could already perform four per cycle, but our test shows only two of them could be vector loads, regardless of if they were 256 or 512 bit loads. Zen 6 raises 256-bit loads to four per cycle on both cores while leaving 512-bit loads at two, so both widths now reach the same 128 bytes per cycle which matters because most shipped vector code still targets AVX1/2. The Out of Order Engine: Where Zen 6 and Zen 6c Split In the past the difference between the Classic cores and the Dense cores in terms of the architecture were, for all intents and purposes, functionally identical with the biggest changes being in the number of cores on a CCD and the amount of L3 cache per core. With the Zen 6 family, that has changed. Starting inside of the core, the changes occur after micro-op dispatch and seemingly end after the load queue. The main differences between Zen 6 and Zen 6c lie in the capacities of their out-of-order structures. Several of these structures are larger on Zen 6c, allowing it to keep more work in flight and absorb more latency than Zen 6. The reorder buffer grows from 576 to 640 entries, the integer register file from 288 to 352, the vector scheduler from 138 to 180, and the load queue from 280 to 330. The differences suggest that AMD is specializing the two designs. Zen 6 appears tuned for high frequency, while Zen 6c has more capacity to tolerate comparatively high memory latency. Zen 6 and Zen 6c use 12-core and 32-core CCDs, respectively, but both provide 4 MB of L3 cache per core. That gives the 12-core CCD 48 MB of L3 cache and the 32-core CCD 128 MB. L3 latency has increased from about 47 cycles on Zen 5 to 55 cycles on Zen 6 and 66 cycles on Zen 6c. The larger caches and greater number of mesh stops likely contribute to the increase. In nanoseconds, Zen 6’s higher clock hides most of the increase, at 10.7 ns against 10.3 ns on the Zen 5-based EPYC 9355P, while Zen 6c’s lower clock and larger CCX put it at 16.4 ns. Moving over to bandwidth, we see that Zen 6 fixes Zen 5’s odd L2 bandwidth behavior, where a core pulled only about 42 bytes per cycle across most of the L2’s capacity, in Zen 6 the read path now reliably delivers 64 bytes per cycle. The rest of the cache hierarchy is largely unchanged in bandwidth per cycle. Load/Store Store-to-load forwarding is seemingly unchanged from Zen 5 and is where the behavior of Zen 6 and Zen 6c re-unify. EPYC 9686F (Zen 6) STLF test EPYC 9996 (Zen 6c) STLF test Zen 5 STLF test A 32-bit load from the same address as a 64-bit store completes with effectively zero latency which lets Zen 6 handle two dependent store-load pairs per cycle. Loads fully contained within the store complete in 7 cycles regardless of alignment with partial overlaps costing 14 cycles, matching Zen 5. SPEC CPU 2026 Performance The EPYC 9686F is near the top of our estimated single-threaded SPEC CPU 2026 results. It roughly matches the Ryzen 9 9950X3D2, AMD’s highest-end client CPU from the previous generation, in integer rate and beats it in floating-point rate. At a matched 4.1 GHz, the 9686F leads the 9950X3D2 by about 4% in integer and 11% in floating point, despite the X3D part’s much larger L3. The EPYC 9996 is no slouch either. It roughly matches the previous-generation EPYC 9575F in single-threaded performance, despite running at lower clocks and having four times as many cores. It also edges out NVIDIA’s Vera in integer and leads it by about 20% in floating point. The EPYC 9686F leads on almost every subtest and finishes about 18% ahead of the EPYC 9996 in both suites. It scores 6.20 versus 5.25 in integer and 10.6 versus 8.99 in floating point, with some of its largest leads in 714.cpython, 766.femflow, and 772.marian. Against the Zen 5-based EPYC 9575F, the 9996 scores 5.25 versus 5.13 in integer and 8.99 versus 9.01 in floating point while running about 900 MHz slower. The 9996 also edges out the 9686F in 721.gcc and 765.roms, two subtests where the 9686F’s higher clock provides no advantage. Top-down breakdowns of pipeline slots on the two Zen 6 chips show where the 9686F’s lead comes from. The integer-rate profiles look almost identical in core-bound subtests. In 750.sealcrypto, 710.omnetpp, 735.gem5, and 753.ns3, retiring slots account for nearly the same share on both chips, with differences of less than one percentage point. Memory-heavy subtests show larger gaps. Moving from the EPYC 9996 to the EPYC 9686F, backend memory stalls rise from 37.9% to 50.0% of pipeline slots in 729.abc, from 19.0% to 34.1% in 723.llvm, and from 24.8% to 33.2% in 708.sqlite. The share of retiring slots falls accordingly. Zen 6c’s lower clock and larger shared L3 cache may help explain its lower memory-stall share. The floating-point profiles look similar for most subtests. The retiring share in 731.astcenc, 772.marian, and 767.nest differs by about one percentage point or less, and 709.cactus spends over half its slots stalled on front-end bandwidth on both chips. The larger gaps again appear in memory-heavy subtests. Moving from the EPYC 9996 to the EPYC 9686F, backend memory stalls rise from 42.5% to 55.3% of slots in 765.roms, from 60.9% to 67.6% in 749.fotonik3d, and from 17.8% to 33.8% in 782.lbm. These are also tests where the 9686F’s higher clock helps least: it trails the 9996 in 765.roms, roughly ties in 749.fotonik3d, and leads by about 11% in 782.lbm, despite clocking up to roughly 29% higher. Running the 9686F at 4.1 GHz to match the 9996 removes the clock advantage, and the overall picture flips: the 9686F scores 4.92 and 8.64 at that clock, putting Zen 6c about 6.7% ahead per clock in integer and 4% in floating point. At the same clock speed, Zen 6 and Zen 6c look almost identical in core-bound integer subtests. In 750.sealcrypto, retiring slots account for 67.3% of the total on the EPYC 9686F versus 67.6% on the EPYC 9996.The floating-point profiles also look similar in several subtests at matched clocks. Both chips spend over half their pipeline slots stalled on frontend bandwidth in 709.cactus. Their retiring shares differ by about two percentage points in 722.palm and 766.femflow. The 9686F still spends a larger share of its pipeline slots stalled on memory. Backend memory stalls account for 50.3% versus 42.5% on the 9996 in 765.roms, 24.9% versus 17.8% in 782.lbm, and 63.3% versus 60.9% in 749.fotonik3d. Zen 6c’s 128 MB L3 cache is likely serving more of these requests than Zen 6’s 48 MB cache, reducing the need to access main memory. The clearest difference is in frontend latency stalls, which account for a much larger share of slots on the 9686F in subtests with large codebases. In 727.cppcheck, that share is 35.2% versus 16.6% on the 9996; in 721.gcc, it is 25.8% versus 10.0%. With clock speed matched and both designs sharing the same frontend, those stalls most likely reflect differences in the cache and memory hierarchy. The floating-point profiles also look similar in several subtests at matched clocks. Both chips spend over half their pipeline slots stalled on frontend bandwidth in 709.cactus. Their retiring shares differ by about two percentage points in 722.palm and 766.femflow. The 9686F still spends a larger share of its pipeline slots stalled on memory. Backend memory stalls account for 50.3% versus 42.5% on the 9996 in 765.roms, 24.9% versus 17.8% in 782.lbm, and 63.3% versus 60.9% in 749.fotonik3d. Zen 6c’s 128 MB L3 cache is likely serving more of these requests than Zen 6’s 48 MB cache, reducing the need to access main memory. Final Words The Zen 6 Family improves upon its predecessor in various ways, an upgraded frontend allows one thread to utilize both decoders, while a faster branch predictor makes it more forgiving on misses, all tied together with larger OoO structures allowing it to better hide memory stalls. All of this coming together to provide a generational uplift from Zen 5. However, I think the more interesting change is the split between Zen 6 and Zen 6c. The classic and dense cores now differ within the out-of-order engine, with Zen 6 appearing tuned for higher clocks and Zen 6c providing more capacity to absorb latency. The shared foundation is still clear, but those differences make the choice between them more dependent on workload behavior. The performance results are encouraging as well with the estimated single-threaded SPEC CPU 2026 scores, the EPYC 9686F leads the Zen 5-based EPYC 9575F by about 21% in integer and 18% in floating point. The EPYC 9996 roughly matches the 9575F despite running about 900 MHz slower which are strong results for both core designs. AMD’s answer to the classic-versus-dense question used to be the same core at two densities but now with Zen 6 it is two cores, each shaped for where it will run. That now leaves me wondering what AMD will do with the Zen 7 Family and if we will see even more specialization of the same basic core design or if we will see a larger split of the designs. 53 2 7 Share Previous Next Discussion about this post Comments Restacks Nathan Gabriel 2h thanks for this! title: Tracking Anthropic-discovered vulnerabilities
body_text: After 7-months, Glasswing Overwelms Maintainers with Underwhelming Findings | Blog | VulnCheck Products Government Resources Community Company Partners Sign In / Join Sign In Go back November 9, 2026 After 7-months, Glasswing Overwelms Maintainers with Underwhelming Findings Patrick Garrity in/patrickmgarrity/ ai cve kev VulnCheck Community gives you free access to VulnCheck KEV, NVD++, Initial Access Community, and VulnCheck XDB Join Now Key Takeaways: Seven months into Project Glasswing, VulnCheck has tracked 442 CVEs attributable to Anthropic, roughly 0.5% of all CVEs published this year, with only two identified as exploited in the wild. Of Anthropicâs 37,966 reported findings, only 7,349 (19.4%) have been made public and just 217 have been marked fixed. Since September, Anthropic has added nearly 12,000 findings while recording just 15 additional fixes, widening the gap between discovery and remediation. Roughly 1,654 findings (4.4%) have been marked as duplicates, nearly eight times the number fixed, and another 419 have been withdrawn. Anthropicâs claimed true positive rate has risen from 90.8% to 94.2%, raising questions about how it accounts for duplicates and withdrawn findings. Anthropicâs OSS Scanner shifts validation work to maintainers, with curl rejecting 19 of 34 published reports as vulnerabilities, confirming six as low severity and leaving nine awaiting assessment. Also putting Anthropic's true positive rates into question. We're seven months into Anthropic's flagship Project Glasswing, and it's time for another update on the results. I've been tracking the project to see whether its claims are overhyped or grounded in reality. As we all recall, Anthropic launched Project Glasswing on April 7th, claiming, "We have identified thousands of additional high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities that we are working on responsibly disclosing to open source maintainers." What surprised me was how little evidence the project offered, which made me wonder whether this was more of an overhyped marketing campaign. That said, we shouldn't overlook that AI is an effective tool for finding vulnerabilities. But that story goes well beyond any single frontier model's capabilities. If you're just catching up, this builds on my earlier posts: Tracking CVEs Attributed to Anthropic Researchers and Project Glasswing - April 15 Observations on Anthropic's Vulnerability Disclosure Ledger - June 9 1H-2026 State of Exploitation Report - July 28 The Anthropic Glasswing Receipts Are Starting to Trickle In - September 8 So let's look at the resultsâ¦ Tracking Anthropic-Discovered Vulnerabilities I started tracking Anthropic's discovered vulnerabilities on April 17th, shortly after launch, in an open source repo called Anthropic Credited CVEs . The goal was to see whether Anthropic's claims lived up to the hype. This was before Anthropic launched its own disclosure ledger , which is only updated in infrequent bulk batches. My repo tracks every vulnerability attributable to Anthropic using CVE records, GHSAs, Linux kernel commits, and Anthropic's own ledger. I also manually audit advisories to catch CVEs that might otherwise get overlooked. After seven months, I've tracked 442 CVEs attributable to Anthropic. That's an average of just 63 per month. Out of the 93,450 CVEs published this year, that's only about 0.5% of all CVEs. For comparison, Anthropic's own public ledger lists just 217 fixed vulnerabilities, so I've tracked more than twice as many as Anthropic has disclosed itself. The Danger Narrative Isn't Adding Up You may recall that Glasswing launched with the message that we'd entered the Mythos era of vulnerability discovery. But are these vulnerabilities actually useful to attackers? To find out, I've been tracking Anthropic-discovered CVEs against VulnCheck KEV. So far, only 2 of the 442 have been exploited in the wild, just 0.45%. (CVE-2026-61500 and CVE-2026-26980) Anthropic's Ledger Continues to Underwhelm When Anthropic first launched its ledger in May, it reported 23,019 findings and a 90.8% true positive rate. As of its most recent update on November 2nd, there are 37,966 findings and just 217 fixes. That looks like a staggering failure to me, but let's take a closer look. Of the 37,966 findings Anthropic reports, only 7,349 (19.4%) have been made public. Just 217 of those have been marked fixed. The more glaring number is that 4.4% (1,654) of the project's findings have already been marked as duplicates, 7.5x more duplicates than fixes. On top of that, 419 findings have been withdrawn. It seems odd that the ledger now claims a 94.2% true positive rate, up from 90.8% at launch, when more findings have been withdrawn or marked as duplicates than fixed, likely a feedback loop missing to the triage rates listed as âTrue Positivesâ. The trend since my September update is even more telling: September 8 November 2 Change Total findings 26,153 37,966 +11,813 Made public 2,736 (10.5%) 7,349 (19.4%) +4,613 Fixed 202 217 +15 Withdrawn 245 419 +174 Duplicates 2 1,670 +1,668 Claimed true positive rate 91.4% 94.2% +2.8 pts In two months, Anthropic added nearly 12,000 findings and fixed just 15 more. Duplicates went from two to thousands, which is exactly what I warned about in September: the longer findings sit, the more likely someone else finds and fixes them first. I don't know how anyone can read these numbers as anything but damning. You may also notice a correction in my visual. There appears to be a bug on Anthropic's ledger that inflates the number of findings marked as disclosed. Check for yourself using the "disclosed" filter. Anthropic's Pivot to OSS Scanner Having humans triage every finding clearly didn't scale, and Anthropic has said as much. In its OSS Scanner launch post on October 8th, Anthropic said it had found more than 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities but had manually reviewed only about 6,000, and that it remains "bottlenecked on our human capacity to validate these findings." It had also already sent nearly 5,000 unverified reports to maintainers who asked for everything in bulk. So with the Glasswing open source initiative hitting a wall, launching a self-service OSS Scanner that projects can opt into makes sense. Maintainers can now request a scan and triage the findings themselves. Anthropic is upfront that these reports are "fully model-generated, without human review or triage" and that "it is possible reports will be incorrect or invalid." In other words, the triage bottleneck didn't go away. It moved to the maintainers. If the true positive rate is really as high as Anthropic claims, that shouldn't be a problem. curl Gives Anthropic's OSS Scanner a Reality Check Three days ago, Daniel Stenberg , who maintains curl, announced that the project had received a batch of 45 vulnerability reports from Anthropic. Anthropic rated only one as medium severity and the rest as low. Daniel is moving them over to GitHub at a deliberate pace "to soften the impact for the team," with plans to have them all published by the end of the week. This gives us a rare look at what Anthropic's findings look like once a maintainer actually validates them. Of the 34 reports published so far, 19 have been marked as not a vulnerability, 6 have been confirmed as low severity, and 9 are still awaiting assessment. That puts the false positive rate at 55.9% so far, and only 17.6% of findings have been confirmed, all of them low severity. That's a lot of work dumped on open source maintainers for a small handful of low-impact bugs, and when a maintainer has to pace reports just to protect his team, that says plenty about the burden. This also isn't new for curl. Back in May, Daniel wrote that five Mythos findings boiled down to a single confirmed vulnerability. It's a far cry from the 94.2% true positive rate Anthropic currently claims on its ledger. It also undercuts the "high- and critical-severity" framing Glasswing launched with. In September, I found that Claude rated 91.5% of ledger findings as critical or high, while maintainers rated only 51.3% that way. I'm curious whether other open source projects are seeing the same thing. curl took a bold move by deciding to publish low and medium vulnerabilities findings publicly as issues for full transparency and we encourage other open source maintainers to follow their lead. Takeaways After Seven Months AI is a valuable tool for finding vulnerabilities, and I'm not discounting that. But seven months in, the evidence still doesn't match the launch narrative. The CVEs are a sliver of this year's total, almost none are being exploited, fixes have stalled while duplicates and withdrawals pile up, and the triage burden is shifting onto the open source maintainers Glasswing promised to help. The receipts keep coming in. They still don't reconcile. title: Scion is back and is going to sell a kei truck in America
body_text: Scion Is Back! And It's Going To Sell A Freaking Kei Truck In America - The Autopian Skip to content Youtube Facebook-f Twitter Instagram Rss Sign in Register Sign out Account Sign in Register Sign out Account Night Panel Disable Night Panel News Reviews Merch Toys Tips Glovebox Become a Member Menu News Reviews Merch Toys Tips Glovebox Become a Member Home » Scion Is Back! And It’s Going To Sell A Freaking Kei Truck In America Scion Is Back! And It’s Going To Sell A Freaking Kei Truck In America By Leslie Hanna November 10, 2026 11:07 am 99 Comments When Toyota first introduced the Scion marque in 2003, it had one primary goal – sell cars to the younger generation. Its cars were cheaper and available in fun colors with fun names like “High Voltage Yellow” and “xPRESSO.” When I was a kid in the early 2000s, I often dreamed of one day owning a tC in Black Cherry Pearl and enjoyed lovingly calling xBs “toaster cars.” Over half of new Scions sold were to people under 35, and the tC boasted the youngest average buyer age in the entire industry at a sprightly 29. Their sales numbers peaked in 2006, but dropped nearly 75% by 2010. After sustained financial struggle, Toyota retired the marque in 2016. But now, a decade later, everyone’s favorite toaster brand is seemingly back. Today, Toyota announced the official revival of Scion, but instead of being a quirky and budget-conscious line, they are becoming Toyota’s cornerstone of curiosity. Now called “Scion by Toyota,” it is being launched as a “freedom lab” where drivers can, and are encouraged to challenge conventional ways of thinking about mobility through design, vehicle concepts, and features. “Okei,” let’s go. Toyota Their first production vehicle is the KEI-01, an ultra-compact utility truck, otherwise known as a kei truck. Toyota will be using its existing manufacturing infrastructure in Indiana to “produce” them for sale in the American market. “Produce” is in quotation marks because the KEI-01 is quite literally a rebadged Toyota Pixis, which is a rebadged Daihatsu Hijet Jumbo Cab. Based on its initial imagery it is seemingly also still right-hand drive, and there’s no word on if a LHD variant will be available in the future. With its friendly little 660cc engine and CVT transmission, the KEI-01 was certified to meet American low-speed vehicle safety standards, meaning it has a limited top speed of less than 25mph and is only legal on roads with a posted speed limit of less than 35mph. This makes it not really usable as a daily driver, but keeps it in this beautiful sweet spot where it has a shocking number of commercial and agricultural uses. Toyota The KEI-01 has a 600-pound payload (which means cargo and passengers) and a three-way fold-down cargo bed, making it a well-equipped workhorse for use on farms and in warehouses. It’s only about 5 feet wide and 11 feet long, which makes it great for use as a delivery or work vehicle in dense, urban areas like New York City. Believe it or not, it also has 4WD, which means it can traverse uneven terrain in more rural areas with ease. And don’t worry if it’s hot outside, because heat and air conditioning are standard. Toyota It’s worth noting that, while Kei trucks are currently sold new in the U.S. as “mini trucks” through independent distributors, this one is sold directly by Toyota. Before you rush to your local Toyota dealer to place a deposit, I’m going to have to burst your bubble a bit. Initially, the KEI 01 is only going to be available in a low-volume, niche pilot program entirely focused on fleet usage beginning in late 2027. Depending on performance and owner feedback, availability of the KEI-01 may eventually be expanded, but no further information is available from Toyota at the time.   View this post on Instagram   A post shared by The Autopian (@theautopian) The Hybrid Side-By-Side Toyota Two other mobility concepts accompany the KEI-01 in the Scion by Toyota lineup, the SxS Concept and the BXE Concept. The SxS Concept was unveiled at the 2025 SEMA Show as a purpose-built side-by-side all-terrain vehicle ( click here for our coverage). Developed by Toyota North America, the off-road concept is outfitted with a turbocharged four-cylinder from the Tacoma making in the realm of 300hp. You won’t have to worry about your turbo spool scaring away local fauna, as it is equipped with a “Silent Mode,” which allows the driver to switch from the boisterous internal combustion system to a much more civilised fully electric driving mode. Unlike the KEI-01, the SxS Concept is still just that – a concept, with no current plans to have a version available to the public. Toyota Last, but not least, is the BKE Concept. The BKE concept is entirely focused on personal mobility in the outdoors, filling the gap between the utility of the KEI-01 and the pure performance of the SxS Concept. Its small form factor and rugged tires make it an ideal off-roader for traversing narrow paths while being portable enough to stow away when not in use or easily tote around in the back of a car. I deleted all my SSH keys
body_text: I deleted all my SSH keys Alex Haydock Home | Posts | Blogroll | About | RSS | GitHub | Mastodon I deleted all my SSH keys 2026-11-04 11:00 security I’ve been using ed25519-sk keys with YubiKeys since practically the moment they were available. But because of some specific use-cases (and because, frankly, YubiKeys are expensive) I’ve had a few traditional on-disk keys hanging around for a while just waiting for me to finally decide to get rid of them. This post documents how I’m using various secure enclaves (YubiKey, TPM, Apple Secure Enclave) to hold/encrypt SSH key material and achieve the goal of not having any unprotected key material living on-disk. First – Isn’t using a passphrase enough? Probably. I don’t intend to imply that this post is the only way that anyone should be doing SSH keys. Using a passphrase will encrypt the key with bcrypt & AES which keeps it protected even if the on-disk keyfile leaks somehow. And with a functioning ssh-agent, the passphrase should only need to be entered once per session, with the decrypted key material being held in RAM after that point. So yes, the ’traditional’ method is probably fine for most threat models. But I’m still keen to move to hardware-backed keys anyway, mostly for the satisfaction. About hardware-resident keys When I say ‘hardware-resident’ keys, I mean keys that use a secure enclave or purpose-built hardware like YubiKeys to store or protect the key material. The theoretical benefit here is that the hardware used to generate the SSH key is needed in order to use the key. There’s no mechanism that allows leaking or exfiltrating keys that generated using this method. Any material that does exist on-disk is useless without the hardware. Goals So I want to: Switch to using hardware-resident keys entirely Do so as natively as possible, avoiding additional software where I can Test these in various real-world scenarios, such as running within an LXC or noninteractively mounting an SSHFS server Hardware I’m going to try three different hardware methods for achieving this, which I think will cover all of my needs: Method 1: YubiKey Method 2: TPM Method 3: Apple Secure Enclave Method 1: YubiKey With a YubiKey (5 and newer), SSH keys can be directly enrolled into the device using ed25519-sk (where the -sk stands for “Security Key”). This doesn’t require any additional software beyond OpenSSH itself. To store a new SSH key on a YubiKey, insert it and run: ssh-keygen -t ed25519-sk -O resident -O application = "ssh:yournamehere" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519-sk The application tag set in the command is arbitrary and can be set to whatever memorable string you prefer to differentiate between multiple SSH keys if you want to create multiple keys on the same YubiKey. If you have ykman installed, you can now inspect the list of credentials enrolled in the device: $ ykman fido credentials list Enter your PIN: Credential ID RP ID Username Display name 0f41fb61... ssh:yournamehere openssh openssh If ykman complains that you haven’t set a FIDO PIN on the YubiKey yet, you can do this with ykman fido access change-pin . Note that you don’t actually need ykman to enrol or use SSH keys with a YubiKey but it does make managing the device more convenient. Once the key has been created, you can retrieve the public key from disk: $ cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519-sk.pub sk-ssh-ed25519@openssh.com AAAAGnNrLXNzaC1lZDI1NTE5QG9wZW5zc2guY29tAAAAIA9B+2GGCkQvBzpa4WobQhfC9YU5Su3pKXBmVLSXEqfRAAAAEHNzaDp5b3VybmFtZWhlcmU= alice@hostname This key can be used like any other SSH public key – added to authorized_keys on a host, copied with ssh-copy-id , or pasted into services that depend on SSH like Git forges. You will also find a ~/.ssh/id_ed25519-sk file on disk (without the .pub extension). Note that although this looks like a private key, it doesn’t actually contain the key material. This is just a handle to find the relevant key on the hardware device. To configure the key for authentication, it can be enrolled with ssh-add like a regular key, or specified directly in ~/.ssh/config : Host blog.infected.systems IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519-sk From here, you can now SSH into the destination host as with a regular key. SSH will ask you to tap the YubiKey to confirm presence when the SSH command runs. Unattended YubiKey usage When using an ed25519-sk key created with the default settings as above, you will be asked to confirm your presence whenever the key is used by physically touching the YubiKey. It’s probably a good idea to keep this default, but if you have a specific use-case that requires unattended key usage, you can generate a no-touch-required key as follows: ssh-keygen -t ed25519-sk -O resident -O no-touch-required -O application = "ssh:nameyourkey" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519-sk When using a no-touch-required key, although it isn’t possible for a malicious actor to exfiltrate the key even with root access to the host the YubiKey is plugged into, a malicious actor with access could use the key without requiring any presence detection or human interaction. So do make sure this is actually suitable for your risk appetite before doing it. To use a no-touch-required key for unattended authentication to remote servers, you need to prepend the entry in the authorized_keys file on the destination host with no-touch-required , otherwise OpenSSH’s default security settings will reject the key. For example: $ cat ~/.ssh/authorized_keys no-touch-required sk-ssh-ed25519@openssh.com AAAAGnNrLXNzaC1lZDI1NTE5QG9wZW5zc2guY29tAAAAIA9B+2GGCkQvBzpa4WobQhfC9YU5Su3pKXBmVLSXEqfRAAAAEHNzaDp5b3VybmFtZWhlcmU= alice@hostname Method 2: TPM YubiKeys are nice, though fairly expensive. It would be useful if we could use the TPM we already have on our host to protect key material instead. Well, it turns out we can! Unfortunately this does require additional software, but it’s a fairly minimal Golang package – ssh-tpm-agent . It can be installed with Go directly from GitHub, but is natively packaged by Ubuntu and I’m working on packaging it for Fedora . To create a TPM-backed SSH key with a PIN, run: ssh-tpm-keygen -N "your-pin" The process will ask you where to store the key. From here, once again we have a keypair with a .pub file that we can use in authorized_keys or copy however we wish. To use the TPM-backed key we need to use the TPM-aware SSH agent provided by the ssh-tpm-agent package. If you installed the native Golang package rather than something vendored by your distribution, you can enable the systemd socket unit for the agent as follows: ssh-tpm-agent --install-user-units && systemctl --user enable --now ssh-tpm-agent.socket To ensure the socket for the agent can be discovered by SSH processes run within your shell session, add the following to your .bashrc or the equivalent for your shell: export SSH_AUTH_SOCK = " $( ssh-tpm-agent --print-socket ) " Again, we can now use this key to authenticate to servers as if it were any other traditional on-disk key. Unattended TPM usage If you want this key to be available unattended, or to services that don’t use a full shell such as systemd mount units , you can create a new key without a PIN (pass -N "" to the ssh-tpm-keygen command) and specify the socket path in ~/.ssh/config instead of relying on SSH_AUTH_SOCK (although this relies on the socket address being predictable – i.e. your UID being stable): Host blog.infected.systems IdentityAgent /run/user/1000/ssh-tpm-agent.sock IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa Note that ssh-tpm-agent does not account for the values in the TPM Platform Configuration Registers (PCRs) which record the state of the booted system – firmware versions etc, so changes of hardware/firmware/OS will not cause the system to refuse to unseal the key (unlike, say, something like BitLocker). So ensure that using a PIN-free key is appropriate for your risk model before doing so. A caveat regarding TPM keys You will notice though that the private keyfile held on disk uses a .tpm extension this time. This is where an important caveat of the TPM method comes in – Unlike the YubiKey approach, the private key material is actually being stored on disk here. This is because TPM devices do not natively support enrolling SSH keys. So what is happening is that the private key material is being stored on disk in encrypted form, and the TPM is being used to decrypt it. This is still a device-bound credential as the key cannot be used without the TPM device even if the keyfile is leaked or exfiltrated but it is a relevant distinction compared to device- resident credentials such as -sk keys. Method 3: Apple Secure Enclave As of macOS Sequoia, the Smart Card Auth system within macOS is able to natively handle SSH keys as identities. We can generate one as follows: sc_auth create-ctk-identity -l "ssh-labelyourkey" -k p-256-ne -t bio The options above: -l labels our key. Choose a unique and useful name here as we’ll need this to find the right key handle file on disk later. -k p-256-ne creates a non exportable ( -ne ) key. This is important to ensure we’re actually creating a key that will stay resident in the enclave. -t bio requires TouchID to use the key. Then we can list the key: % sc_auth list-ctk-identities Key Type Public Key Hash Prot Label Common Name Email Address Valid To Valid p-256-ne B15235464F87EC7C8DEE89BFA06399FFD6678E99 bio ssh-labelyourkey ssh-labelyourkey 04/11/2027, 09:29 YES To export a handle to disk that allows OpenSSH to use the key from the secure enclave, you can do: ( cd ~/.ssh && ssh-keygen -w /usr/lib/ssh-keychain.dylib -K -N "" ) When prompted for a pin during export, you can leave it blank as it isn’t used here. A public key and private key handle file will be created on-disk in the ~/.ssh directory. Note that the command above will export a key handle for all of the SSH keys you have enrolled in the Secure Enclave (you can create many if desired by repeating the process above). I wasn’t able to find a way to export individual key handles despite Apple’s docs suggesting that you should be able to with KEYCHAIN_CERTIFICATES . Your best bet will be to use a clear label using the -l flag when creating the key so you can easily find the handle for it after it has been exported to disk. Once we have our pubkey and handle file, we can process these as we normally would – copying the public key to an authorized_keys file on a remote host or adding it to whatever services we prefer. To use SSH keys from the Secure Enclave, we need to set SSH_SK_PROVIDER in our shell. We can add this to ~/.zshrc : export SSH_SK_PROVIDER = /usr/lib/ssh-keychain.dylib After a restart of the shell, the key will work like any other – though you may need to specify it directly as in my case it wasn’t being autodiscovered by macOS’s SSH agent: Host blog.infected.systems IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa_sk_rk_ssh-labelyourkey Running a Mac in ‘clamshell mode’ If you run your Mac in what Apple calls ‘clamshell mode’ (i.e. a laptop with the lid shut), then the initial create-ctk-identity command will fail with an error like this: Error: Error Domain=com.apple.LocalAuthentication Code=-4 "Touch ID is not available in closed clamshell mode." UserInfo={BiometryType=1, Subcode=10, NSDebugDescription=Touch ID is not available in closed clamshell mode., NSLocalizedDescription=Authentication canceled.} Unfortunately it seems that keys created with -t bio do actually require full TouchID in order to generate or use – unlike other operations such as unlocking the Safari Keychain or using Apple Pay which fall back to a user password when in clamshell mode. There is an option to use -t none to create a key without presence confirmation enabled at all. This carries the same risk as I discussed in the section about using YubiKeys unattended so you’ll have to decide whether it works for your risk model. If, like me, you use the machine in clamshell mode basically all the time there are some alternative options that still retain presence detection though: You could buy one of Apple’s expensive bluetooth keyboards with Touch ID . Or, the YubiKey 5C Nano is tiny and can sit almost flush in the side of a closed MacBook and can be used with Method 1 including presence detection. Final note With a mix of these three approaches, I’ve finally been able to deprecate on-disk keys from all my setups. Hopefully some of the info in this post is helpful to people! It’s nothing that can’t already be found online but I’ve gathered it into one place mostly for my own convenience. The main gotcha to be aware of with hardware-resident keys is that they’re, well, hardware resident. Hardware malfunction/loss/change can render keys unusable. So it’s probably better to make sure you at least have multiple keys. Remember, authorized_keys can take as many keys as you care to put in it so redundancy is the best move here I think. In Six Math Essentials, the renowned mathematician and Fields Medalist Terence Tao introduces readers to six central concepts that have guided mathematicians from antiquity to the frontiers of what we know today and now help us make sense of our complex world. This slim, elegant volume explores numbers as the gateway to quantitative thinking; algebra as the gateway to abstraction; geometry as a way to calculate beyond what we can see; probability as a tool to navigate uncertainty with rigorous thinking; analysis as a means to tame the very large or the very small; and dynamics as the mathematics of change. title: Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers
body_text: Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers [LWN.net] LWN .net News from the source Content Weekly Edition Archives Search Kernel Security Events calendar Unread comments LWN FAQ Write for us Edition Return to the Front page User: Password: | | Log in / Subscribe / Register Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers [LWN subscriber-only content] By Joe Brockmeier November 10, 2026 Mike Lothian owns a docking station (or dock) that uses a DisplayLink chipset that had, at least in his opinion, subpar performance on Linux. He decided to try improving the Linux driver, with LLM assistance, but ran into one problem that he could not solve—so he asked for help, hoping that Synaptics's developers would lend a hand. (DisplayLink was acquired by Synaptics in 2022.) Rather than help him in improving the driver, however, the Synaptics legal team responded with patent infringement claims, a demand that he cease unauthorized implementation of DisplayLink technology, and threats of expensive legal penalties. For now, it appears that Linux users of the company's docks will have to continue to live without feature parity with other platforms. Synaptics and Displaylink The dock that he was trying to support is a Dell device that connects to a system via USB 3 and allows users to connect multiple monitors and other devices to their computer. It provides its DisplayLink Manager (DLM) software for Linux for the devices via an APT repository for Ubuntu. The company only provides DLM software in binary form, and only for x86-based platforms. The software is proprietary, but the company does maintain an open-source, out-of-tree kernel module that is included with DLM, the Extensible Virtual Display Interface (EVDI) project. It provides a driver that's compatible with Linux DRM and allows users to manage their docked displays with standard tools used for display settings, such as xrandr or GNOME and KDE Plasma's utilities. Stay on top of Linux kernel development with a one-month free trial subscription to LWN, no credit card required. A short article explains why the company has not released source code for DLM: the software uses a proprietary graphics technology called DL3 to create a compressed stream of the various channels (e.g., USB, DisplayLink video, audio) over a communication channel (USB 3 in this case) and decode it again for output to the user's devices. Unfortunately, the vendor-supplied software did not work well for Lothian. I spoke and chatted with him via Signal while writing this article; he said that the driver kept crashing under Linux, so he decided to use his Claude subscription to try to develop a new driver and support software. Vino He posted the first patch series for Vino—his Rust-based DRM/KMS driver—to the kernel's dri-devel list as an RFC on June 17. Lothian noted that it was in an incomplete state, and asked for help with a blocker that he had run into trying to communicate with the dock's control plane. " If you have knowledge of the DisplayLink DL3 control-plane engagement sequence, or ideas for isolating a whole-bus timing/ordering property a per-channel diff cannot see, help would be very welcome. " He received feedback from a few developers, including guidance from Danilo Krummrich to rework the driver to use the Rust KMS bindings , but no advice specific to the problem he was trying to solve. Lothian also opened an issue on the EVDI GitHub repository on June 17. It explained the work he'd done so far, outlined the approach in trying to reverse-engineer the DL3 protocol, provided links to his GitHub repository with the Vino code, and asked for clarification on a few issues. There was no reply to his issue. He also reached out to Łukasz Spintzyk of Synaptics directly by email; his correspondence with the company between July 5 and October 7 is available in this PDF compiled by Lothian . He noted that he had found a few bugs in EVDI and opened a pull request (that went unreviewed for several months), and also asked for assistance where he was blocked on Vino. On July 20, he received a reply, not from Spintzyk, but from Michal Lukaszek of Synaptics: The reason I'm writing is that DisplayLink is not an open standard. The protocol, codec, and other technologies used by DisplayLink devices are proprietary to Synaptics and are protected by a substantial portfolio of patents in a number of jurisdictions, including the UK. From what you've published, it appears that the VINO project is progressing beyond interoperability work and toward implementing technology that we believe is covered by those patents. While many developers understandably focus on avoiding copyrighted source code, patent law is different. An independently written or clean-room implementation does not necessarily avoid patent infringement if it implements patented inventions. Lukaszek said it was entirely possible that Lothian was unaware of the " intellectual property landscape surrounding DisplayLink ", so he wanted to make him aware now rather than " have the situation become more formal later ". Lothian lives in Scotland and has a ".co.uk" email address, which explains why the email made reference to the UK. Cease and desist On August 17, Andrew Bateman, an assistant general council of intellectual property for Synaptics, sent a cease-and-desist notice . The letter stated that Lothian had not " substantially responded " to Lukaszek's communication, and had continued with " public statements and further development activities ". It included an appendix with a list of 125 patents that " cover fundamental aspects of DisplayLink's architecture and operation ", but did not specify which patents might be infringed by the work. Synaptics included a list of eight demands it expected immediate compliance with, including ceasing development of " any software or other implementation that infringes any Synaptics patent ", withdrawing submissions of materials " made to Linux kernel maintainers, mailing lists, code-hosting platforms, package maintainers, distributions, or any other person or organization ", and to identify in writing every location " in which the relevant materials have been published, submitted, stored, or distributed ". It also demanded that he provide Synaptics with a signed confirmation, by August 28, that he had complied with its demands. Lothian, instead, posted version three of his Vino work for the DisplayLink docks to the dri-devel list on August 26. He said that the previous two versions had " never lit a panel ", but the new work could control three generations of DL3 docks without any vendor software. There were no substantive reviews of the patch set posted to the list, though there were some automated reviews from Sashiko. On August 27, Lothian responded to Bateman and asked him to elaborate on the patents that Synaptics thought were being infringed. " A claim chart mapping the relevant claims to the relevant code would make it much easier for me to understand and properly respond to your concerns. " He also expressed confusion about Synaptics's position that his work was being treated as patent infringement. Synaptics is a member of the Open Invention Network (OIN), which was created to help open-source developers and vendors deal with the threats of expensive patent litigation. It holds a large, cross-licensed portfolio that serves to provide patent protection to individuals, open-source projects, and large vendors alike. Lothian said that he was now an OIN licensee as well, and he thought that it was supposed to " reduce exactly this sort of patent problem around Linux and open source software ". He asked Bateman to explain how Synaptics claims " interact with our respective OIN commitments ", and expressed a desire to sort things out with Synaptics constructively. " I don't think a public dispute between Synaptics and an individual open source developer would be particularly helpful for either of us, especially within the Linux and open source communities ". Lothian did not think he could " reasonably provide the signed undertaking " Synaptics had demanded by August 28 without understanding which patent claims it was alleging. He asked for an extension to the deadline. There was no response from Bateman, so Lothian sent a follow-up email on September 18. He said he was concerned there was no acknowledgment to his last email, and wondered it was safe to assume he could continue his work. He had been running the Vino driver himself for quite a while, and was eager to move it upstream without having patent threats hanging over the work. Bateman responded the next day and said that he should be concerned: As you previously requested, we have been documenting your ongoing patent infringement by mapping your Vino driver to specific claims of our DisplayLink patents. I will provide this claim mapping documentation to you within the next two weeks. I will also be sending to you our demand for substantial monetary compensation to recoup the cost and effort required to create such documentation of your infringing acts. I previously gave you the opportunity to stop your infringement, but you decided to push back and not heed my warnings, and so now we are escalating as we deem appropriate. The letter continued to claim that Lothian would be " single-handedly eviscerating DisplayLink's competitive advantage in this crowded market by educating our competitors and other third parties as to how we implement our proprietary technology ". He said that DisplayLink is not a member of OIN, and none of its technology is licensable through OIN or any other organization. Bateman sent a follow-up letter , dated October 5, that included two claim charts for UK patents: GB2484736B ("Display control device") and GB2485613B ("Image generation"), both filed in 2010 and published in 2012. He reiterated Synaptics's demands from its previous letter, and said that the deadline was now October 11; failure to comply would result in the company seeking " monetary compensation from you in the amount of US$25,000 to recoup the costs and effort required to create the attached documentation of your infringing acts ". That amount would be increased by $25,000 each week until the company's demands were complied with. Lothian responded the next day, by email, to say that he was on vacation, and would not be back home until October 13. He asked for an extension of the deadline to return home and go through the claim charts " ideally with someone qualified to help me read them ". Bateman replied that Synaptics would agree to extend the deadline to October 18, though no further extensions would be granted. He reiterated that " DisplayLink is not a member of OIN " and none of its technology was licensable through OIN. OIN to the rescue? Synaptics is a member of OIN, and is listed in the community directory . In addition to joining OIN, Lothian had reached out to the organization to try to solicit its help and has been in communication with some of the staff there. OIN indicated that it would look into the matter and see if he had any protection as an OIN member. That process took longer than Lothian hoped, though OIN did eventually provide its conclusion. OIN's portfolio covers a wide range of software that matches its Linux System Definition , but it does not cover everything that might be implemented for a Linux system. In particular, its definition specifies that codecs (" a component of a program capable of performing transformations of a video, still image or audio data stream or signal ") are not covered unless specifically mentioned in this list of components. I spoke briefly to OIN CEO Keith Bergelt on October 23, shortly after OIN staff informed Lothian of the result of their research. Bergelt said that OIN's conclusion was that, since codecs are explicitly not covered by OIN's Linux System Definition, its protections did not extend to Lothian's attempted kernel contributions. OIN had recommended that Lothian reach out to a lawyer in the UK, and provided a recommendation. Status Unfortunately, that referral did not pan out, Lothian said. He has not given up entirely, but he has taken down the GitHub repository to comply with Synaptics's demands. For now, he may continue working on some of the components that are not affected by the patent claims, but the work on Vino will not be submitted to the kernel. " Vino itself has to remain local until this is sorted out, I just can't afford to defend myself against Synaptics. " Perhaps amusingly, Lothian told me that someone from Synaptics finally replied to the pull request on October 7. Lothian told me he does not intend to follow up on the comments: " You can't threaten to sue me and then say 'can you update your pull request?' " For the time being, Synaptics has succeeded in shutting down an effort to improve the way DisplayLink docks work with Linux. It is an unpleasant reminder that, while much of the current conversations in open-source communities are concerned with LLM-driven development, software patents still pose problems for free-software developers and users. to post comments Surely there is plenty of very old prior art on these? The lawyer is just saber rattling. synaptics doesnt understand what patents are Posted Nov 12, 2026 3:04 UTC (Thu) by felixfix (subscriber, #242) [ Link ] You're both right: patents are supposed to describe something so clearly that it can be reproduced, but then it is illegal to do so. Pretty bizarre, to my mind. I despise intellectual property for other reasons, but I once worked up an alternate patent system which seemed fairer and might actually encourage its alleged justifications. From memory ... A patent includes: 1. The recipe to reproduce the object. 2. The royalty schedule. 3. A time limit. This can end in two ways: If no one reproduces the object within the time limit, the patent fails. If someone reproduces the object, the interval from patent to reproduction establishes the patent length. The incentives work out correctly: Inventors want as long a time limit as possible to get a longer patent. Inventors want as complex a patent as possible to prevent copycats. But if it's too complex and no one reproduces it, they have no patent. Copycats want to reproduce as soon as possible to get a shorter patent. Copycats may decide to reproduce it internally but not sell it, thus being ready to start selling the instant the time limit expires. There has to be some maximum time limit; otherwise inventors would choose 100 years. The multiplier from copycat time to patent length can be by legislative policy or vary per patent. (This is from memory. I may have forgotten some subtle aspects.) I believe this to be true, but get actual advice or read the statute and come to your own conclusions. In the USA, patent infringement is covered under USC 271. There are several ways to infringe. Writing open source software isn't one of them: 271(a), direct infringement: Doesn't apply because you're not "making" or "selling" the entire invention. Are you "using" the invention? Well, I don't know: did you just write the code, or did you also run it in an infringing manner? And, if you did just write the code, if you're purely a hobbyist, the "experimental use" defense should cover you. If you do somehow lose on the experimental use exception, and they can prove it's willful, then oh God no! Treble damages! But you know how much treble damages would be for a single unit of a shit product like DisplayLink? Something like $0.60. So you'd probably be able to get the lawsuit thrown out of court based on the de minimis doctrine before it even got to trial. 271(b), inducement: Lots of ways this fails for the plaintiff. One way is that you have to actually talk to the person you're inducing to infringe. So, throw the code over the wall, talk only to other developers and not users, and you're good. 271(c), contributory: You have to sell or offer to sell it. You're not selling anything: you're giving your code away for free. Case closed. 2771(f), extraterritorial: There's a very nice case, Microsoft v. AT&T, where the facts were that Microsoft mailed a copy of Windows to a customer, on a CD or DVD or something like that, and AT&T said, "waaaah, Windoze is a component that infringes our patuntz, so you owe us under 271(f)!" and Microsoft said, "LOL GTFO luzer! Software's intangible and can't be a component of a patented invention!" The Supreme Court agreed with Microsoft. So, yeah, someone in the US should be good to pick up the torch here. body_text: Introducing Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 \ Anthropic Skip to main content News Research Policy Commitments Company Try Claude Introduction Performance and efficiency Coding Cybersecurity Science and engineering Safety and alignment Data privacy Availability November 9, 2026 Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 [1] Introduction [2] Performance and efficiency [3] Science and engineering [4] Safety and alignment [5] Availability We’ve upgraded Claude Fable and Claude Mythos—models that are designed to tackle the most daunting technical challenges. Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision. During prerelease testing they’ve helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours—among many other applications we’ll discuss below. Claude Fable and Claude Mythos are the same underlying model. Fable has strong cybersecurity and biology safeguards to guard against misuse, which allows us to make it available to all users. Organizations pursuing beneficial applications in cybersecurity or biomedical research can apply for access to Mythos through our recently expanded Life Sciences and Cyber Verification Programs. Testers have found that Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 communicate more clearly than past Fable and Mythos models. They generate outputs up to 30% faster than Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, and they’re available at a lower price: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 also come with an optional fast mode, which speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times. Fast mode is available for $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens. Safety and alignment. To help ensure safety and alignment keep step with growing model capabilities, we ran extensive prerelease safety testing on the model that underlies Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. This included developing novel evaluations that give deeper insight into specific concerning behaviors like sandbox escapes. We believe high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low, and the model performed as well as, or better than, our recent models on most alignment measures. Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards are as robust as those of Fable 5.1 but produce fewer unnecessary blocks, and we have implemented our strongest-ever protections against distillation attacks. We describe more about our safety testing below, and full details can be found in the Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card . When to use Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. Fable and Mythos are best for the most ambitious, open-ended technical work. For most coding and knowledge tasks, we recommend that users start with Claude Opus 5.5, our strongest daily driver, and then switch to a different model as required, depending on the scope and complexity of their work—upward to Fable or Mythos, or downward to Claude Sonnet 5.5 or Claude Haiku 5.5. Fable 5.2 can also play the role of Advisor (where Haiku, Sonnet, or Opus models consult it to help solve harder problems) or Orchestrator (where it delegates simpler tasks to smaller models).
