Coding Over 90% of the changes merged into Anthropic’s core codebase are now written by Claude (with human guidance). We’ve used Fable 5.2 to fix stubborn bugs in minutes, optimize performance across all of our services, and complete high-value software projects that would otherwise have been too slow or too costly to attempt. A team of agents running an earlier version of Fable 5.2 migrated a critical production service from Python to Rust—the service is now more efficient, more reliable, and starts about 26 times faster. We’ve found that Fable 5.2 exercises strong engineering judgment and can produce high-quality results from even ambiguous requests. As an experiment, one Anthropic engineer gave Fable 5.2 the task of designing a prototype operating system. Starting from an empty folder, the model coordinated over 1,000 subagents, working around the clock for eight days writing, testing, and reviewing code. It produced a working operating system that boots on a laptop, with its own core that runs the machine, drivers for the disk, keyboard, and network, permanent file storage, windows, a login screen, an installer, and built-in Claude functionality (see the video below). Early testers have been impressed at how successfully Fable 5.2’s coding skills can be applied to a wide range of tasks: Vercel Shopify Datadog Unity Uber Oracle iGent Snowflake Cognition Vercel Shopify Datadog Unity Uber Oracle iGent Snowflake Cognition Quote “The model is in my head. It understands the intent behind every prompt I’ve given it. I haven’t had to say ‘No, I meant…’ a single time. Projects we’ve been pushing along with other models for weeks got finished and approved by our teammates in a few days with Claude Fable 5.2, and the humans reviewing its code had less to say.” Company Vercel Author Joe Haddad, Member of Technical Staff Quote “Claude Fable 5.2 is great for taking a loose idea and refining it. Its answers are really well-considered, and within a few turns I can almost always say ‘ok, go do that,’ and trust that it’ll complete it with little intervention. It feels like working with another staff-level engineer.” Company Shopify Author Tom Pritchard, Staff Engineer Quote “You can just throw Claude Fable 5.2 at new, ambiguous systems it has never seen before, and it will figure out how to actually work within them. It’s almost like an incident commander that can send out faster models to get quick signals and coordinate, which removes that burden from me as an operator.” Company Datadog Author Matt Lee, Senior Staff Engineer Quote “Claude Fable 5.2 can complete tasks that previous models struggled with. The clearest examples so far are building higher-quality 3D scenes from scratch and rebuilding an experience from a visual reference. It’s very strong on the harder game-dev tasks, where it keeps iterating and improving instead of getting stuck.” Company Unity Author Sam Zhang, Creative Technologist Quote “I had Claude Fable 5.2 run a 10–12 hour security audit. It sent out about 170 reviewer agents and came back with a write-up, fix pull requests and a policy proposal. It works until the job is actually complete instead of stopping at a plausible checkpoint. Its self-correction and honesty about gaps impressed me. At High effort, I’d use this over what I run today for long unattended audits and doc-heavy work.” Company Uber Author Andrew Mager, Staff Engineer, Agentic Systems Quote “In one test combining country debt summaries, repayment history, and regional benchmarks, Claude Fable 5.2 generated SQL that returned the expected results. The SQL generated by two other models also ran successfully, but incorrectly summed country-level summary amounts, producing values 5–8x the expected amounts. Getting these business calculations right is why we see value in using Fable 5.2 for enterprise SQL generation.” Company Oracle Author Liyu Gong, Senior Manager of Machine Learning Quote “In a single session, Claude Fable 5.2 built a hypervisor, the software that walls off virtual computers sharing one machine. Its core is mathematically proven to keep them apart. More than 3,500 machine-checked proofs cover every case, not just the ones you test. It’s the first model I’ve seen break a problem this large into pieces it can prove, fit them together, and keep taking on more ambitious work. A very clear upgrade from Fable 5.1.” Company iGent Author Sean Ward, Co-Founder and CEO Quote “Claude Fable 5.2 is the strongest model we have measured on data-eng-bench, our open-source benchmark of 103 data-engineering tasks. It solved tasks consistently across repeated runs and passed every interactive coding task we gave it.” Company Snowflake Author Bala Kasiviswanathan, VP of AI and Developer Experience Quote “Claude Fable 5.2 says it doesn’t know things instead of hallucinating. At one point it told me its last estimate was wrong and that it wouldn’t give a number until it had measured the change. Very impressive!” Company Cognition Author Adhyyan Sekhsaria, Member of Technical Staff Cybersecurity Claude Mythos 5.2 is our most capable model for cybersecurity engineering. It catches more vulnerabilities than our previous models, and is better at reproducing and fixing them (note that Claude Fable 5.2’s safeguards will block most cybersecurity-related tasks). A security company found that one in six confirmed bugs found by Claude Mythos 5.2 were missed by all of the other frontier models they tested. On our internal evaluation, CVE Rediscovery,¹ Claude Mythos 5.2 found 10.2% more vulnerabilities than Claude Opus 5.5 and 14.4% more than Claude Mythos 5.1. Claude Mythos 5.2 also shows better judgment and calibration—one tester found that previous models had overstated the seriousness of about 1 in 20 findings, whereas Claude Mythos 5.2 hadn’t overstated any.² CVE Rediscovery Accuracy vs. cost Mythos 5.2 Opus 5.5 Mythos 5.1 55 60 65 70 75 80 85 90 95 0 Advisories found (%) 0.10 0.20 0.50 1 2 5 10 Cost per attempt (USD, log scale) Low Med High Xhigh Max CVE Rediscovery is an internal cybersecurity evaluation that assesses how many published CVEs (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) a model can independently find when given a snapshot of the project before a CVE was fixed. Our October 2026 run against 1,829 CVEs showed Claude Mythos 5.2 outperformed Claude Mythos 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 at every effort level. Claude Mythos 5.2’s cyber capabilities are accessible through our Cyber Verification Program , which we’re continuing to expand and improve. Claude Enterprise customers (even if they aren’t members of the Cyber Verification Program) can access Claude Security , which scans codebases for vulnerabilities using our most capable models—which now includes Claude Mythos 5.2. A recent update to Claude Security helps it watch repositories as code is updated, track any findings to ensure they’re fixed, learn from additional context, and connect to a user’s tools through an API and MCP. Rubrik Mozilla Rubrik Mozilla Quote “We have worked closely with Anthropic’s new model, Claude Mythos 5.2, to do a next round of high-fidelity threat discovery and elimination within our own systems for potential issues we did not uncover with earlier Mythos models. The output is more readable and empowered our team to spot-check faster and more easily. We built our Code Guardian harness with Mythos 5.1, and we’d switch to Mythos 5.2 to give our customers more powerful cyber capabilities.” Company Rubrik Author Arvind Nithrakashyap, Co-Founder and Chief Technology Officer Quote “Claude Mythos 5.2 is astonishingly good. We’ve worked closely with the Anthropic team all year to harden Firefox with successive generations of Claude models, and each round has left fewer, subtler bugs to find. Even so, Mythos 5.2 roughly doubled the vulnerability discovery metrics of Mythos 5.1 across respective scanning campaigns.” Company Mozilla Author Brian Grinstead, Distinguished Engineer Science and engineering Important tasks in science, engineering, and mathematics increasingly depend on coding: analyzing data, modeling molecules, designing parts, and controlling instruments are all done through software. Below, we discuss how Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 have helped researchers make progress on difficult problems in these areas. Theoretical physics Claude Fable 5.2 solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes, and the effort to unite the two linchpin theories of modern physics, relativity, and quantum mechanics. Both of Claude’s results rely on holographic duality, the idea that certain universes containing gravity can be precisely described by a quantum theory containing no gravity at all. In the first problem, physicists in 1983 had shown that as these universes heat up, black holes form abruptly, like water boiling; but their method worked only in large universes that were big enough for relativity to apply. A calculation to determine whether the same was true in very small universes, where only the quantum description can be used, was laid out in 2003 but was too laborious to complete. Fable 5.2, working largely autonomously, completed it and found the transition is abrupt there, too. In the second problem, Fable 5.2 found the exact limit of a technique physicists have used for more than 15 years to rule out candidate theories of quantum gravity in a simplified universe. Read more about these results in their respective preprints, here and here . Protein folding Adeno-associated viruses are small, harmless viruses whose protein shell, the capsid , can be used to deliver gene therapies. The protein structure of the capsid is important—for example, it affects whether the therapy will be blocked by a patient’s immune system—but it’s also highly complex. Existing protein-folding models like AlphaFold can predict individual proteins, but a capsid is built from dozens of them. Building on two open-source protein-folding models, Claude Mythos 5.2 found a novel way to accurately predict a whole capsid’s structure. It wrote code that ran these models on overlapping groups of protein chains, and used the information on the known symmetries of the capsid to merge them together. Claude’s method worked across several capsids, both natural and engineered (in our tests, it accurately modeled 28 of the 34 it attempted).³ Three computational biologists shared the following reflections on how Claude’s skills could be used to speed up their research into gene therapies: Dyno Therapeutics Columbia University Biohub Dyno Therapeutics Columbia University Biohub Quote “This acceleration could save meaningful time and cost from our capsid folding pipeline, enabling us to deploy compute more efficiently across many capsid properties that are needed for a genetic medicine. We are excited to help Anthropic push the reasoning capabilities further to reduce the cost of designing capsids overall.” Company Dyno Therapeutics Author Sam Sinai, Cofounder and Head of AI Quote “Large protein assemblies, including capsids, remain an open problem for protein modeling, due to the complexity of accurately predicting and positioning the structures of dozens of individual macromolecules, not to mention the inordinately high computational costs involved. Claude’s approach cleverly tackles this problem for symmetric assemblies, making it possible for individual scientists to model systems on personal workstations that would otherwise require dedicated clusters.” Company Columbia University Author Mohammed AlQuraishi, Assistant Professor of Systems Biology and Computer Science Quote “Biohub’s goal in open-sourcing ESMFold2 was to enable the scientific community to build on the biology it has learned. We are excited to see Claude prototype a new sampling procedure that enables predictions of large, symmetric complexes such as AAV capsids—a protein used to deliver gene therapies. We will continue to incorporate such contributions from the community that extend our tools to important application domains.” Company Biohub Author Zeming Lin, Principal Research Scientist Mathematics Mathematical formalization. Formalization is the process of translating a mathematical proof into a language that a computer can check step by step. It can help human mathematicians gain confidence in results without having to check them by hand (this matters even more when AI models generate results that are hard for humans to verify). Because formalization is such a laborious process, if AI could assist with it, mathematicians could spend more time exploring novel ideas. Our first formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem , performed by an unreleased research version of Claude, took 11 days. It relied on a purpose-built harness along with guidance from a human researcher. By contrast, a team of 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents fully formalized the theorem in just 30 hours, with minimal human intervention. Fable 5.2 started from minimal prompts, and built its own ways to coordinate.⁴ It needed one-third as many action tokens as our first formalization and produced a proof seven times shorter. As can be seen in the figure below, Opus 5.5 (with the same 1,000-agent setup) completed only 26% of the formalization in 18 hours, and barely made any more progress after 30. Read more about the formalization here . Fermat’s Last Theorem proof formalization Completion over time Fable 5.2 Opus 5.5 0 0.2 0.4 0.6 0.8 1 Completion (0–1, weighted share of statements proved) 0 6 12 18 24 30 Time elapsed (hours) Resumed with 12 more hours 0.86 1.00 0.26 0.27 Formalizing the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in the mathematical programming language Lean. Each line shows the proportion of the full formalization that Fable 5.2 (green line) and Opus 5.5 (orange line) had completed over 30 hours with about 1,000 agents, and a single run per model. At the dashed line (18 hours), both teams resumed from their last save with 12 more hours. Hardware and robotics Many of AI’s potential benefits—for example, in speeding up laboratory research—depend on it being able to act in the physical world. Claude Fable 5.2 continues our models’ trend of increasing usefulness in the real world , showing promising results on tasks such as designing hardware devices and substantial advances in controlling physical robots. Hardware engineering. We tested Fable 5.2’s skills in hardware engineering, asking it in a one-paragraph prompt to design and produce three working electronic devices with their own circuit boards, 3D-printed enclosures, and software. The devices, shown below, were a home voice-assistant hub, a USB speakerphone, and a handheld virtual pet. We collaborated on this project with Diode , a company that designs and manufactures circuit boards. Claude wrote its own specifications, selected available electronic components from US distributors, routed each device’s four-layer circuit board, modeled the enclosures with computer-aided design, and programmed the devices’ software. Each board was ready for manufacturing in under a day, with minimal human input. Once Diode had built the boards, Claude guided the company’s engineers through the testing and assembly of the devices. All three devices worked without needing any electrical modifications. Read more about Claude’s hardware engineering skills here . Robotics. Compared with earlier Claude models, Fable 5.2 shows substantially improved skills in controlling physical robots—even for robotics tasks on which it has never explicitly been trained. The video below shows robots controlled by Fable 5.2 completing a variety of tasks, including solving a puzzle cube, unscrewing a bottle cap, and drawing a picture of a robot. On the public RoboDojo benchmark, which tests how AIs can control a simulated two-arm robot from camera images, Fable 5.2 outperformed other frontier models that were run on the same harness, as well as most AI systems built specifically to control robots. RoboDojo (average) Max score by model Gemini 4 Argon GPT-6 Astra Fable 5.1 Opus 5.5 Fable 5.2 0 10 20 30 40 50 60 70 Average success rate (%) Gemini 4 Argon (our run; High effort) GPT-6 Astra (our run; Max effort) Fable 5.1 (Max effort) Opus 5.5 (Max effort) Fable 5.2 (Max effort) 34.2 29.8 27.6 39.4 64.9 RoboDojo Sim tests control of a simulated two-arm robot. Scores are based on our internal runs for each model using the highest available effort level. At Max effort, Fable 5.2 scores 64.9%, more than double GPT-6 Astra (29.8%) and Fable 5.1 (27.6%). Research and analysis Early testers using Claude Fable 5.2 for research and analysis tasks found that it can handle more ambiguous, data-heavy tasks than previous models and has better judgment on ambiguous tasks—particularly those that require abstract reasoning and design. Proprietary trading firm Jump Trading tested Fable 5.2 on proxy evaluations that resemble some of its quantitative research tasks, embedding it in a harness similar to the one the firm uses for its own research. In one run, Fable 5.2 effectively played all the necessary roles: code-writer, coordinator, planner, and job-submitter. Previous models had required substantial investments of time to manually rebalance roles to accommodate different models’ strengths and weaknesses. Other testers from research and analysis organizations sent us the following statements on their experiences with Fable 5.2: Jump Trading Balyasny Asset Management Discovered Materials IMC Harvey Fundamental Research Labs XTX Markets Box Jump Trading Balyasny Asset Management Discovered Materials IMC Harvey Fundamental Research Labs XTX Markets Box Quote “Claude Fable 5.2 is incredible at playing every major role within a research system: defining questions, interpreting, coordinating, and of course finding and implementing the key ideas. Definitely one of the strongest on taste and judgment that we’ve seen. In an internal research automation benchmark, it achieved a full 10% lower error than the next best model.” Company Jump Trading Author Lucas Baker, Head of LLM R&D Quote “In a recent evaluation, we asked Claude Fable 5.2 to investigate how one organization tested a new integration in its core technology systems. It traced the answer to the right sources and didn’t overstate what the evidence showed. It also flagged that the question’s framing could be misleading. In investment research, that restraint makes clear what remains unknown and where the market may be mispricing risk or opportunity.” Company Balyasny Asset Management Author Ashish Malik, AI Researcher Quote “Phonon calculations are one of the most expensive routine steps in computational materials science, which is why labs often skip stability checks when screening new materials. Claude Fable 5.2 made Quantum ESPRESSO’s phonon code about 36 times faster on average than stock on the same GPU, taking our 13 benchmark cases from 3.3 hours to under four minutes. That beats Fable 5.1’s speedup by 3–4 times.” Company Discovered Materials Author Akash Ramdas, Co-Founder Quote “With Fable 5.1 we saw the first glimmers of a model coming up with truly innovative research ideas. Claude Fable 5.2 continues that trend. It had the same insight we were impressed with from Fable 5.1 and then came up with a second, entirely new angle. It achieved new best scores on three of the four quant research problems we’ve finished. We’d like to use it for high-impact, long-running research tasks, or for coordinating teams of other models.” Company IMC Author Marquis Wong, Principal AI Engineer Quote “In an I-9 compliance review, Claude Fable 5.2 gave the client clearer direction than Fable 5.1. It identified the employees needing immediate attention and explained how to correct each issue and who should act. It’s an exciting improvement in the model’s ability to give practical legal guidance.” Company Harvey Author Niko Grupen, Head of AI Research Quote “On one task, Claude Fable 5.2 had to pull a company’s financials out of its 10-K into a forecasting model, and the template didn’t say whether a metric should be the reported figure or calculated. It inferred the author’s intent from the cell formatting, caught that the regional numbers didn’t sum to the reported total, and got every cell right. Better judgment calls like that are the main reason it scored 91% on our eval versus 86% for the next best model.” Company Fundamental Research Labs Author Jeffrey Liu, Member of Technical Staff Quote “In our quantitative research work, Claude Fable 5.2 delivered very strong improvements versus Fable 5.1, especially in the setup with multiple coordinating agents. Its maths research capabilities represent another meaningful advance, too.” Company XTX Markets Author Alex Gerko, Founder and CEO Quote “Before putting AI to work across workflows, you need to trust its approach and conclusions. In our testing, Claude Fable 5.2 identified inconsistencies, drew on context across entire document sets, and adjusted recommendations based on relevant evidence. For example, when reviewing files attached to a loan application, it flagged that the salary deposits and the bank statement’s balance didn’t match, so the underwriter could focus on what to check.” Company Box Author Yashodha Bhavnani, VP of AI Products Safety and alignment No single test can tell us how a highly capable model will behave once it’s deployed, so we rely on many different tests and many different types of evidence before release. For the model underlying Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, our predeployment safety work included alignment training and testing, newly designed evaluations on the model’s propensity to take unhelpful actions, building stronger safeguards against misuse, and scaling up our behavioral monitoring. The model was also tested before release by external evaluators, including the UK AI Security Institute , Frontier Design , and METR . See the Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card for a summary of their reports⁵ and for a full description of our own safety and capabilities testing. Alignment testing We ran a suite of evaluations for how well-aligned Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 are in behavioral terms, testing how often they behave in unintended and potentially unsafe ways. Weighing everything we’ve seen across a range of evaluations, we’ve assessed the risk of these models behaving in unsafe ways in high-stakes situations to be low (as with our other recent models). We tested Claude Mythos 5.2 (the same underlying model as Fable 5.2 without certain cybersecurity or biology safeguards), on our automated behavioral audit, which tests how a model behaves across approximately 1,900 scenarios. Claude Mythos 5.2 performed as well as, or better than, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Mythos 5.1 on most measures. For example, it scored better than all three on most measures that involve misleading users. Hallucinating inputs, falsely claiming to have completed a task, omitting important information, and failing to disclose bad or lazy work were all lower in Claude Mythos 5.2.⁶ Automated behavioral audit Overall misaligned behavior score Mythos 5.1 Opus 5.5 Sonnet 5.5 Mythos 5.2 0 0.5 1 1.5 2 2.5 3 3.5 4 Score (1–10, lower is better) Mythos 5.1 Opus 5.5 Sonnet 5.5 Mythos 5.2 3.28 2.79 3.10 2.67 Overall score from our automated behavioral audit, a composite of many undesirable behaviors including cooperation with human misuse and autonomous actions across a range of scenarios. Lower scores are better. See Section 6.4.1 of the Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 System Card for full details. We paid particular attention during our testing to behaviors that contributed to recent notable cybersecurity and alignment incidents. For example, we found that Claude Mythos 5.2 has a lower propensity than Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Mythos 5.1 to engage in biased or motivated reasoning (such reasoning might mean it “explains away” evidence that it isn’t in a simulation and thus takes actions without a realistic understanding of the consequences). We ran multiple different evaluations to test the model’s tendency to attempt escaping its sandbox. In two evaluations we’d used previously, Claude Mythos 5.2 made substantially fewer attempts at sandbox escape than any other model we’ve tested. In a dedicated evaluation—an adversarial experiment including over 1,800 scenarios, most of which could not be solved without escaping a sandbox, and where the sandbox has a deliberate weakness—Claude Mythos 5.2 made use of credentials or files that we had placed outside its sandbox in 3.1% of scenarios, about as often as Opus 5.5 (3.3%), less often than Sonnet 5.5 (5.1%), and well below previous iterations of Claude Mythos (5 and 5.1, which scored 39% and 21%, respectively). We found that other techniques, such as describing the sandbox and adding tools to report weaknesses, reduced Claude Mythos 5.2’s escape attempts even further. On other measures—one, for example, involving taking harmful actions after erroneously concluding it was in a simulation—Claude Mythos 5.2 scored slightly worse than Opus 5.5, and about level with Claude Mythos 5.1. The problem of building evaluations that reliably catch every failure before a model is deployed remains unsolved. The complexities of evaluating highly capable models often muddy the picture—for example, Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow. That is why we do not rely on these evaluations alone to provide a holistic picture of safety: we draw on monitoring during training, reviews of transcripts from internal use, testing by external evaluators, and interpretability techniques for examining what is happening inside the model. We are also working to make our evaluations more realistic and to better understand what they miss. Safeguards Cybersecurity and biology safeguards. Consistent with previous Claude Fable models, Fable 5.2 comes with safety classifiers that block high-risk cyber activities, including penetration testing, exploit generation, and binary-based vulnerability, as well as most tasks in research biology. When a query is blocked, users will instead receive a response from Opus 4.8 for cybersecurity and Opus 5 for biology. Since the release of Claude Fable 5.1, we have continued to reduce false positives for our safety classifiers. Based on early testing across claude.ai, Claude Code, and Cowork, we observed about 55% fewer blocks with Fable 5.2 compared with Fable 5.1—about 60% fewer in cybersecurity and 40% fewer in biology. Claude Mythos 5.2 is available to vetted organizations that work in these dual-use areas. AI research and development. The model that underlies Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 is a step forward in general capabilities. However, during the model’s training, we took steps to limit advances in the specific research capabilities that could most directly accelerate AI development. Thus, in relevant areas, including accelerator kernel optimization and improving large language model architectures, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 perform at about the level of Opus 5.5. Importantly, we ensured that the training changes did not affect related capabilities like agentic coding, hardware development, and traditional AI or machine learning research (including interpretability research). We do not alter these capabilities as the model is being served to users (that is, at inference time). As described in Section 1.5 of the System Card and similarly to previous models, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 also include transparent fallbacks to Opus 5 for a small set of topics in this domain, including kernel development on certain nonstandard accelerators. Anti-distillation. Distillation, where a model is trained on the outputs of a more advanced one to extract the advanced model’s capabilities, occurs illicitly on an industrial scale, often involving thousands of fake Claude accounts. Since distillation allows for advanced capabilities to be released without the safeguards we’ve built into Claude, it creates safety and national security risks (see our September 2026 threat intelligence report for details on illicit distillation activity we’ve detected and disrupted so far). Fable 5.2 has the strongest protections against distillation of any model we’ve released; it uses the techniques we described in a recent report , which have reduced the data harvested by distillers by 90% to 99%. We are also expanding the rollout of an API feature that helps guard against illicit distillation: preserved thinking now applies to all accounts. Preserved thinking prevents distillers from editing Claude’s prior context in an attempt to extract its reasoning (developers can refer to our preserved thinking docs to learn how to update integrations with new API features). Data privacy and Enterprise Frontier Safeguards Some more complex forms of AI model misuse can be detected only when observing patterns across multiple requests. For this reason, powerful models like Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 rely on safeguards that monitor a window of usage data (as opposed to individual responses). With Enterprise Frontier Safeguards , automated safety monitoring is run on prompts and responses that are stored in a customer’s infrastructure, making it compatible with zero data retention (ZDR). Enterprise Frontier Safeguards is now in private beta with customers like Bridgewater, Salesforce, and Stripe. Enterprise customers can request access to Enterprise Frontier Safeguards by contacting their account team or by completing this form . Eligible customers can continue using Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 with zero data retention before implementing safety monitoring with EFS. For other customers, we have 30-day retention for safety monitoring. Availability Claude Fable 5.2 is available today on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Developers can get started with claude-fable-5-2 on the Claude Platform. This week, we’re giving subscribers on eligible paid plans extra Fable usage. Plans and seats that include Fable models get one to three Fable resets based on how long they’ve subscribed, and Fable is included for up to 50% of weekly usage limits for Pro plans and standard seats on the Team plan. Learn more about the Fable 5.2 launch promotion here . Cybersecurity professionals can apply for access to Claude Mythos 5.2 through the Cyber Verification Program . Claude Enterprise customers can also use Claude Security , powered by our full family of models, including Claude Mythos 5.2. Life sciences researchers can also apply for access through the Life Sciences Verification Program . Fast mode for Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 is available on Claude Code, the Claude Platform, Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed and Google managed), and Microsoft Foundry (Anthropic hosted). Note that access to Claude Mythos fast mode is available only to organizations who are part of our Verification Programs. Edit 11 November: Amended a sentence and added a footnote to the “Mathematical formalization” subsection to more accurately describe the information we provided to the model. Footnotes 1 CVE refers to Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures , a system that enumerates software vulnerabilities. 2 The counts are raw findings from one tester’s audit, although testers consistently found that Claude Mythos 5.2 identified more vulnerabilities than earlier models. On our own evaluations, vulnerability identification is roughly on par with Opus 5.5 (see the system card ). 3 Earlier work on modeling AAV capsids and other large symmetric protein systems includes FoldaVirus , EvoDOCK and its symmetric extension , SymProFold , CapBuild , MoLPC , CombFold , Uni-Fold Symmetry , Apodex Discovery , and the “big bang” initialization (the last of which was referenced in the prompt we gave to Claude Mythos 5.2). These methods typically assemble the full structure from separately predicted chains or small groups of chains. Claude was permitted to use known symmetries but was instructed not to rely on assembly. Note that accuracy is measured by comparing Cα RMSD with the experimental structure: 1.2 Å for OpenFold3-preview2 and 1.4 Å for ESMFold2 on AAV2 ( PDB:1LP3 ). A capsid counts as accurately modeled if either model came within 3 Å. For AAV2, Claude’s method required about 58 minutes of inference on one NVIDIA H200 GPU for OpenFold3-preview2 and about seven minutes for ESMFold2. 4 As described in our accompanying post , we “gave the agents a list of 60 statements, a one-sentence sketch of the classical route, the definitions those statements use, and 47 proved lemmas from our earlier formalization, and assigned lead and helper roles. We offered no other guidance on how to prove the theorem or organize themselves.” 5 None of the external organizations reviewed the contents of this blog post or the contents of the System Card. Those organizations do not necessarily agree with any of the claims made in either publication. 6 We ran these tests on Claude Mythos 5.2 because testing the model with reduced safeguards provides the most comprehensive look at model behavior. We expect Fable 5.2 to behave similarly; in some cases, more potential pathways for misuse should be blocked given its stronger safeguards. Introducing AlphaProof Code: a breakthrough in verifying complex software at depth Pushmeet Kohli and Swarat Chaudhuri Read the technical paper Share Copied How Google DeepMind researchers built a new agentic framework that formally verified the code of Signalâs cryptographic protocol â long considered to be a grand security challenge Today, weâre sharing a milestone in software security long considered to be a grand challenge: Google DeepMind researchers guided AI agents to mathematically prove key security properties of the actual code underlying the Signal protocol, the technology that protects billions of private conversations in apps like Signal and Google Messages. This breakthrough discovery was made using AlphaProof Code , a novel agentic framework for formal verification at unprecedented depth that combines human expertise with AI agents. Formal verificationâmathematically proving code runs correctly without flawsâis the highest standard of security assurance; however, it is difficult and often labor-intensive. Our work marks the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth. It's also the first time the implementation of a widely deployed protocol like this has been formally verified by any method, with or without AI. How we verified Signal AlphaProof Code is a multi-LLM agentic framework that splits the work of formal verification the way a research team would: human experts work with AI to decide what to prove, and a group of AI agents does it. First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signalâs security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code. Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human â just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most. Cryptographic protocols underpin nearly all digital communication, from online banking to web browsing, and a single flaw can expose millions of people at once. That's why experts have spent decades formally analyzing them. But most protocol verification stops at the design level. Our agents went further, proving that the compiled code fulfills the key security properties â such as keeping messages protected before and after a device is temporarily compromised â down to the exact code running on devices. Because real-world vulnerabilities often hide in the gap between design and implementation, bridging this gap makes these proofs vastly more complex. Even at this complexity, our verification process took just four weeks â a task that historically takes expert teams years â proving that Signal's core cryptographic code delivers the security protections our experts specified. To confirm that AlphaProof Code can tell correct code from buggy code, we reintroduced two real, previously fixed bugs into an isolated version of Signal's code. In both cases, the system produced a machine-checked proof that the buggy version was insecure. In AlphaProof Code, AI agents help users write a specification, then autonomously prove that the implementation meets it. Every proof is checked by Lean to verify the agents' work. While prior formal verification focused on smaller portions of the code, Google DeepMind's approach enables significant expansion,â said Ehren Kret, Chief Technology Officer of Signal. âUsing AI agents to translate live code into valid Lean theorems is a major breakthrough. As AI-driven security threats grow, rigorously verifying the Signal protocol implementation gives us even greater confidence in our code's privacy guarantees. Ehren Kret Chief Technology Officer of Signal While prior formal verification work has necessarily focused on smaller scopes, this new approach enables a significant expansion. Traditionally, verifying that production code strictly matches its cryptographic design required extensive manual effort, making the use of AI agents to automatically translate live code into valid Lean theorems a great breakthrough. As AI-driven security threats grow, having the core Signal protocol rigorously verified with automated theorem proving gives us even greater confidence that our code delivers on its privacy guarantees. The future of security Achieving this long-standing challenge demonstrates how AI can bring elite security assurance to businesses, governments, and critical infrastructure, helping defend against agent-driven cyber threats. Verifying Signal's core cryptography lays the groundwork to secure other vital systems, from medical device firmware to power grid software. Scaling these techniques requires continued research. Paired with automated defense agents like CodeMender , formal verification can help counter the speed and scale of modern cyber threats to create software with mathematical proof that its protections work. We are open-sourcing our formal verification artifacts for community use. Read the technical paper below. Read the technical paper Acknowledgements This research was developed by Swarat Chaudhuri, Andrew Ferraiuolo, Anton Kovsharov, Tej Chajed, Sam Schlesinger, Karn Seth, Jonathan Katz, Charles Sutton, and Pushmeet Kohli. We thank Eric Wieser for help with open-sourcing our code, Owen Jones for program management support, and MartÃ­n Abadi, Christopher Henson, Katerina Hristova, Henryk Michalewski, Jonathan Protzenko and George Tsoukalas for helpful discussions. We thank Signal's Rolfe Schmidt, Michael Rosenberg, and Ehren Kret for their feedback on our methodology. We also thank Tulsee Doshi, Four Flynn, Kate Olszewska, Alicia Huang, Andy Liu, Benoit Schillings, Raluca Ada Popa, Melvin Johnson, Koray Kavukcuoglu, Demis Hassabis, and Sundar Pichai for their support of the project. Carr Onstott , Mehul Jaiswal , Strands Agents Team For a while, Amazon and AWS teams relied on Claude Sonnet 4.6 to label tickets in an internal system without breaking the bank. Sonnet 4.6 fit the goldilocks choice of balancing intelligence with cost. Considering it dealt with one of the world’s largest internal ticketing systems, the nine month old model did well. However, two Amazon engineers recently swapped out Sonnet 4.6 for Strands Decider , a decision model we launched a month ago, that performed just as well at 98% less cost . This change will save millions of dollars of token costs in a year. Carr and Mehul, who work on the internal ticketing system, walk through how this happened below. Replacing an LLM’s job with a decision model We had Sonnet 4.6 labeling tickets at enormous scale. The tickets could be customer escalations, capacity requests, automated alarms, security findings, or anything else across the company that needed to fit within 20 category types. The agent ran with a long system prompt on every ticket, generating JSON and reasoning against a fixed set of labels. A decision model can’t generate text. It’s first given some state and a question with a set of options, then the decision model returns a probability for each option plus a confidence score. We saw this method fit perfectly with ticket labeling: the state is the ticket, the options are the label catalog. We started with the original Strands Decider 2B . On a test set of tickets, the E4B Gemma 4 build got clearly better results, so we switched to it. Afterwards, we tuned how confident the model needed to be before applying a label. The results showed E4B beating production Sonnet on a separate set of our tickets. We ran E4B on SageMaker ml.g5.xlarge instances (one A10G, 24 GB each). The model used about 19 GiB, and one request took about 640 ms on one instance. The endpoint autoscales with traffic, but its network was isolated, preventing outbound access to the container. SageMaker copies the model weights in from S3 before start-up. Customers can do this too! Apart from our ticketing APIs, everything in the path is a standard AWS service. Ticket events land in an SQS queue that then triggers a Lambda function. It reads the ticket data and calls the model, a SageMaker AI Endpoint with Strands Decider. AppConfig holds the switch (described below), and CloudWatch carries the logs, metrics and alarms. The stack is defined in CDK with deployment stages for Beta, Gamma, and Prod. Running Sonnet 4.6 and Strands Decider on the same tickets We didn’t want to flip a switch and hope. The labeling Lambda reads a three-way setting from AWS AppConfig on every message: BEDROCK : Sonnet labels every ticket, but Strands Decider isn’t called. DUAL : Both the Sonnet and Strands Decider models are called in parallel. The results from the Sonnet model are applied to the ticket and compared with Strands Decider results. DECIDER : Strands Decider labels every ticket and Bedrock isn’t called. What we measured Claude Sonnet 4.6 Strands Decider E4B % Improvement Average time per call 4,215 ms 897 ms 78% Input tokens per ticket 6,554 2,009 Output tokens per ticket 170 1 Total tokens, per ticket 6,724 2,010 70% The token drop had two sources. Strands Decider produced one output, the choice, instead of a JSON answer. Its prompt was also much shorter than Sonnet 4.6’s. Production’s label descriptions alone are longer than Strands Decider’s 4,096-token window, so we rewrote each of the 20 labels as a one- or two-sentence criterion and sent them as the options of a single choice question, plus a “none” option. The ticket data is the same as what Sonnet gets, except that on long tickets Strands Decider drops the oldest comments to fit. Below is a graph of our Lambda durations on the day we turned off the Sonnet usage, showing the average Lambda execution duration dropping 74%. What it costs At published us-east-1 on-demand prices: Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Bedrock, global endpoint) Strands Decider E4B (SageMaker, ml.g5.xlarge ) Price $3.00 per 1M input, $15.00 per 1M output tokens $1.408 per instance-hour Per ticket $0.0222 about $0.0005 Per million tickets about $22,200 about $500 Sonnet’s cost per ticket comes straight from the token counts above. Strands Decider’s depends on how busy each instance is. At about 640 ms per request, one instance can handle about 5,600 tickets an hour, which would be $250 per million tickets at full use. We keep headroom for bursts, and in practice it comes to about $500 per million. That is about 44 times cheaper than Sonnet, a 98% reduction. These are published list prices. They leave out the Lambda, which also runs for less time per ticket now. One thing that surprised us was that JSON key order changed the answer. Sending the same content with keys in a different order moved the output probabilities by up to 0.19. We now send every request with sorted keys, so if you serve a decision model behind an API, check this before you compare runs. Our lessons This worked because the task is a closed choice from a known catalog, the volume is high, and the latency of the old path mattered. If your labels need explanation text, if the catalog changes weekly, or if you can’t fit the useful context into a few thousand tokens, a decision model probably can’t replace the LLM’s job. The part we’d copy regardless of model is the three-way switch. Running both on real traffic, then judging every disagreement, told us more than any offline eval would have. It also meant going back was a 45-second config change. The world of agents gets a lot more exciting (and less costly) with decision models. If you’re running a classification agent, try the Strands Decider repo and its serving notes . title: Your TV can see through walls (2025)
body_text: Your TV can see through walls: Navigation: Homepage      Index      Yearly archives Fun Astrophotography      (catalog) About this site Real pages Dark Light TTY Your TV can see through walls: 2025-08-02 — 2026-02-23 This is a spectogram of the signal from a local TV station: ATSC digital TV signal. (Recorded using an Ettus USRP B200) Walking between the receiver and TV station causes a slight disturbance to the signal, but it's nothing to write home about: Walking through the signal path For this capture, I moved the antenna a few centimeters: Where'd my signal go? This is selective fading : The direct signal is being canceled out by a strong reflection. Because the phase of the reflection depends on frequency, this effect is not uniform over the whole signal. Apart from being annoying if you're trying to watch TV, this state is extremely sensitive to any nearby movement. Here's what happened to the signal when I got up from my chair: ... and here's me walking around in a neighboring room: Stripes! The gaps between the stripes happen when my reflection perfectly cancels out the residual signal, which happens each time the path length changes by one wavelength. Let's use this to figure out how fast I was walking: The gap between each stripe is around 70 pixels, and the waterfall has an update rate of 150 Hz... 70 pixels * 1 second/150 pixels = 0.47 seconds = 2.1 Hz speed of light / 490 MHz * 2.1 Hz = 1.3 m/s = 4.6 km/h I was walking perpendicular to the direct signal path, so the speed can be used as is, without any adjustments for geometry. So, a simple radio reciever is able to detect motion and provide an estimated speed — and it's not just TV that works for this: any wideband radio signal like WiFi or LTE can be used in much the same way. Those make worse demonstrations because they have a messy waterfall, but it's possible extract the same data with a bit of work. Happy paranoia! Site wide RSS feed . Proudly supporting IPv6! title: AI usage generates a fragile codebase
body_text: AI usage generates a fragile codebase Evan X. Merz Programmer / Master Gardener / Doctor of Music / Curious Person AI usage generates a fragile codebase 2026-11-07,  Evan X. Merz programming , artificial intelligence , ai , llm , web programming I can only speculate as to the reasons why I was laid off from Meta in May, but I suspect that one of the reasons is that I was a little bit more resistant to adopting AI/LLMs as coding tools than some of my peers. Don't get me wrong, I generated at least 90% of my code using AI in my last few months there, which was the minimum for a decent rating. But AI didn't 10X the amount of code I was writing. It didn't even 2X it. I was focused on code quality. I saw the code being pushed by some of my peers who were heavily reliant on AI, and I saw that it was brittle code. There were many subtle issues that would lead to tech debt in the long term, and even some glaring issues were ignored by very good programmers. For instance, I saw one of the best programmers on my team try to merge code that used javascript events for mouseover CSS effects rather than using the :hover selector, which is a totally unscalable way of writing mouseovers. Now I'm employed at another large tech company and I've fully made the switch to generating 100% of my code using AI because that's the expectation today. Still, I can see lots of people becoming aware that this isn't a sustainable way to continue development of a large scale SaaS product. AI tends to solve the problems that can fit within its context window very well, but it's totally oblivious to the long term issues that can't be understood in that relatively small frame. In this post I'm going to list four ways that AI usage results in a fragile codebase that isn't resilient to the demands of highly available and highly scalable SaaS applications. By the way, every word of this article was written by a human. Even though the following image was generated by AI, this article isn't AI slop. Four ways AI makes codebases fragile Here are the four most common ways that I have seen AI generating a fragile codebase. 1. AI writes shallow tests One of the most obvious failures of modern LLMs is that they tend to write simplistic automated test cases that don't cover the things that matter to humans. Frequently I see AI agents writing lots of tests of get/set methods which are trivial and don't typically require much testing. When AI writes e2e tests, they tend to only cover the cases which are already covered in the codebase. In other words, the AI writes tests only covering one type of user, or only covering surface level interactions. This creates massive gaps in the test coverage that are invisible to developers because they aren't captured by the line level coverage metric. 2. AI writes overly complex ccode AI also tends to write overly complex code. It frequently uses two or three helper methods when a single one would suffice. It tries to follow coding guidelines, such as DRY, to a fault, without realizing that the added complexity of that rigidity makes the code more difficult for human developers to debug or understand. 3. Reliance on AI decreases human understanding And that's the third issue with AI codebases: Humans don't understand them. The longer a company relies on AI agents to generate the code, the fewer developers are going to understand the codebase. This means that developers can't do the things that are necessary to build a resilient codebase. They don't understand the data structures and algorithms well enough to see when a pull request contains a new abstraction that doesn't work with the pre-existing structures. 4. AI moves too quickly to maintain a high quality bar AI moves too quickly for human developers to maintain a high quality bar. Each pull request comes faster than the prior one and has to be reviewed in even less time. This leads to developers skimming the code and missing crucial details that result in long term tech debt. Small quality issues like testing gaps and poorly named variables accrue in the codebase until it becomes a morass of spaghetti code. Four signs that you have a fragile codebase If you're unsure whether coding agents are harming your codebase or not, then you might look for the following symptoms of a fragile, AI-generated codebase. 1. AI generated codebases have more incidents When you switched the department over to agentic coding did the number of incidents slowly start rising? At first when we were all using agents to generate massive amounts of code, it didn't seem that different from traditional coding. The PRs came and were merged and everything seemed alright. But oh, there was that one p0 that came in at the end of the month, then there were two SEVs the following month. Then even more the next month. Now, after a year or two of agentic coding, it seems like there's an incident every weekend. AI coding agents are the reason why there are more incidents impacting customers. 2. Recovery from incidents takes longer in AI codebases Not only are there more incidents, but the incidents take longer to be mitigated. The fact is that the human developers on your team now have a more shallow understanding of the codebase. If your coding agent can't find the issue that your customers are facing, then humans are going to have to dig through a codebase that is highly complex and poorly tested. They will essentially be entering unfamiliar territory, so it takes longer for them to figure out what is going wrong. Hence, companies lose more and more money to incidents that take longer to resolve. 3. AI generated codebases create errors that are only visible to users When humans don't spend time in the code, they fail to see all of the use cases. They fail to understand how actual humans are using the code because they aren't ensuring that the AI is instrumenting analytics and catching all the errors properly. Hence, invisible errors start appearing in the codebase. Errors are uncaught and only visible to real world users, as opposed to the types of users that are being tested in automated tests or in developer manual testing. 4. AI results in a poor user experience And that leads to the ultimate problem with AI codebases: they weren't made for humans. AI codebases are software made by AI for AI. They aren't being tailored to the way that human users use the product, and they aren't being tailored for the way human developers need to maintain the product. The experience degrades on both the user and the developer side, leading to a vicious cycle of enshittification. Products made for humans require a human touch The fact of the matter is that for a product to satisfy human customers, it has to be informed by a human perspective. Nobody likes ordering from machines at a restaurant. Shopping for clothes from a website always results in worse fits than shopping in person. The same is true of SaaS products. Any time you leave your SaaS product in the hands of a machine, you are losing the human touch that is valuable to your users and your developers. This may work for the cheapest products that only compete on price, but high quality software products will continue to have a human touch. The best, most expensive products will be tailored for human users by human developers. They will be charming and enjoyable to use. They won't be fragile because they won't be primarily developed by AI. About me Buy my art

It helps to steer your coding agents away from legacy patterns, and instead toward solutions that harness the power and capabilities of the modern web platform. Stewarded by the Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox, and MDN teams, alongside the web development community. Documentation · Eval Dashboard · Source Code · Report an Issue Quickstart npx modern-web-guidance@latest install This command runs an interactive wizard to install Modern Web Guidance. See Alternative Installation Methods below. Try it out (without installing) # Search for relevant guides npx modern-web-guidance@latest search " animate a dialog modal backdrop " # Retrieve a guide by ID npx modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve " animate-to-from-top-layer " # Scan a codebase for legacy patterns to modernize npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan . Why? Coding agents often default to older patterns because LLM training data contains vast amounts of legacy code. This often leads them to generate bloated JavaScript for tasks that now have native, high-performance web platform solutions. Even if a model knows an API exists, it often lacks the density of real-world, modern implementation patterns required for production-ready code. Modern Web Guidance bridges this gap. Our skill's CLI returns targeted, expert-curated guidelines directly into your agent's context window, focusing on: Modern Browser APIs : Helping models correctly structure APIs they frequently misuse. Performance & Accessibility : Preferring platform-level APIs that can be optimized by the browser and include built-in accessibility affordances. Responsible Fallbacks : Guiding models to use sensible, lightweight fallbacks instead of heavy polyfills or legacy libraries. What's Included? We cover the past several years of the web platform's new features, all the way up to the cutting edge. The guides are designed to be token-efficient ; we run evals enabling us to prune lowest-common-denominator content that models already know. Core Disciplines 🎨 User Experience Smooth visual states (View Transitions, entry/exit animations, parallax scroll, CSS scrollbar-color ). 📐 CSS Layout Modern layout systems (container queries, subgrid , modern color spaces like oklch , text-wrap tuning, and line-height trimming). ⚡ Performance Speed optimizations (instant preloading, Interaction to Next Paint (INP) diagnostics, and scheduling tasks via scheduler.yield ). 📝 Forms & UI Native components (Anchor Positioning for tooltips, Popover API, dialogs, :user-invalid validation, and auto-sizing fields). ♿ Accessibility Important considerations (screen reader and keyboard operability, content navigation and discoverability). 🤖 Built-in AI Local client models (native translation, summarization, and language detection APIs). Safe Adoption of Modern Features Progressive Enhancement & Nuanced Fallbacks : We distinguish between purely additive enhancements (like speculative preloading) which are safe to let older browsers silently ignore, and critical behaviors (like dialog controls or network beacons) where we write highly considered, low-overhead fallbacks. Responsible Fallbacks : We prioritize lightweight, case-specific custom fallbacks (<50 LOC) or conditionally-loaded polyfills instead of heavy third-party bundles. Gotchas & Quirks : We document hidden platform limitations, such as the 64KB payload quota for fetchLater() or macOS-specific scrollbar behaviors. Baseline-Aware Integration : We leverage real-time compatibility data from the Baseline project so agents dynamically adapt to current browser support. Origin Trial & Volatile Feature Gates : Guides covering experimental Origin Trial APIs or volatile features (single-engine features shipped within the last 3 months or still stabilizing) remain discoverable via search , but are gated on retrieve so agents do not adopt unstable APIs without explicit developer consent. Project Configuration ( .mwgrc ) Configure Origin Trial and volatile feature opt-ins for a repository with an optional .mwgrc JSON file in your project root (or ~/.mwgrc as a user-level fallback), which you can commit to share across your team: CLI Command .mwgrc Key Effect npx modern-web-guidance@latest set-allow-origin-trials "allowOriginTrials": true Unlocks guides for experimental Origin Trial APIs. npx modern-web-guidance@latest set-allow-volatile-features "allowVolatileFeatures": true Unlocks guides for volatile single-engine features. How It Works Activation : The coding agent activates the modern-web-guidance skill because of a relevant task. The agent is instructed to use the modern-web-guidance CLI for web platform queries. Local Semantic Search : The agent runs modern-web-guidance search "<query>" . The tool matches the query to the best guide using an offline, zero-dependency embedding model and BM25 search engine (no network calls, no API keys). Guide Fetch : The agent retrieves the guide via modern-web-guidance retrieve <guide-id> , inserting targeted code patterns, gotchas, and fallbacks directly into its context window. Tip Note: We use npx to ensure the content doesn't go stale, but the CLI works offline, completely private and local. The npm package is self-contained, with no extra dependencies to ensure both low-latency and supply-chain security. Evals to prove this works well We developed a robust eval harness to ensure that the content is empirically proven and continuously calibrated so AI agents write better code. We run automated evaluations using a closed-loop validation pipeline: [ Expert-authored guidance and demo ] │ ▼ [ Target generation ] ──> Tasks on real webapps, Golden solutions, Playwright graders │ ▼ [ Calibration loop ] ───> Runs Grader on Golden Solutions (Must Pass 100%) │ Runs Grader on Unmodified Base App (Must Fail 100%) ▼ [ E2E agent evals ] ────> Runs coding agents in guided vs. unguided modes Compares pass rates and accessibility w/ and w/o the skill Simulated Developer Tasks : We define realistic developer prompts against full base applications ( daily-grind , devtools-times ) that mimic real-world requests (e.g., "make my images load faster"). Prompts avoid naming APIs or features, testing whether the agent can naturally discover and apply the right guides. Static & Browser-Based Assertions : Playwright graders verify that each implementation requirement was followed—checking source patterns, computed styles, runtime DOM behaviors, and accessibility states. Self-Healing Calibration : Graders are calibrated against multi-agent (Claude/Codex/AGY) golden solutions (100% pass target) and an unmodified baseline application (0% pass target). E2E Testing : We measure coding agent performance on real tasks with and without guidance. The opportunity (100% - unguided pass rate) and uplift (guided - unguided pass rate) are key: if models already succeed without guidance, we prune redundant advice; where agents struggle, we refine guides to maximize uplift.
