title: Announcing .NET 11
body_text: Announcing .NET 11 - .NET Blog Skip to main content Dev Blogs AI All .NET posts .NET MAUI ASP.NET Core Blazor Entity Framework C++ C# F# TypeScript NuGet Servicing .NET Blog in Chinese Microsoft for Developers Agent Framework Develop from the cloud Xcode ISE Developer TypeScript PowerShell Python Java Java Blog in Chinese Go Microsoft Edge Dev Microsoft 365 Developer Microsoft Entra Identity Developer Microsoft Entra PowerShell Visual Studio Visual Studio Code Aspire All things Azure Azure SDK Azure VM Runtime Team Microsoft Azure Azure Cosmos DB Azure DocumentDB Azure Data Studio Azure SQL DevOps DirectX Microsoft Foundry Power Platform OData Unified Data Model (IDEAs) Windows Command Line #ifdef Windows Inside MSIX MIDI and music React Native The Old New Thing Foundry on Windows Windows Developer Dev Blogs .NET Blog Announcing .NET 11 November 10th, 2026 19 reactions Announcing .NET 11 .NET Team Show more Today, we’re excited to announce the release of .NET 11! This year’s release makes building modern applications faster, more productive, and has improvements across C# 15, ASP.NET Core, .NET MAUI, and Windows development. With hundreds of runtime optimizations, more responsive SDK tooling, and less overhead in everyday commands, you can spend less time waiting and more time creating. Build richer web and cross-platform applications, take advantage of new C# language features, and explore AI-powered development with improved tools and agentic capabilities. Download .NET 11 .NET 11 support .NET 11 is a Standard Term Support (STS) release with two years of support under the .NET support policy . STS and Long Term Support (LTS) releases have the same quality and servicing policies; the difference is the length of support. .NET 10 remains a supported LTS option. Stay current with servicing updates whichever release you choose. Join us at .NET Conf, November 10-13 Explore .NET 11 with the product teams and community at .NET Conf 2026 . The conference includes product team sessions on November 10 and 11, followed by two days of community sessions. Watch the Day 1 livestream, including the keynote , or browse the conference session playlist . Announcing .NET 11 Watch on YouTube Watch .NET Conf What’s new in .NET 11 Some of the changes we’re most excited for you to try: C# 15 union types and closed hierarchies help you express the possible states of your application and handle them with compiler-checked patterns. A Native AOT CLI host and a warm MSBuild server reduce overhead in everyday developer workflows. ASP.NET Core brings asynchronous validation, OpenAPI 3.2, and new capabilities for Blazor and SignalR applications. Experimental Blazor AI components integrate with the Agent User Interaction Protocol (AG-UI) for advanced agentic web experiences. Build AI-powered, agentic applications with Microsoft.Extensions.AI (MEAI) for model access, MCP for tool integration, and Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) for agents and workflows. Put agentic development tools to work with .NET Skills for .NET-specific guidance, .NET MAUI DevFlow for inspecting and testing running apps, and the .NET Upgrade canvas for reviewing modernization progress. .NET MAUI adopts CoreCLR as its default runtime and improves XAML iteration and native controls. The libraries add built-in Zstandard compression, simpler process execution, richer JSON support, and new ways to work with in-memory data without copying it first. The what’s new in .NET 11 overview links to the full details. Here are the changes behind those headlines and how to start using them. Languages C# 15 C# 15 is the default language version for projects targeting .NET 11. Union types are one of its biggest additions: a value can be one of a declared set of case types, with conversions from those types and exhaustiveness checking in switch expressions. Consider a product lookup that either finds a product or reports that it wasn’t found: ProductLookup result = new Product(42, "Mechanical keyboard"); string message = result switch { Product product => $"Found {product.Name}", ProductNotFound missing => $"No product with ID {missing.Id}", }; Console.WriteLine(message); public sealed record Product(int Id, string Name); public sealed record ProductNotFound(int Id); public union ProductLookup(Product, ProductNotFound); The result type tells a caller which outcomes it needs to handle. There’s no need to use object or an unrelated base class just to put those outcomes behind one return type. C# 15 also adds closed hierarchies . A closed class limits direct derivation to its declaring assembly, giving the compiler the information it needs to check patterns over the hierarchy. Unions are useful when you want to combine existing types; closed hierarchies fit models where you own the inheritance relationship. Smaller language features help with everyday code, too. Collection expression arguments let you pass constructor or factory arguments without giving up collection expression syntax: HashSet<string> names = [with(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase), "Alice", "ALICE", "Bob"]; Console.WriteLine(names.Count); This prints 2 : the comparer controls equality, so "Alice" and "ALICE" are one entry. Other additions include extension indexers and labeled break and continue . These features don’t require the preview language version. The separate memory safety work remains in preview ; see the C# 15 feature documentation for its opt-in requirements. F# 11 F# 11 improves compiler memory use and reduces allocations in FSharp.Core collection operations. It also adds ways to bound concurrent asynchronous work, useful when a collection operation would otherwise start more work than a service or machine can handle comfortably. The F# release notes distinguish the default-language updates from preview capabilities, including Runtime Async support for custom computation-expression builders. Platform SDK The SDK now enables a Native AOT CLI host by default. Commands such as help and version queries can run without starting the managed CLI, and tool launches can avoid that startup path too. Commands that need managed execution still use it. The MSBuild server also stays warm between CLI invocations by default, reducing repeated startup work. SDK installers on Linux and macOS are smaller through assembly deduplication. File-based apps can grow across source files with #:include , and solution filters can be created and edited from the CLI. dotnet watch adds Aspire app-host integration, crash recovery, and device selection for mobile projects. For teams using Microsoft.Testing.Platform, dotnet test gains run-level timeouts, failure limits, clearer progress reporting, and per-module results directories. The test runner matters: these switches aren’t interchangeable with the VSTest command-line options. Container publishing adds reproducible image digests through SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH and avoids redundant layer uploads when the target manifest already exists. NuGet source configuration gains a minimum package publication age setting, which lets teams wait before newly published package versions become eligible for selection. This is an additional policy control, not a replacement for vulnerability checks or reviewing dependencies. See what’s new in the SDK and tooling for command examples and configuration. Runtime and performance Performance work in .NET 11 reaches both the code you deploy and the tools you use to develop it. Stephen Toub’s Performance Improvements in .NET 11 takes a detailed tour through hundreds of runtime and library optimizations, with benchmarks and code examples. The just-in-time (JIT) compiler improvements remove more redundant bounds checks and branches, improve devirtualization, and fold more operations into constants. For example, the JIT can optimize additional SequenceEqual calls when it knows the inputs at compile time. These changes improve generated code without requiring you to rewrite the corresponding application logic. Native AOT interface dispatch uses a shared helper that reduces the code needed at interface call sites and improves throughput for interface-heavy workloads. Hardware support also expands, including FP16 instructions for Half operations on supported x64 and Arm64 hardware and new vector construction and composition APIs. There’s useful work on diagnostics, too. In-process crash report logging can capture a managed stack trace, module information, and runtime state before a process exits. Previously available on mobile platforms, this reporting path now also supports Linux and macOS. As always, measure the effect on your own application. Throughput, startup time, memory use, and deployment size depend on the workload and publishing options you choose. Runtime Async has been a recurring theme throughout the .NET 11 previews. It moves asynchronous suspension and resumption into the runtime instead of relying on compiler-generated state machines. One especially useful result is a clearer live call stack. Profilers and debuggers can show the asynchronous methods themselves instead of the infrastructure used to execute them. This is a distinction from exception stack traces, which already hide much of that infrastructure. Runtime Async remains a preview feature. To try it in a project targeting net11.0 , add: <PropertyGroup> <Features>runtime-async=on</Features> </PropertyGroup> You don’t need to enable EnablePreviewFeatures for this scenario. The .NET runtime libraries themselves are built with Runtime Async, but opting your application’s code into the new compilation model is a separate choice. See the Runtime Async documentation for its behavior and current guidance, and test your application’s dependencies and diagnostics before adopting it. AI libraries and tools The .NET 11 SDK includes an MCP server template . MCP gives AI applications a common way to discover and call tools and services. The template uses the official MCP C# SDK and includes a working sample tool, so you can start exposing your own functionality without first installing a separate template package: dotnet new mcpserver -o MyMcpServer For applications that consume AI services, Microsoft.Extensions.AI (MEAI) provides abstractions such as IChatClient and IEmbeddingGenerator . These libraries let you compose model access with dependency injection, caching, and OpenTelemetry using familiar .NET patterns. They’re available as NuGet packages, rather than features that require you to move all of your application code to a new framework version. Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) builds on these abstractions with agents that call tools and maintain conversation state, plus workflows that coordinate agents and application code. Connect agents to MCP tools to give them access to your application’s capabilities, and expose an agent through an ASP.NET Core AG-UI endpoint to build an interactive Blazor experience. The AG-UI hosting integration is currently prerelease. For hands-on examples, start with .NET AI Essentials: The Core Building Blocks Explained and continue with our Microsoft Agent Framework walkthrough . Libraries The .NET libraries add capabilities that previously required extra setup, intermediate buffers, or custom helpers. The Process API expansion includes one-shot methods to run a process and capture its output and exit status. More advanced APIs give you control over inherited handles, suspended starts, and process signaling. Build tools and developer utilities can spend less code on process plumbing while still inspecting how a child process finished. See Process API Improvements in .NET 11 for examples. Zstandard compression joins the existing compression formats in System.IO.Compression . New span-based compression APIs support callers that manage their own buffers, and ZIP improvements include CRC32 validation when reading entries. Four new in-memory stream adapters bridge existing data to APIs that accept a Stream : ReadOnlyMemoryStream , WritableMemoryStream , ReadOnlySequenceStream , and StringStream . For example, a pipeline’s segmented ReadOnlySequence<byte> can be read as a stream without first flattening it into a new contiguous buffer. System.Text.Json adds support for C# unions, F# discriminated unions, and JSON Lines output from asynchronous sequences. F# union support uses reflection and doesn’t support source generation, trimming, or Native AOT, so check the documented limits before choosing it for a trimmed application. LINQ adds FullJoin , which preserves unmatched elements from both inputs. This is useful for reconciliation work, such as comparing two inventories where you need to see missing items on either side. The libraries also expand numeric types, DNS resolution, cryptography, and tracing configuration. The library overview covers the complete set of changes and marks APIs that remain experimental. Entity Framework Core 11 Entity Framework Core 11 improves how your model becomes a query and how that query becomes SQL. EF Core removes unnecessary joins in more reference-navigation and split-query scenarios, improves GroupBy translation, and translates the new LINQ FullJoin operator on relational providers that support it. These changes can simplify generated SQL while letting more queries stay in LINQ. Complex types and JSON columns can now be used on entities mapped with table-per-type or table-per-concrete-type inheritance. Other improvements include migrations tooling and additional provider-specific JSON capabilities. For SQL Server applications, EF Core adds support for vector indexes and approximate vector search. The SQL Server features and corresponding EF APIs are experimental. See the vector search documentation and limitations before evaluating them. EF Core 11 requires .NET 11. When upgrading, check your database provider’s compatibility and the EF Core 11 breaking changes as well as the runtime changes. Developer tools The new dotnetup toolchain manager lets you install and update .NET SDKs and runtimes in your user account. It’s currently in public preview and helps you manage side-by-side versions and keep up with servicing updates. .NET Skills gives coding agents task-specific guidance from the .NET team. Our .NET Skills introduction explains how to add these skills to your coding agent. The experimental .NET MAUI DevFlow toolkit exposes a running app’s visual tree, screenshots, and interaction tools, so an agent can inspect and test the UI rather than work only from source code. For modernization, the .NET Upgrade canvas gives you a visual view of a GitHub Copilot upgrade session. Review assessment findings and dependency compatibility, follow implementation tasks, and monitor failures and progress as the upgrade agent works. Our modernization walkthrough in the GitHub Copilot app covers the workflow from assessment through execution. Workloads Web: ASP.NET Core and Blazor Application types are most useful when the rest of the stack understands them. ASP.NET Core supports C# unions wherever it uses System.Text.Json , including JSON request and response bodies in Minimal APIs and MVC. Generated OpenAPI documents describe the union’s alternatives with an anyOf schema. This support applies to JSON bodies, not to route, query, header, or form binding. When multiple union cases have the same JSON shape, configure a classifier so deserialization can distinguish them. The ASP.NET Core union documentation explains those boundaries. Validation also becomes more practical for rules that need to do I/O. Asynchronous validation works with the new asynchronous DataAnnotations APIs, so a validator can await a database lookup or a remote call instead of blocking a thread. Minimal APIs and Blazor forms can use this support. OpenAPI 3.2 is now the default for generated documents. Among other improvements, it lets the document describe the per-event payload of a server-sent event stream. If a client generator or another part of your toolchain doesn’t yet support 3.2, you can explicitly select an earlier document version. For long-lived connections, SignalR authentication refresh lets a connection refresh authentication without reconnecting. Blazor Interactive Server components can receive the updated identity and react when claims change. Blazor adds capabilities for both statically rendered pages and interactive applications. The new CacheView component caches the rendered output of a component subtree during static server-side rendering. On a cache hit, Blazor replays the markup without creating those child components or running their lifecycle methods. That gives you a smaller unit of caching for expensive, mostly static sections of a page. Interactive Server apps can opt into automatic circuit pause when a browser tab becomes inactive . After a configurable delay, pausing frees the server memory and SignalR connection held by an inactive user. The feature requires an additional package and explicit configuration; upgrading doesn’t silently change your application’s circuit behavior. Forms gain client-side validation for static server rendering and asynchronous validation support. QuickGrid and Virtualize add ways to move to a particular item, useful when returning a user to their place in a large collection. Blazor also adds components for agentic user interfaces. The new Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.AI package includes components for streaming chat, tool rendering, approval flows, and shared UI state. Basic chat works with any IChatClient . For advanced experiences with a remote agent, the AG-UI .NET integration carries streamed responses, tool events, approval requests, and shared-state updates between an ASP.NET Core agent endpoint and the Blazor UI. The Blazor AI components package is experimental and remains prerelease throughout .NET 11. It’s an opportunity to try the direction and give feedback, not a stable part of the ASP.NET Core shared framework. See the Blazor AI components documentation . The AG-UI .NET SDK introduction covers the protocol’s client and server APIs. Build Agentic UI with the new Blazor AI components puts them together in a working app. See what’s new in ASP.NET Core for the Blazor features, configuration examples, and compatibility details. Client: .NET MAUI .NET MAUI in .NET 11 makes CoreCLR the default runtime across its platforms. The move to CoreCLR brings mobile and desktop apps onto the same runtime foundation as other .NET workloads. On Apple platforms that don’t allow JIT compilation, the runtime uses precompiled code and the interpreter rather than generating native code at runtime. Native AOT is an opt-in publishing alternative; its Android support remains experimental. Review the platform-specific runtime guidance and test your app’s libraries when choosing a deployment model. The UI development loop gets attention, too: XAML Incremental Hot Reload is a preview feature in .NET 11. It updates live instances of pages and controls, including supported structural edits, without requiring you to navigate away and back. It’s enabled by default in Debug builds. Implicit XAML namespace declarations remove the need to repeat the standard namespace declarations at the root of every file. Windows uses the new CollectionView2 handler by default, while Android Shell adopts a handler-based architecture. New mobile test templates and dotnet test device selection bring testing into the CLI workflow. These are meaningful runtime and handler changes, so exercise navigation, custom handlers, and trimmed publishing as part of your upgrade. The optional Microsoft.Maui.Controls.Compatibility package no longer ships; apps that still reference it need to migrate off it. .NET MAUI follows its own support policy , separate from the .NET runtime’s STS and LTS lifecycle. Windows: WinUI, Windows Forms, and WPF For new Windows desktop apps, WinUI 3 is the recommended native UI framework, pairing C# and XAML with modern controls and the Fluent Design System. It’s delivered through the Windows App SDK , which also makes modern Windows APIs available to existing WPF and Windows Forms apps. To add UI tests, see UWP and WinUI 3 apps: UI testing with MSTest . Windows Forms in .NET 11 adds an opt-in modern visual styles mode that you can select at the application or control level. It also adds ways to react to system visual and accessibility settings, defer revealing a form until it’s ready, and suspend painting during bulk updates. These controls let you introduce refreshed rendering where it makes sense for your application instead of treating a framework upgrade as an automatic visual redesign. WPF updates focus on reliability, including fixes for Fluent window backdrops, window manager failures, and weak-event cleanup. Self-contained Windows publishing also includes a native dependency needed by apps that load mixed-mode WPF assemblies. Get started and plan your upgrade Install the .NET 11 SDK . Use a compatible, up-to-date Visual Studio 2026 installation, or Visual Studio Code with C# Dev Kit . To create and run a console app: dotnet new console -n HelloDotnet11 -f net11.0 dotnet run --project HelloDotnet11 You can replace the generated program with either of the C# examples above to try the new language features. For an existing application, plan the upgrade across your development and deployment environments: Update the SDK selection in global.json if your repository pins it, and install the matching SDK on development machines and build agents. Update target frameworks to .NET 11, preserving platform-specific target framework suffixes where applicable. Update packages and workloads to compatible versions. Review the .NET 11 breaking changes , including the updated minimum CPU requirements . Installing a new SDK alone doesn’t retarget your app. Run your tests and measure the application under a representative workload. Validate your actual publishing mode, container base images, native dependencies, and deployment hosts. Upgrading from .NET 8 or .NET 9 .NET 8 and .NET 9 reach end of support on November 10, 2026. Move to a supported release to continue receiving fixes. Choose .NET 11 for the latest capabilities, or .NET 10 if its LTS lifecycle fits your requirements better. See the .NET support policy for dates and servicing requirements. If you’re upgrading from a .NET 11 release candidate, update to the final SDK, runtime, and compatible package and workload versions rather than staying on a prerelease build. Thank you for building .NET with us .NET 11 is the work of over 7,000 contributors . Thank you to everyone who contributed code, tested previews, reported issues, and helped us make better design decisions throughout the year. Your feedback across the previews and release candidates helped shape what we’re shipping today. The .NET ecosystem continues to grow, with more than 589,000 unique packages on NuGet and over 1.1 trillion package downloads . Download .NET 11 , try it with an application you know well, and join us at .NET Conf to learn directly from the people building it. title: Horible public key tricks
body_text: Horrible public key tricks: Navigation: Homepage      Index      Yearly archives Fun Astrophotography      (catalog) About this site Real pages Dark Light TTY Horrible public key tricks: 2026-11-08 — 2026-11-09 So, I've always been somewhat annoyed at SSL/TLS. It requires everyone to go through a complex "ACME" dance just to put up a public website. Worse, certificates expire every few months, so it's not a one and done thing: even with automation, maintaining a certificate requires care to ensure the ACME client always has access to DNS records or the web server. ... and the whole system doesn't even work because certificates are issued over plaintext connections, and trusted certificate aurthorities use very secure keys like "4" There is prior art of protest SSL implementations , but I do actually want to encrypt web traffic. Passive eavesdropping is a real risk... but preventing it doesn't require the whole certificate thing: therefore, the best choice is a protest certificate. The only part of the certificate I directly control is the public key. Therefore, the simplest way to obtain a bad certificate is use a vanity private key such as 313333333337 (one of the most eleet primes). However, while the resulting public key would be weak, no one would know unless they try to break it. A good protest should be obvious: # openssl s_client -connect maurycyz.com : 443 /dev/null \ | sed -n /BEGIN/,/END/p | grep -zE '////.?*////' --color= yes -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- CERTIFICATE----- First, let's look at mathematical framework of RSA. To generate a key, pick two large prime numbers (p and q) and multiply them to yeild the modulus (n). Pick a small number, e as public exponent. The RSA public key is composed of the modulus (n) and the public exponent: # Encryption requires knowing e (public) cyphertext = plaintext^e mod n The private key contains the modulus and the private exponent (d) which is chosen to be the multiplicate inverse of e modulo n. Exactly how d is found is not relevent, but the process requires knowing p and q. # Decryption requires knowing d (pivate) = cyphertext^d mod n = plaintext^e^d mod n = plaintext^(e*d) mod n = plaintext^1 mod n = plaintext --> Ok, back to vanity keys. The standard value for e is 65537 (0x10001), because the small number of set bits makes encryption faster. In fact, the CA I used will refuse to sign keys with a non-standard public exponent, so I can't do anything funny there. The modulus, n, is either 2,048 or 4,096 "user controlled" bits, so it's the ideal place to hide a message. However, to use the certificate, I'll need to find two large primes that multiply out to the vanity modulus. My method starts by picking two random primes and calculating the resulting n value. Then, the bytes of n are modified to introduce message into the base64 encoding. Of course, the modified n is not the product of p and q, but this is fixable by setting q to n/p. The resulting q value is very unlikely to be a prime (or integer), so I round it and find the next prime after the ideal q: which usually only requires changing the value of q by a few hundred. Since p and q are similar in size, a small change q only affects the least-sigifiant half of the product: 58174124 * 918491824 = 53432457262362176 (incrementing until the next prime...) 58174124 * 9184918 43 = 5343245836 7670532 As long as the message is embedded into the upper half of n, it's likely to survive undamaged. The original p and newly selected q can now be used to construct a functional RSA private key in the usual manner. From here, it's really just a matter of getting a certificate aurthority to sign the key: # Single domain openssl req -new -key priv.pem -subj '/C=US/CN=example.com' > cert_request certbot certonly --manual --csr cert_request # Wildcard cat > config <<EOF [ req ] req_extensions = req_ext [ req_ext ] subjectAltName = @alt_names [ alt_names ] DNS.1 = *.example.com DNS.2 = example.com EOF openssl req -new -key priv.pem -config config -subj '/C=US/CN=example.com' > cert_request certbot certonly --manual --csr cert_request ... although since base64 operates on groups of three byte, it is possible for the message to be misaligned and not readable. However, since the layout of the certificate is static, it is possible to adjust the message's placement until it works: this should take less than four attempts. The result is a functional, trusted certificate with a longish message hidden in the public key. Renewal is done by resumbitting the CSR and repeating the ACME chalange, which can be automated. Base64 is missing most punctuation, but it provides the full ASCII alphabet, and the ~150 (RSA-2048) or ~320 (RSA-4096) available charaters provides plenty of space for jokes. Another option would be to target the base16 displayed in most browser's certificate viewer: this would provide a lot more space (2 chars/byte instea of 0.75), but requires careful word choice. As for security , this trick obviously reduces the entropy in the private key. However, it should still be secure: nearly identical methods have been considered as a form of compression. If the top-half of the modulus is fixed to a well known value, it doesn't have to be sent or stored as part of the key. A reduction of around 1/2 can be achieved through division, but the state of the art can fix 2/3 of the key, reducing the size to 1/3 of standard RSA while retaining a similar level of security... although I should note that such tricks have largly been abandoned in favor of other crytosystems which can directly use small keys. The manipulation of q may produce primes that are very close together, which makes it possible to factor n and recover the private key. A very small d value can also be a problem. Both of these are unlikely, but my script doesn't check for insecure values However, regardless of the key's security, it should be perfectly fine for a public website: modern TLS provides forward secrecy, so eavesdropping requires a man-in-the-middle attack even if the private key is compromised. title: The Web Is More Than Enough
body_text: The Web Is More Than Enough, by Paul Ford (Ftrain) Ftrain , by Paul Ford Home / Publications / Print, Web, and Newsletters / The Aboard Newsletter Oct 21, 2026 The Aboard Newsletter The Web Is More Than Enough Web browsers enable incredibly rich app development—and that’s radically easier than it used to be. You can have it all, my empire of alert(). Last week was fun. We launched tinylittleoffice.com —you heard it here first!—and it turned out that lots of folks were in the market for an “office suite that stores data in the URL.”  So many people visited that the server went down (well, I maxxed out the CloudFlare free plan), and ultimately, after I put in my credit card, a couple hundred thousand people came by to check it out. People on Hacker News insisted it was a pointless waste of time, and folks on GitHub started asking for features and fixes, all of which we’re considering, and some of which we’re doing. The Register wrote an article about it , and it also made it, for a little while, to the top ten of Product Hunt . So all good; we will continue to support and enhance it, bit by bit, while we also do stable software development work for our customers and clients. But I did want to pause for a second and point out something that surprised me about the process. It’s this: The web browser is very, very, very powerful software for building applications. I know that is obvious and is the sort of thing I could have said any time in the last 20 years. But now there’s an addendum to the statement:  The web browser is very, very, very powerful software for applications, and the cost of accessing that power is going down seemingly every day. I put maybe twice as much effort into building a web-based office suite as I might normally put into writing a long newsletter post. I’m not telling you this because I am a very special boy. I’m telling you because if you want to, you can learn to do it, too. Fast, cheap, good, right? But even after I had to put in my credit card, CloudFlare hosting costs…$0. Partly because I optimize for cheapness, but partly because that’s just how it goes these days. Fast? Dear God, computers are fast, and software development is also fast compared to the past. But as I code web apps, I keep finding new corners of the browser I didn’t know well. Things are just…wild in there. The Web Crypto API is a first-class security platform in the browser. The Web Assembly platform lets you run native-speed code in your browser. WebGL provides for high-quality 3D and 2D graphics in your browser. The Web Audio API lets you mix sound in your browser. And on and on. The web is really the greatest distribution platform imaginable right now. It’s inherently multilingual—I released TinyLittleOffice in 21 languages (the most common NYC ones, which is why it has Creole and Yiddish), with lots of infrastructure for accessibility. Plus, of course, JavaScript is a full-featured programming language, and HTML can represent most things a document can do on a computer; if you need something more old-school, PDF.js lets you deal with PDFs in the browser. I think you can even hyphenate text reliably these days, although I refuse to believe it. I knew these things existed. I’d even programmed with them. But I’d never really looked closely; I just downloaded whatever open-source code would make it easier to build and tried to drag software across the finish line. My quirky 1990s-vintage office suite might not convince you—it’s weird and small. So take a look at Simon Willison’s new web-based browser 3D game, Battle Drones . He’s hosting it on GitHub. He wrote it himself. He’s not a games builder. It just pops right up in the browser and you play it. It’s multiplayer, and it works offline. Time to place your Fab Plant. As he wrote about it : … but I can now see a path to vibe coded games like this being taken seriously. Battle Drones is fun, it looks good, it has innovative features (the multiplayer-over-audio thing is a first for an RTS as far as I can tell). I’d love to see what someone with better taste than me and a driving passion to produce something truly exceptional could build! All the various cool browser technologies have been around for years. But they are each extremely vast. If you get good at Web Audio, you probably don’t have time to get good at Web Crypto and Web Assembly and WebGL.  The reason they were so complex is, basically, because they were built for teams like those at Google, not for individuals. In the past, the web was for people to build web pages—and, yes, in the present, you can still do that, but for more than a decade, the web has been designed for giant companies so they can deliver software securely to billions of people who buy things with credit cards. These huge mega-libraries were dropped into the web browser to enable large teams to build big things, and the little guy was a bit of an afterthought. But now you can make a game in 3D with sound, and it can work just fine on a plane. This is one of the places where “are we in an AI bubble” gets fuzzy for me, because it’s totally clear all these giant AI companies are huffing AGI paint fumes, but at the same time, if we actually unlocked the economic transformation of, say, 100 times as many people making software for each other, that would blow an enormous crater into the current tech economy. Don’t like the way your giant industrial looms make carpet? Hack your own firmware and make each carpet totally personalized! Turn any Instagram post into a huge floor covering! Suddenly all the carpet companies have to hack their own firmware to compete. What’s that going to be like?  This also destabilizes the app store economy. The high tax of building for app stores seems less worth paying when you can just test an idea in the world from a web server for $0 after a couple weeks. Perhaps Mozilla should take another swing at launching a mobile phone! (Forget I mentioned that.) In any case, what used to be a large industrial process is now a personal one, if you so desire. Web browsers enable incredibly rich app development—and that’s radically easier than it used to be. It’s a mixed blessing. I’ve been a writer for years, and software development feels more and more like writing to me every passing week. The awkward part of the comparison is, in general, people do not want to pay writers any money at all. As a writer, you get used to it. But for software people, being perpetually devalued is pretty novel. Then again, if you need software to do something—like our clients!—say, to fix a process, organize a database, get more value out of a big piece of industrial equipment, it’s a pretty amazing time, because you can do just about anything. I’m pretty confident we’ll all meet in the middle, but it’ll take a while, and it will be different on the other side. Play Device Slots video Expand Core Library Updates Production-ready effect presets and Racks for vocals, guitars, mixing and mastering. Play Core Library Updates video Expand Softube Effects Shape dynamics and tone with five Softube effects modeled on sought-after studio hardware. Play Softube Effects video Expand 00:00 FAQs What’s new in Ableton Live 13? Ableton Live 13 adds new audio and MIDI workflows, sound design tools and mixing effects. Highlights include: A built-in Step Sequencer, ARA 2 support for compatible audio-editing plug-ins, Capture Automation, and Contextual Browsing for adding devices and swapping presets directly from the device chain. Drum Synth, new Multiband and Mid-Side Racks, expanded Rack controls, and Envelope Clips for automating and modulating effects on return tracks. Device Slots in the mixer, and new Core Library Drum Racks, instrument presets, Audio Effect Racks, samples, and MIDI clips. Arrangement Sync for Ableton Link, support for exporting tempo automation and time signature changes, and more precise event timing in exported MIDI files. Mixer improvements including Send sliders, a persistent Mixer Configuration menu for choosing which sections are visible, smoother mixer resizing, and an Unsolo button on the Main track, plus an updated Phaser-Flanger interface. Live 13 Suite also includes Melodyne essential, Looplet, Clipper, Transient Shaper and the Classic Dynamics & EQ Pack by Softube. See the full Release Notes for every change. What’s new for Push? Push 3 gains Custom Layouts, a new Step Sequencer layout, a new Performance Mixer, and Device Mode upgrades. Custom Layouts combine Session View, note areas, XYZ and mixer controls on a single page. The Step Sequencer brings the step editing experience from Live to the hardware. Device Mode adds jog wheel navigation and up to 32 Rack Macros. Push 2 supports the new Step Sequencer and most Device Mode improvements (except jog wheel navigation), but not Custom Layouts, Performance Mixer or Expressive Step Editing. See the full Release Notes for every change. What’s the difference between Ableton Live 12 and Live 13? Live 13 is the next major version of Ableton Live, following Live 12. It adds audio and MIDI workflows including ARA 2 support, Step Sequencer and Capture Automation, plus instruments and effects, expanded Rack controls, updated Core Library content, and more. Everything you can do in Live 12 you can still do in Live 13. What’s the difference between Live 13 Intro, Standard and Suite? Ableton Live 13 comes in three editions: Intro, Standard and Suite. They share the same core workflow but differ in their features and included instruments, effects and sounds. Live Intro is limited to 16 tracks and Scenes. Standard allows unlimited tracks and Scenes, and adds many more built-in instruments, effects and sounds.  Suite includes everything in Standard plus Max for Live, the complete instrument and effect collection, and Live’s full Core Library. Suite also comes with Melodyne essential for ARA 2 editing, plus the Classic Dynamics & EQ Pack by Softube and Looplet as free downloads at release. Compare editions in detail . When is Ableton Live 13 released? Ableton Live 13 will be released in early 2027. Subscribe to our Newsletter to be notified at release Can I pre-order Live 13? Yes, in two ways: If you already own Live 12 – pre-order Live 13 at 20% off. If you don’t own Live 12 yet – buy or upgrade to Live 12 at 20% off during the announcement offer and get the corresponding Live 13 edition free when it’s released. How do I upgrade to Live 13? Log in to your User Account and visit the Ableton shop to see the upgrade options for your license. From now until the release of Live 13, you can buy or upgrade to Live 12 and get the corresponding Live 13 edition for free on release day.  What happens to my Live 12 Rent-to-own license when I upgrade? You can extend your existing plan to cover the cost of upgrading to Live 13 Suite and start using it as soon as it’s released. Visit the Ableton shop to see your upgrade options. How do I get access to the Live 13 beta? Limited places for the Live 13 public beta are available to Live Standard and Suite owners. Learn more about the  Ableton Live beta program . Which ARA plug-ins work with Live 13? Most ARA 2 plug-ins work with Live 13, including Melodyne. Live 13 Suite comes with Melodyne essential. A small number have known compatibility issues. See the full Release Notes for more information. One ARA plug-in can be used at a time, across multiple clips and tracks. Read the Release Notes Save 20% on Live 12 now, upgrade to Live 13 for free. It provides a live process tree, lower-pane module/handle/thread inspection, rich per-process properties, system-wide performance graphs, code-signing inspection, and macOS-specific equivalents for Process Explorer workflows. The app is built with Swift, SwiftUI, and AppKit, with sampling backed by public macOS APIs such as libproc , sysctl , Mach host statistics, Security.framework, IOKit, Metal, and optional privileged helper support. Features Live process tree with Process Explorer-style colors for services, own processes, new/deleted processes, suspended processes, sandboxed processes, and packed images. Frozen process-name pane with horizontally scrollable metric columns. Persisted process-list column widths, ordering, column sets, and selected columns. Type-to-select in process and lower-pane lists. Immediate tooltips for truncated cells and process path/command-line detail. Pause/resume refresh with the spacebar. Native menu bar with File, Options, View, Process, Find, Window, and Help commands. Toolbar actions for refresh, save, process properties, kill, lower pane, find handle/DLL, target-window picker, and System Information graphs. Lower pane modes for DLLs/images, handles/file descriptors, and threads. Lower-pane row highlighting for newly appeared and deleted items. Per-process Properties window with Image, Performance, Performance Graph, Threads, TCP/IP, Security, Environment, and Strings tabs. TCP/IP tab with local address, remote address, async reverse-DNS remote name lookup, TCP state, and column persistence. Security/signature detail with signer, publisher, certificate chain, Team ID, notarization status, platform/ad-hoc status, validation reason, SHA-256, and VirusTotal integration. Module/image detail windows with metadata, signature verification, VirusTotal, Reveal in Finder, and Search Online. Handle/file-descriptor detail windows. System Information window with Summary, CPU, Memory, I/O, Network, and GPU pages. System Information graphs for CPU, memory, swap, disk I/O, network I/O, GPU, and per-core CPU usage. Performance vs. efficiency core labeling and coloring on Apple Silicon. Hardware details for CPU topology/cache, memory/page information, storage, network interfaces, GPU device capabilities, and OS/machine data. Menu-bar CPU history item. Process actions: kill, kill tree, suspend/resume, set priority/nice, restart, bring to front, sample process, Search Online, Check VirusTotal. Optional privileged helper architecture for cross-user and privileged operations. Release scripts for DMG creation, signing, and notarization. Requirements macOS 14 or later for the GUI app target. Xcode 26.6 or later recommended for the current project configuration. Swift 5.9 toolchain or later. xcodegen for regenerating ProcexpMac.xcodeproj from project.yml . Install xcodegen if needed: brew install xcodegen Build Generate the Xcode project and build the Debug app: xcodegen generate xcodebuild -scheme ProcexpMac -configuration Debug build The Debug app is written under Xcode DerivedData. On this machine the path is typically: ~ /Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/ProcexpMac-czqddcuyalgzfgebjezrhssregtw/Build/Products/Debug/ProcExp \ \( Dev \) .app You can also open the generated project in Xcode: xcodegen generate open ProcexpMac.xcodeproj Run After a Debug build, launch the app with: open " $HOME /Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/ProcexpMac-czqddcuyalgzfgebjezrhssregtw/Build/Products/Debug/ProcExp (Dev).app " If your DerivedData suffix differs, locate the product with: find ~ /Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData -path ' */Build/Products/Debug/ProcExp (Dev).app ' -print To relaunch a freshly built app from this workspace: app= " $HOME /Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/ProcexpMac-czqddcuyalgzfgebjezrhssregtw/Build/Products/Debug/ProcExp (Dev).app " pids= $( pgrep -f " $app /Contents/MacOS/ProcexpMac " || true ) if [[ -n " $pids " ]] ; then kill $pids 2> /dev/null || true ; fi open -n " $app " Bundle identity: development vs. official Unqualified Xcode and local ad-hoc builds use ProcExp (Dev).app with bundle ID com.sysinternals.procexpmac.dev . Its helper uses the separate launchd and Mach service ID com.sysinternals.procexpmac.dev.helper . The development app, helper approval, preferences, and LaunchServices registration therefore do not replace an installed official copy. The official identities are reserved for an explicit Developer ID build or the Azure release pipeline: ProcExp.app , com.sysinternals.procexpmac , and com.sysinternals.procexpmac.helper . The build and signing scripts validate the entire tuple before signing or publishing it. Validate Run the full Swift package test suite: swift test Run the live smoke test: swift run ProcexpSmoke Run focused test suites: swift test --filter ProcexpModelTests swift test --filter ProcexpNetworkTests swift test --filter ProcexpSigningTests TCP/IP Test Fixture The repository includes a small stateful TCP fixture for testing the TCP/IP tab: swift build --product ProcexpTcpFixture .build/debug/ProcexpTcpFixture --duration 3600 --remote-host github.com --remote-port 22 The fixture opens a loopback listener, creates a loopback established connection, and optionally opens a DNS-resolved remote TCP connection. Select the fixture process in Process Explorer and open Properties > TCP/IP to inspect the sockets and remote-name resolution. Privileged Helper The app can use an optional privileged root helper for operations that require elevated privileges, such as richer cross-user process detail (full process list, threads, modules, environment) and privileged process control. The helper is a launchd daemon reached over XPC; the app registers it with SMAppService . macOS gates SMAppService daemon registration on the app's code signature and on an explicit user approval. The app must be signed with a stable, non-ad-hoc identity — a Developer ID Application certificate for distribution, or a self-signed identity for local development — and you approve the daemon once in System Settings ▸ General ▸ Login Items & Extensions . The sections below cover both the Developer ID install and a local self-signed test. Testing with a Developer ID certificate (real install) This is the same experience end users get. DEV_SIGN_IDENTITY= " Developer ID Application: NAME (TEAMID) " \ bash Scripts/dev_install_helper.sh This builds a Release app, embeds the helper and its launchd plist at Contents/Library/LaunchDaemons/ , signs everything inside-out with the Hardened Runtime and entitlements, installs /Applications/ProcExp.app , and launches it. Then, in the app, choose ProcexpMac ▸ Install Privileged Helper… and approve the daemon in System Settings ▸ General ▸ Login Items & Extensions . After approval the app adopts the privileged provider and shows all processes. Testing without a Developer ID certificate (local self-signed) For local development you can exercise the same privileged code path with a throwaway self-signed identity. On first run the script creates the identity in a dedicated keychain (no login-keychain involvement), builds a signed, helper-embedded app, installs it to /Applications , and launches it: bash Scripts/dev_install_helper.sh Then, one time only, choose ProcexpMac ▸ Install Privileged Helper… and approve the daemon in System Settings ▸ General ▸ Login Items & Extensions . After that, every subsequent run of the script rebuilds and relaunches the signed app with the helper already enabled, so the elevated path is available on each iteration: bash Scripts/dev_install_helper.sh # Debug (default), fast CONFIGURATION=Release bash Scripts/dev_install_helper.sh RESTART_HELPER=1 bash Scripts/dev_install_helper.sh # after changing helper code Notes: The script defaults to a Debug build signed with the "ProcexpMac Dev" self-signed identity. It installs /Applications/ProcExp (Dev).app with the .dev app and helper identifiers. SMAppService ties daemon registration to the app's signature and location, so reinstalling the same-identity build keeps the development helper registered. The app changes take effect on relaunch; the root helper keeps running its already-loaded binary, so pass RESTART_HELPER=1 (prompts for sudo) when you change the helper's own code. A corporate-managed Mac can prompt for a keychain password when codesign touches your login keychain and reject your account password if the login keychain drifted out of sync after a rotation. The dedicated keychain the script creates avoids that entirely. Verifying and cleaning up Check whether the daemon is registered and running as root: launchctl print system/com.sysinternals.procexpmac.dev.helper For an explicit Developer ID install, inspect the official service instead: launchctl print system/com.sysinternals.procexpmac.helper If registration succeeded, the process list shows previously hidden cross-user and system processes. If the daemon is registered but not yet enabled, approve it in System Settings ▸ General ▸ Login Items & Extensions and it becomes active. Repeated reinstalls can clear a previously remembered approval, in which case macOS asks you to approve it again. If registration is refused outright (for example, an ad-hoc signature), the app reports that the helper could not be registered and continues in unprivileged mode. Remove the installed app and unregister the helper: bash Scripts/dev_uninstall_helper.sh The cleanup script defaults to the development tuple. To remove an explicit Developer ID test install instead, run: PROCEXP_LOCAL_FLAVOR=official bash Scripts/dev_uninstall_helper.sh Remove the throwaway signing keychain when finished: security delete-keychain " $HOME /Library/Keychains/procexp-dev.keychain-db " See Helper/README.md and docs/RELEASE.md for the helper architecture and the full Developer ID signing/notarization pipeline. Release Build Build a release DMG: bash Scripts/build_release.sh This local ad-hoc command creates build/ProcExp-Dev.dmg containing ProcExp (Dev).app . To prepare the canonical app for Developer ID signing: PROCEXP_BUILD_FLAVOR=official PACKAGE_DMG=0 bash Scripts/build_release.sh Sign and notarize a release build after configuring Developer ID credentials: bash Scripts/sign_notarize.sh See docs/RELEASE.md for the full release pipeline. Project Layout App - SwiftUI/AppKit GUI application code. Sources/ProcexpModel - shared model types, providers, formatting, columns, and coloring rules. Sources/ProcexpSampling - unprivileged process sampling with libproc and sysctl . Sources/ProcexpNetwork - socket enumeration and system GPU utilization. Sources/ProcexpSigning - code-signing, SHA-256, Keychain, and VirusTotal support. Sources/ProcexpGraphs - AppKit graph views and SwiftUI wrappers. Sources/ProcexpActions - process actions and confirmation metadata. Sources/ProcexpAutostart - launchd/autostart detection. Sources/ProcexpPrivileged and Sources/ProcexpHelper - privileged helper client and daemon. Tests - Swift package tests. Scripts - build, icon, signing, notarization, and release scripts. docs - implementation, release, and project notes. Notes macOS does not expose every Process Explorer data source through public APIs. Where macOS denies access or a metric is not available through supported APIs, the UI leaves values blank rather than fabricating data. Some details become available only for same-user processes or when the privileged helper is active. title: Payments Canada announces launch of Canada's Real-Time Rail (RTR) payment system
body_text: Canada launches the Real-Time Rail, bringing 24/7 payment infrastructure to the national economy | Payments Canada Skip to main content A new source of strength for Canada’s economy: Canada's Real-Time Rail (RTR) is now live. Learn more × Canada's Real-Time Rail is here Top Contact Careers Subscribe Search Français Payments Canada Systems & services Main Navigation Payment systems Real-Time Rail payment system Retail batch payment system High-value payment system - Lynx Payments Canada fees System closure schedule Payment services Payment file validation service Message validation service Financial institutions file Corporate creditor identification number database APIs Rules & documentation Payment resources Main Navigation Directories Support guides Consumer guides Business guides Financial institution guides Cheque printer guide ISO 20022 Automatic funds transfer High-value payment system - Lynx Real-Time Rail payment system Glossary Education Insights Main Navigation News & research Corporate reports Modernization Connect Main Navigation Careers Annual conference Events Membership Payment service provider participation Contact About Main Navigation Who we are Our members & stakeholders Members Stakeholders Our leadership Governance & risk Board of directors Legislation & by-laws Risk management Menu Menu Home Insights News & research Canada launches the Real-Time Rail, bringing 24/7 payment infrastructure to the national economy News Canada launches the Real-Time Rail, bringing 24/7 payment infrastructure to the national economy November 9, 2026 The new system will enable participating financial service providers to clear and settle payments in real time, providing a made-in-Canada platform for future innovation and prosperity. OTTAWA, ON, November 9, 2026 – Payments Canada today announced the launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail (RTR). This new national payment system will transform day-to-day payments for Canadian businesses and consumers by enabling instant speed and settlement, real-time cash-flow visibility and data-rich messaging through existing banking and payment channels. The launch of Canada’s RTR marks a major milestone in modernizing the critical infrastructure that underpins Canada’s economy and future growth. The RTR will enable participating members, including financial institutions, credit unions and payment service providers, to exchange, clear and settle payments securely in real time for their customers, 24 hours a day, every day of the year. “A stronger, more productive economy relies on modern financial infrastructure that can match our ambition,” said the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne, Minister of Finance and National Revenue. “The launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail lays the foundation for a more dynamic and competitive digital economy, driving innovation, expanding choice and creating new opportunities for Canadians while positioning our country for long-term growth.” “The launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail marks the beginning of a new era for payments in our country,” said Susan E. Hawkins , President and CEO, Payments Canada. “As a national asset that’s designed specifically for our country, the RTR gives the payment ecosystem a modern foundation to build on. By collectively leveraging this rail, our ecosystem will unleash its full potential, enabling our members to build capabilities that drive innovation, resilience and growth for businesses and consumers across the nation.” Image Ron Morrow, the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne and Susan E. Hawkins The RTR will drive significant cost savings and economic growth in Canada over the next decade. The C.D. Howe Institute projects that, with its functionalities at launch, the RTR will generate up to $14.5 billion in cost savings from lower processing costs, reduced use of cash and cheques, and reduced float (the period during which funds are temporarily unavailable to the recipient). Extending beyond these cost savings, the RTR is expected to generate $16 billion in economic gains , growing to $27 billion as new functionalities are introduced over time. “The Real-Time Rail is an important step in modernizing Canada's payment infrastructure and ensuring it keeps pace with Canadians' evolving needs,” said Tiff Macklem, Governor of the Bank of Canada. “The Bank will oversee the system so that it operates safely and reliably while ensuring Canadians can benefit from innovations in financial services.” Owned and operated by Payments Canada, and built in collaboration with delivery partners CGI, Deloitte Canada, IBM Canada and Interac Corp., the RTR leverages ISO 20022 data-rich messaging. Through this shared technical language, the RTR holds the potential to strengthen Canada’s economic sovereign autonomy and support its global competitiveness. Fraud safeguards from day one Canada is the first G7 country to deploy a real-time payment system with mandatory centralized fraud services for use at launch. These services will be used alongside participants’ existing fraud controls to mitigate the risk of fraud for Canadian businesses and consumers at multiple levels. Fraud controls required at the launch of Canada’s RTR include: Confirmation of payee (available for consumer accounts on day one) A fraud transaction “safety” score A risk list or repository of fraud risks and indicators A fraud reporting and intelligence platform While no system is entirely immune to risk, these measures establish a strong, coordinated layer of defence across the payment network. At-launch member participants The initial cohort of active RTR system participants includes: Wealthsimple Questbank Peoples Trust Company Paramount Commerce KOHO DoBusiness.com™ Digital Commerce Bank Bank of America Canada’s deliberately sequenced RTR rollout pairs day-one security with rapid scalability. With additional participants onboarding continually in the coming months, including all major Canadian financial institutions and other members applying for access, the RTR will be available to more than nine in 10 Canadians within the first year after launch. Made-in Canada, for Canada The launch of the RTR reflects our ‘Team Canada’ approach, bringing together regulators, members, stakeholders and delivery partners around a shared vision . Built in Canada and designed to serve all Canadians, the RTR provides accessible payment infrastructure through existing banking and payment channels. This infrastructure supports a diverse country and a broad range of communities, including small businesses, newcomers and people in rural areas.  Payments Canada research found that 60 per cent of Canadian businesses are ready to adopt real-time payments to address everyday challenges such as forecasting cash flow and waiting to send and receive funds. More than half of surveyed consumers (52 per cent) also expressed interest and intent to use real-time payments. To meet this evolving need, the RTR serves as a secure platform for innovation. With it, system participants can build and offer products and services that benefit consumers and businesses across the country, supporting a changing economy and Canada's future prosperity. An infrastructure for the future Canada’s Real-Time Rail is an important step toward a more productive, innovative and inclusive economy, and the work will continue to ensure the country’s payment infrastructure meets Canadians’ evolving needs. Learn more about Canada’s Real-Time Rail Contributed quotes At-launch member participants "When Canada embraces new technology, innovation and competition follow, and consumers benefit. Canadians deserve instant, seamless, low-cost financial products to power their businesses and their lives. The Real-Time Rail can transform how money moves in this country, with payments that arrive in seconds instead of days. We’re proud to be among the first institutions to join the RTR and bring this technology to the millions of Canadians who trust us with their money." Mike Katchen, CEO and Co-Founder Wealthsimple "Canadians deserve a modern financial system that operates at the speed of everyday life. The launch of the Real-Time Rail is a pivotal turning point—it puts individuals in direct, immediate control of their money around the clock. We are proud to join Payments Canada in unlocking a safer, more dynamic financial ecosystem for everyone across the country." Rob Galaski, President Questrade Financial Group (Questbank) "The launch of the Real-Time Rail is a transformative milestone for Canada’s financial ecosystem. As a proud member of Payments Canada and a settlement agent at launch, Peoples Group is pleased to support the foundational clearing and settlement that brings real-time payments to life. We are committed to supporting innovative businesses across the country, and look forward to direct participation as the rail expands to serve even more Canadians." David Raju, President and CEO Peoples Group "Being first-to-market on the Real-Time Rail lets our merchants and partners benefit immediately from 24/7 settlement, higher transaction limits and proactive fraud defence. As one of Payments Canada's first payment service provider (PSP) members, we’re proud to have worked alongside their team to help advance Canada’s payment infrastructure and support the next chapter of payments innovation." Sereena Boparai, Chief Revenue Officer Paramount Commerce "The Real-Time Rail is a significant step forward for the integrity and resilience of Canada's payment infrastructure. Building payment systems that are instant, secure and always on takes real rigour, and it's the kind of foundation a modern financial system depends on. We're excited to be part of this work with Payments Canada, and to help ensure Canadians benefit from payment infrastructure built to the highest standards.” David Merriby, CEO The future KOHO Bank “DoBusiness.com™ is honoured to be one of the very first participants on Canada’s Real-Time Rail. The RTR's launch represents a milestone in how money moves across Canada and its payments sovereignty. For us, faster payments and superior fraud prevention belong together. This is an opportunity for us to help Canadian businesses modernize how they pay and verify account details before money moves.” Shayle Rothman, CEO and Co-Founder DoBusiness.com™ “We’re proud to be part of the Team Canada effort that brought the Real-Time Rail to life. For years we’ve helped fintechs and other corporate clients build and launch the payment services Canadians use every day. With the RTR, those companies can now give their customers faster, more robust ways to move money, right from launch.” Jeff Smith, CEO DCBank "The Real-Time Rail is an important investment in Canada's economic future. Instant, data-rich payments will give Canadian businesses and their trading partners more visibility and control over their cash, and we look forward to bringing those benefits to our clients.” Lyndsay Langford, Head of Global Payments Solutions for Canada Bank of America Delivery partners “Canada’s Real-Time Rail is a significant milestone and a powerful example of what national collaboration can achieve. More than a modernization of payments, it represents an investment in critical infrastructure that will support Canada’s digital economy for generations to come. CGI is proud to have contributed alongside Payments Canada, Interac and our fellow delivery partners to this made-in-Canada initiative. Together, we’re laying the foundation for faster, more secure and resilient payments, opening new opportunities for businesses, financial institutions and Canadians. Through this work, we’re helping build what’s next for Canada’s digital economy.” Michael Godin, President, Canada Operations CGI “Deloitte is very proud to have supported Payments Canada and its members deliver the technical solution for the Real-Time Rail project. This ‘made-in-Canada’ initiative will be a critical foundation for innovation and productivity in Canada while better protecting Canadians against financial crimes. We look forward to welcoming new members to the RTR and continued collaboration for the benefit of Canadians.” Todd Roberts, Global Payments Leader Deloitte Canada “Canadians expect payments to be fast and easy, but behind that experience, the infrastructure has to be secure, resilient and built for the future. Building a real-time payment system at this scale takes deep payments and technology experience, relentless testing and close collaboration. As the technology implementation partner, IBM Canada has worked alongside Payments Canada and its partners to bring that experience to the Real-Time Rail, helping build a strong foundation for the next generation of payments and innovation in Canada.” Matthew Wetmore, Managing Partner and Market Leader, Consulting IBM Canada “As the RTR’s Technical Operator and first Fraud Services Provider, Interac is proud to support Payments Canada and the wider payment ecosystem in achieving this historic launch milestone. We bring more than 40 years of experience to these roles, and our commitment is clear: to operate always-on infrastructure Canadians can trust. As Interac e-Transfer payments begin to clear and settle on the RTR, we will put this world-class infrastructure to work for consumers and businesses.” Jeremy Wilmot, President and CEO Interac Corp. Payments Canada Member and Stakeholder Advisory Councils “The launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail is a significant milestone for Canada’s payment ecosystem and reflects the sustained commitment and collective effort of members in bringing it to launch. The RTR establishes a modern, made-in-Canada foundation for real-time, data-rich payments that will support innovation, efficiency and improved payment experiences. As members build on this foundation, the focus will be on delivering new capabilities and experiences that create real value for consumers and businesses across Canada." Michael Liberty Vice President, Global Money Operations, CIBC Payments Canada Member Advisory Council Chair “The launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail is an important milestone for the stakeholder community and for the future of payments in Canada. By creating greater access to real-time payment infrastructure, the RTR opens new opportunities for stakeholders across the ecosystem to participate, innovate and compete. The RTR is a platform that enables new ideas, products and services that can deliver more seamless payment experiences for Canadians, and on behalf of the Stakeholder Advisory Council, we look forward to seeing what new possibilities this creates for payments in Canada.” Daniela Aubry Chief Payments Officer, Metrolinx Payments Canada Stakeholder Advisory Council Chair “We are very proud to contribute to this major milestone in the modernization of payments in Canada. This is a true collective effort, made possible through outstanding collaboration among the various industry stakeholders. This initiative demonstrates what we can achieve together to advance financial infrastructure for the benefit of businesses and Canadians.” Patrice Roy Head of Payments, National Bank Payments Canada Member Advisory Council Vice-Chair Key member program contributors “The Real-Time Rail is a powerful foundation for new business models, greater competition and economic growth across Canada. We're thrilled that Brim Financial is a future participant in Canada's Real-Time Rail. Brim's Payments-as-a-Service platform capabilities will enable real-time money movement, payments and intelligent commercial workflows in one unified ecosystem. This empowers our clients to accelerate innovation, unlock new opportunities, optimize liquidity and deliver transformative customer experiences.” Rasha Katabi, Founder and CEO Brim “The launch of the Real-Time Rail is a significant milestone in the modernization of Canada’s payment systems. Central 1 has invested in the infrastructure, capabilities and expertise to enable our clients to participate in real-time payments without the complexity to build and operate the underlying infrastructure themselves. Through that investment, we’re helping our clients unlock the benefits of real-time payments and extend those benefits to millions of Canadians.” Sunny Soin, Vice President, Product and Platform - Payments Central 1 “In today’s high-velocity commercial environment, there is need for instant, frictionless settlement backed by world-class technology. By deploying our proprietary Citi Payment Express platform for Canada’s Real-Time Rail, we are giving our clients immediate access to 24/7 real-time settlement and rich ISO 20022 remittance data via a high-availability, low-latency platform designed for instant payments. It is a powerful example of how Citi delivers global-standard technology to solve local market needs.” Mohneet Gujral, Head of Payments Citi Canada “Desjardins is proud to play a role modernizing Canada’s payment infrastructure. The Real-Time Rail will help us better serve the evolving payment needs of our members and clients, today and into the future.” Johanne Duhaime, Senior Executive Vice President, Technology and Organizational Performance Desjardins “The Real-Time Rail represents an important milestone for Canada and the continued modernization of our payment ecosystem. Real-time, always-on payments are changing how businesses move and manage money, from providing greater visibility and control over cash to enabling faster payouts and more seamless payment experiences for their customers. We’re proud to participate in this next chapter for Canadian payments and help our clients capture the opportunities it creates.” Dougal Middleton, Head of Payments and Treasury Services, Canada J.P. Morgan "The launch of the Real-Time Rail is an important milestone in the modernization of Canada's payment ecosystem. Meridian is proud to support this industry-wide effort and the development of payment infrastructure that will help enable faster, more modern payment experiences for Canadians and businesses across the country.” Matthew Seagrim, Chief Growth Officer Meridian Credit Union “The Real-Time Rail holds tremendous potential to empower Canadian consumers and businesses. I want to thank Payments Canada and Finance Canada for turning a sovereign real-time payments network into a reality. The imperative for made-in-Canada infrastructure that protects and supports Canadians, while strengthening domestic dependency, has never been more important. As adoption gains momentum, I look forward to seeing the positive impact that the RTR will have for workers, SMEs and homegrown innovation.” Dan Broten, Senior Vice President and Chief Digital Officer EQB Inc. (owner of President’s Choice Bank) Industry association collaboration “The CBA welcomes the implementation of the Real‑Time Rail, which will expand to include many of our members across Canada and will help modernize Canada’s payment systems and strengthen the backbone of the country’s financial market infrastructure. Innovation in payment technology continues to be a driving force behind payment choice and efficiency, thereby supporting economic growth in Canada. Security and trust remain paramount to the successful execution of real-time payments. Banks in Canada are dedicated to enabling a safe, fast and secure experience for individuals and businesses, while maintaining a resilient and stable financial system.” Anthony G. Ostler, President and CEO Canadian Bankers Association “The Real-Time Rail is a momentous transformation in how payments are done in Canada. Credit unions and their members will see real benefits, including improved convenience and better cash flow management for small businesses. As part of this phased implementation, we welcome the secure, flexible ways that credit unions will be able to participate in the RTR, so that very soon everyone who banks with a credit union or caisse populaire will experience faster, smarter and more flexible payments.” Jeff Guthrie, Chief Executive Officer Canadian Credit Union Association “Congratulations to Payments Canada on launching the Real-Time Rail. This is a milestone for small businesses, consumers and the innovators building Canada’s next generation of financial services. We look forward to seeing fintechs and financial institutions connect, bring more payments onto the rail and build services that give Canadians and businesses more choice.” Adriana Vega, Executive Director Fintechs Canada About Payments Canada Payments Canada enables prosperity, productivity and safety for Canada through trusted, critical national payment infrastructure. As a public-purpose organization, we own and operate: Lynx , our high-value payment system; the Automated Clearing Settlement System (ACSS), our retail batch payment system; and the Real-Time Rail (RTR), our new real-time payment system. We establish the by-laws, rules and standards that govern these systems, which cleared and settled $103 trillion in 2025 — more than $411 billion every business day. Transactions that pass through our systems include debit card payments, pre-authorized debits, direct deposits, bill payments, wire payments and cheques. In collaboration with our diverse membership, we continue to modernize Canada’s payment ecosystem to promote innovation, competition and deliver efficiencies that power a modern economy.
