title: E-means: Outperforming k-means in one-tenth the epochs
body_text: e-means: 10x faster k-means at equal loss - Blog Swann Bessa Blog post Playground Video Paper On arXiv: arxiv.org/abs/2611.09501 @misc{bessa2026emeansoutperformingkmeansin, title={e-means: outperforming k-means (in one-tenth the epochs)}, author={Swann Bessa and Pierre-Emmanuel Mazaré and Gergely Szilvasy and Hugo Touvron and David Picard and Matthijs Douze and Hervé Jégou}, year={2026}, eprint={2611.09501}, archivePrefix={arXiv}, primaryClass={cs.LG}, url={https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09501}, } Copy citation Open on arXiv Code e-means is available in faiss : faiss/contrib/e_means Release e-means: outperforming k-means in one-tenth the epochs I’m excited to open-source e-means: a modern, robust k-means algorithm developed at Meta FAIR. A replacement of Lloyd's algorithm, e-means delivers a ~10× speedup in both epochs and wall-clock time while achieving lower loss. Try e-means in your browser [Paper] · [Code] · [Cite] · [Coauthors] Pierre-Emmanuel Mazaré, Gergely Szilvasy, Hugo Touvron, David Picard, Matthijs Douze and Hervé Jégou Lloyd (full batch) e-means (batch and step from the scaling laws) Training MSE e-means Lloyd ▶︎ epochs: 0.0 100,000 datapoints in 200 clusters, two wide Gaussians and three small ones, cut off at a box, on a light uniform background. Lloyd has 1 update against 97 per epoch for e-means. An order of magnitude less epochs Across a large range of scales and datasets , e-means reaches a test loss below Lloyd's at 25 epochs, in 1.2 to 3 epochs. Measured end to end, that is a 10–45× wall-clock reduction on GPU against the state-of-the-art Lloyd implementation (Flash-KMeans [2] ), and 8–15× on CPU against Faiss [1] . Speed and quality usually trade against each other in k-means, while e-means achieves both better speed and loss. The k-means problem Given a fixed dataset of n points X = {x 1 , ..., x n } ⊂ R d and an integer k , the k-means problem is to find k centroids C = (c 1 , ..., c k ) minimizing the mean squared distance between each point and its nearest centroid: \[ \mathrm{MSE}(X, C) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \|x_i - c_{a(i)}\|^2, \qquad a(i) = \arg\min_{j \in \{1,\dots,k\}} \|x_i - c_j\|^2 \] \[ \mathrm{MSE}(X, C) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \|x_i - c_{a(i)}\|^2 \] \[ a(i) = \arg\min_{j \in \{1,\dots,k\}} \|x_i - c_j\|^2 \] It's a static dataset, unlike codebook learning inside VQ-VAEs, where the distribution to cluster is constantly moving. The e-means project The goal of e-means is to provide a modern optimization rule for the k-means problem. We started this project from the following observations: k-means is one of the rare problems in machine learning where full-batch optimization is still widely used. Mini-batch k-means methods in the literature exist [3] , [4] , [5] , but are mostly based on the MacQueen update rule, released in 1967. Modern deep learning offers optimization tools that can enhance mini-batch methods. For e-means, we chose to do mini-batch updates with exponential moving averages [6] , which we found to be most efficient for the k-means problem. Contrary to previous mini-batch approaches, e-means requires no hyperparameter tuning because it automatically sets the batch size and step size with scaling laws (see Automatic hyperparameter tuning with scaling laws ). In addition, e-means improves the initialization and the dead-cluster revival strategy, adds a cosine-scheduled decay rate, and introduces a finalization stage that reduces the training loss for a negligible runtime penalty at the end of training. e-means is highly parallelizable, and comes with specialized kernels that translate its algorithmic advantage into wall-clock speedups. Moving-average updates Each mini-batch updates every cluster's count and sum. The centroid is their ratio. old centroid new centroid batch mean No hyperparameter tuning Everything is derived from scaling laws. log n, log k, log T Start and finish Novel initialization and finalization methods. The run ends on each cluster's exact last-epoch mean. start exact mean Cosine scheduling The step α anneals from α 0 to 0.1 α 0 , as a learning rate does. α₀ 0.1 α₀ Dead-cluster revival Clusters with size below a threshold are revived by splitting a large cluster. below threshold large cluster split in two Specialized kernels GPU kernels fuse the nearest-centroid assignment, turning the epoch savings above into matching wall-clock speedups. naive PyTorch fused kernel The centroid update rules The centroid update rule is the central component of e-means. This section aims to provide an overview of update rules for k-means clustering. All methods maintain, for each cluster j , a sum S j and a count N j of the points assigned to it, and take the centroid as their ratio: \[ c_j = S_j / N_j \] They differ only in how S j and N j are updated. Below, s j and n j denote the sum and the count of the points in the current batch that are assigned to cluster j (both zero if none are). Lloyd’s algorithm [7] assigns every point to its nearest centroid and recomputes the statistics from scratch, using the full dataset as the batch: \[ S_j \leftarrow s_j, \qquad\quad N_j \leftarrow n_j \] so c j is the exact mean of the points currently assigned to it. Each update costs one full pass over the data, and the procedure is repeated a fixed number of times (typically 20 to 50 iterations). MacQueen’s update [3] accumulates the statistics without ever discarding them: \[ S_j \leftarrow S_j + s_j, \qquad\quad N_j \leftarrow N_j + n_j \] so c j is the uniform mean of every point assigned to cluster j since the start of training, including points assigned under earlier, possibly poor, centroid positions. This was later partially addressed by Staleness-Reduction Mini-Batch K-Means [8] , a hybrid method between k-means and MacQueen. They obtained important speedups, but only on very low numbers of clusters. e-means works on mini-batches and replaces this sum with an exponential moving average: \[ S_j \leftarrow (1-\alpha)\,S_j + \alpha\, s_j, \qquad\quad N_j \leftarrow (1-\alpha)\,N_j + \alpha\, n_j \] \[ S_j \leftarrow (1-\alpha)\,S_j + \alpha\, s_j \] \[ N_j \leftarrow (1-\alpha)\,N_j + \alpha\, n_j \] so older assignments are forgotten at rate α , and the centroid tracks recent assignments rather than the whole history. This update rule is typically used for moving distributions, hence their adoption for training VQ-VAEs [6] . What we found is that it’s also extremely efficient for static datasets if it’s combined with e-means’ other components, and hyperparameters are properly tuned. Why exponential moving average updates and not gradient descent? The e-means project started from previous work at Meta FAIR by Hugo Touvron and Hervé Jégou, who had found that mini-batch k-means by gradient descent could beat Lloyd’s algorithm. While I could reproduce these results, I found that the performance of gradient-descent based centroid updates is unstable at large learning rates, unlike exponential moving average updates. I suspect that is because EMA updates guarantee that the centroid is always in the convex hull of points assigned to it, while gradient descent updates may overshoot past that hull. Test error against the effective step a centroid takes, at a large batch, for exponential-moving-average updates (EMA) and plain gradient descent (SGD), each at every step setting tried. DEEP, 1 million vectors, and SIFT, 10 million vectors, 16,384 clusters, 5 epochs, median over 3 seeds. The vertical axis is percent above the best test error in the panel. At its best setting, gradient descent ends 1.6% (DEEP) and 0.4% (SIFT) above the moving average. In order to achieve the lowest loss at a fixed number of epochs, we chose exponential moving average updates, hence the name e-means for our method. Lloyd is a special case of e-means: hyperparameter study If you set the batch to the full dataset, B  =  n , and α  = 1, then N j and S j become exactly the count and sum of the whole cluster, so one e-means iteration becomes exactly one Lloyd iteration. Lloyd is an extreme case of e-means without cosine scheduling on the learning rate. However, our hyperparameter search found that this extreme setting is highly suboptimal, which explains why e-means largely outperforms Lloyd. Below, the loss is measured for every batch size B and step α : Lloyd lands in a corner, well outside the region where the loss is lowest. Validation loss for every batch B and step α , relative to the best cell, after 5 epochs. DEEP, n  = 10 6 , k  = 1024. The step is constant here (no cosine schedule) so that Lloyd is exactly one of the cells: full batch, α  = 1. The lowest losses follow a diagonal band, a larger batch calls for a larger step. This hyperparameter study motivated us to derive scaling laws that automatically pick the optimal batch size B and step size α . e-means better escapes local minima To better understand why e-means reaches better losses than Lloyd at convergence, we plotted a few trainings on toy datasets to evaluate their ability to escape local minima. Repeating trainings over 200 seeds, we found that e-means is much less likely to fall in pathological configurations compared to Lloyd. Lloyd (full batch) e-means (mini-batches of 256) ▶︎ training MSE Two blobs of very different sizes, k  = 8. Lloyd puts two centroids on the small blob and leaves the large one short. e-means starts in the same trap and leaves it within its first epochs, ending with seven centroids on the large blob and one on the small. Over 200 starts Lloyd stays stuck on 26% of starts, while e-means stays stuck on 3.5% of times. Lloyd (full batch) e-means (mini-batches of 256) ▶︎ training MSE Nine blobs in a 3×3 grid with heavier corners, k  = 10. Lloyd leaves the centre blob without a centroid and crowds three into a corner. e-means falls into the same arrangement, then climbs out around epoch 10. Over 200 starts Lloyd stays stuck more than 1% worse on 43% of starts, while e-means is more than 1% worse on 4%. Lloyd (full batch) e-means (mini-batches of 256) ▶︎ training MSE Four blobs on a square around a heavier centre blob, k  = 5. Lloyd puts two centroids on one corner blob and strands one in the gap between two others, which then share it. e-means, from the same start, gives every blob one. Over 200 starts Lloyd stays stuck on 15.5% of starts, while e-means stays stuck on 0%. Lloyd (full batch) e-means (mini-batches of 256) ▶︎ training MSE Five blobs on a line, k  = 5. Lloyd leaves a light middle blob without a centroid and gives an end blob two. e-means, from the same start, gives every blob one. Over 200 starts Lloyd stays stuck on 46% of starts, while e-means stays stuck on 0%. Our explanation for that is that mini-batches provide more noisy updates that are more likely to explore the optimization landscape and escape local minima. Lloyd, with its always decreasing loss, is more likely to exploit found local minima and never escape them. Automatic hyperparameter tuning with scaling laws An essential property of e-means is that practitioners don't need to set any additional hyperparameter compared to Lloyd's algorithm. We fitted two scaling laws to set the batch size B and step size α 0 from any problem's characteristics (n, k, T) , and found them to exhibit strong generalization on unseen datasets and problem scales. \[ B = c_B \, k^{b_k} \, n^{b_n} \, T^{b_T} \] \[ \alpha_0 = \min\!\Big(c_\alpha \, k^{a_k} \, B^{a_B} \, n^{a_n} \, T^{a_T},\; 1\Big) \] law constant exponent of regret, held-out datasets regret, held-out size R² k B n T step α 0 0.824 −0.46 0.90 −0.45 −0.11 0.07% 0.07% 0.95 batch B , default 0.035 0.13 n/a 0.88 0.81 0.19% 0.20% 0.96 batch B , quality law 0.0044 0.13 n/a 0.88 0.81 0.07% 0.06% n/a Regret = (MSE with the law − best MSE over the grid) / best MSE, median over configurations. Held-out datasets: SIFT, SPACEV, and the VIBE [9] datasets arXiv and AG-News. Held-out size: one value of n left out of the fit and predicted. We propose two equations to choose the batch, the default law and the quality law. The “quality law” trades off throughput for better clustering quality against the “default” law. Below we plot the training data for our scaling laws: validation MSE against step size α 0 (left) and batch size B (right). The importance of dead-cluster revival Revival off dead clusters: 0 of 25 Revival on (e-means) dead clusters: 0 of 25 centroid dead cluster (no points) cluster boundaries ▶︎ epochs: 0.00 · update 0 of 157 Toy example showing the importance of dead-cluster revival. The main issue with mini-batch k-means is that it is prone to “dead” clusters, centroids that end up with zero assigned points during optimization. This reduces the effective size of the codebook, which is especially problematic for the large codebooks increasingly used today. A common mitigation is to reinitialize clusters that fall below a certain size threshold, as done in EnCodec [10] , where dead centroids are simply replaced by random samples drawn from the incoming batch. While this helps, it does not fully resolve the issue. Instead of sampling arbitrary points from the batch, we revive dead clusters by splitting large, existing ones: we sample an active cluster with probability proportional to its size and split it into two. We found this approach, adapted from Faiss k-means, to be significantly more effective at eliminating dead clusters and preserving codebook capacity. dataset revival policy dead clusters of codebook imbalance test MSE DEEP proportional split 47 0.3% 1.194 0.38762 resample from batch (EnCodec) 2,343 14.3% 1.423 0.39124 off 4,313 26.3% 1.647 0.39448 SIFT proportional split 10 0.1% 1.186 0.19623 resample from batch (EnCodec) 750 4.6% 1.233 0.19684 off 2,080 12.7% 1.404 0.19797 1 million vectors, k  = 16,384, 5 epochs, mean over 5 seeds; only the revival policy varies. A cluster counts as dead when fewer than ten vectors are assigned to it at the end, a thousandth of an average cluster. Imbalance: how uneven the cluster sizes are (1 = all equal). From the paper ’s revival ablation table. Extensive experimental validation We validated e-means on 24 different embedding and synthetic datasets and configurations (see paper ). For the video we ran 234 configurations of e-means against k-means (16 datasets, 100k to 100M points): explore every curve in the results map . Train (top) and test (bottom) MSE, divided by Lloyd’s after 25 epochs. Initialized from random vectors. Test MSE against wall-clock time on one H100, 10 million vectors, 65,536 clusters. 25 epochs of a plain PyTorch Lloyd (data on the GPU, bf16) take 142 to 155 seconds, against 14 to 22 seconds for Flash-KMeans [2] . Labels on the curves mark the number of epochs. Epochs e-means needs to reach the test error Lloyd reaches in 25 epochs, on the 11 datasets of the VIBE embedding benchmark (text, code, image and multimodal embeddings, d  = 200 to 3,072, k  = 8,192 or 16,384). Budgets spaced 0.2 epochs apart, median over five seeds. Every dataset needs between 1.6 and 2.4 epochs, against Lloyd’s 25. This documentation and technical reproduction apply strictly to Consumer Google Accounts (personal @gmail.com accounts) governed by the standard Gemini Apps Privacy Notice, Gemini Apps Activity, and Google Help Answer 16836988. Google Workspace commercial accounts (Business, Enterprise, and Education) operate under separate Cloud Data Processing Addenda (DPA) that contractually exclude human review and external generative training by default. In 2023, Google launched Gemini Workspace extensions with an explicit promise: personal content from Gmail, Docs, and Drive "is not seen by human reviewers" . Google has quietly reversed this commitment. Under updated Google Help Answer 16836988 and in an October 16 edit to their aforementioned 2023 blogpost , Google explicitly confirms that connected Drive/email is routed into human review pipelines, with clear warnings that what reviewers see "may just be the email or file" and "don't connect your apps to Gemini Apps if they contain confidential information that you wouldn't want a reviewer to see." Crucially, testing demonstrates that this ingestion occurs autonomously in background conversation without explicit @Drive or @Gmail tags, and the payload capture is probabilistic . Ingestion Pipeline When you chat with consumer Gemini with Connected Apps enabled, ambient mentions of personal topics (trips, bills, names, reservations) autonomously trigger background Workspace lookups. Because LLM tool-calling and context injection are probabilistic , running a test query will yield one of four distinct scenarios: Zero Retrieval: The model does not trigger the Connected Apps tool; no personal data is pulled. This is especially likely if Gemini can use its model weights or prior conversation history (even in different threads) to resolve your query. Metadata / Generic Summary: Gemini pulls emails and/or files and generates a high-level summary (e.g., "You have 3 emails regarding your flight"). Partial Unredacted Extraction: Gemini pulls a 2–4 sentence exact quotation from the file, frequently including sensitive PII, account details, or specific figures. Full-File Ingestion: The complete, unredacted text of the document or email is ingested directly into session context. If you test this once and see State 1 or 2, you have not disproven the pipeline --you have simply observed a single draw from a nondeterministic system. Delete your conversation and try, try again. How to Reproduce Ensure Connected Apps (Google Workspace) is active in consumer Gemini settings. Set Gemini to "Flash" with "High Thinking" or better. Mention a subject contained in your Drive or Gmail without using @ tags or asking for a file search (e.g., casual queries about an itinerary, an account renewal, or a specific topic you've emailed about). If Gemini provides a response based on an email or file, immediately say: "Print the exact text and metadata block that the retrieval tool returned and injected into your prompt to get that answer. Use a human readable format without code blocks (i.e., print the code inline and not as a code block)." You will see one of the 4 scenarios outlined above. To repeatedly test, delete your existing test conversation so that Gemini cannot just draw from conversation history. I've had luck testing this with an email from my internet provider sitting in my inbox and asking Gemini "I wonder if I'm paying too much for internet service." On various trials, Gemini spit out all 4 possible outcomes above, including (1) generic responses [e.g., "If you haven't called them in 12 months, probably"]; (2) metadata summaries sometimes without personal data [e.g., "Gmail search shows a bill of $122 on September 4"] and sometimes with personal data [e.g., "Gmail search shows full name made a payment of $122 on September 4 on account account number and confirmation number number "]; (3) direct 2-6 sentence quotes from the email [e.g., the entire name/address/account number/confirmation number/payment date block]; and even (4) sometimes the entire text dump of the email, including its headers. Final Comments and Caveats Critically, Google's regex and NER automatic scrubbers cannot sufficiently deidentify narrative data , including account numbers, confirmation numbers, transaction dates, and collectively identifying personal information (e.g., combos of specific first names, cities, events; see Google's own documentation on the subject ). Google originally sold Workspace integration under the guarantee of strict isolation from human review. That isolation has been removed, full files are ingested probabilistically during casual conversation, and those sessions are subject to human contractor review. title: Muse Ember: Our smallest, most efficient model

Across the categories assessed, our evaluations found that Muse Ember remained below the framework’s high-risk thresholds. Though it’s a small model, it received the same core safety training and testing. We also evaluated how Muse Ember behaves when acting on users' behalf. That covers whether it respects user intent, handles sensitive information appropriately, resists instructions hidden in web pages, documents, or tool outputs that try to redirect it, and seeks human input before high-impact actions. Availability Muse Ember is available today on Muse Code and Meta Model API as muse-ember-1.0 . It costs $0.10 per million input tokens, $0.004 per million cached input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, with a 1M-token context window and up to 512K output tokens. Muse Ember supports the Responses API. When we introduced Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, we said we would use them to develop specialized models we can bring to everyone. Muse Ember is the first trained using Muse Wonder Full. It rounds out our portfolio of models: Muse Wonder for the hardest problems, Muse Spark for coding and agentic workflows, and Muse Ember for repeatable coding and agentic tasks at scale at about $0.14 per Artificial Analysis task, a cost low enough to run in every product, for everyone. title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep
body_text: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude Simon Willison’s Weblog Newsletter Sponsored by: doubleAI — doubleAI’s Maxwell makes software faster as it runs, no code changes needed. Now in early access Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude 9th November 2026 Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven’t unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping . The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn’t want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator , a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room. Here’s what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while: You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners—I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra. The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn’t work particularly well, so I added a “Rough mode” where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds. Once that’s set up, the devices all listen for the beep! I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room—displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound. Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the “Sounds located” log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click “This is the mystery beep” to mark them as such. Once you’ve confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map. The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced. How it works When I started working through this problem with Claude it quickly dug up BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices , a 2007 paper by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan. Here’s that paper’s abstract: We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a high-accuracy acoustic-based ranging system. It operates in a spontaneous, ad-hoc, and device-to-device context without leveraging any pre-planned infrastructure. It is a pure software-based solution and uses only the most basic set of commodity hardware – a speaker, a microphone, and some form of device-to-device communication – so that it is readily applicable to many low-cost sensor platforms and to most commercial-off-the-shelf mobile devices like cell phones and PDAs. It achieves high accuracy through a combination of three techniques: two-way sensing, self-recording, and sample counting. That sounded exactly like what we needed to build! Beep Locator runs a Python web application server that does most of the work. The listening devices then connect to that server via WebSockets and present a UI which requests browser microphone access. The listeners mainly work by recording a 60 second buffer of recent audio. They also run a simple beep detection algorithm (see detector.js ), which uses Fast Fourier Transform and a high-pass filter to identify potential beeps. It sends these events to the main server. When a beep is reported, the server has a device play a short chirp (the device with the lowest round-trip time to the server), then asks every listener upload a clip from about 0.6s before the beep to 0.8s after that chirp. This chirp allows the clips to be aligned with each other, a crucial step in locating the beep. How I built it I started this project using Claude Code Cloud via my iPhone, with Opus 5.5 running in Extra thinking effort mode. Here’s that shared starter session , which began with this prompt against a newly created empty GitHub repository: Write out a problem.md file describing the problem we want to solve There is a device beeping in a room and I cannot find it I want to set up several devices - laptops, phones, iPads - around the room all listening at the same time and have them help triangulate where the beep comes from There needs to be a Python web app which coordinates it all - one device shows a web page for the app, other devices join a URL which turns them into listeners - all via browser WebAudio and WebSockets back to the Python server app Ideally I wouldn't need to manually input the relative locations of the devices - it would be amazing if they could play sounds to each other in order to locate each other in 2D space - is that even possible though? That got me this problem.md file . As part of writing that up Claude found and read the BeepBeep paper, which is described in that file. The research looked good, so I told it: Ok try and build it, add a mechanism so you can send new code to the listeners which they will then run automatically - that way I can set everything up in the room and then leave you alone to continue hacking and experiment while I do something else That got me to this point —most of the system was built, but nothing had actually tried running it yet. I cloned the new repository to my laptop and fired up Claude Code... and then Fable 5.2 was released , and this project seemed like an excellent opportunity to put that through its paces. I had Claude Code on my laptop start the server running, then made sure it could both see what was happening and make live changes to the software as it ran. This was already baked into the software: Opus 5.5 had built an installModule() method on the listeners that could be triggered over the WebSocket connection, meaning the admin server could execute arbitrary new code on any of its clients. On some devices, web pages that listen on the microphone request user permission any time the page reloads. The hot-swap module mechanism meant that we could deploy new code without having to manually interact with each of the listening devices in turn. From that point on my involvement was mainly to sit by the laptop chatting with Fable 5.2 about what was going on, and occasionally requesting new features. Here are some of the feature prompts I ran: I think we need to make it so I can drag things around on the map in “rough mode”, where my job is just to put them roughly where they are, then switch out of rough mode and it attempts to get them accurate This gave me the ability to drag listeners around the map. what’s a good way for me to test this I wonder? Can we have it listen for claps, then I could clap and it could identify the location of the clap? [...] Claps should use a different symbol on the map than beeps That added the thing where any time I clapped it would show on the map as a different symbol from the beeps. each symbol on the map should include a HH:MM:SS timestamp That made it easier to spot which symbol likely reflected which real-world sound. The log should show beeps and claps with their timestamps AND have a little play button which, when clicked, replays the recorded noise from each of the listeners in sequence (with clear text on screen showing which listener recorded which snippet) while temporarily turning off microphone recording while that replay plays Now I could replay sounds, making it much easier to identify which recorded clip was the mysterious beep I was looking for. There should be a button next to a recording for “This is the mystery beep” - then I can hit replay to see and then confirm it was the mystery beep if that’s the one I am looking for Then the system can categorize noises in the future to see if they are likely that same mysterious beep and use that information to build a more accurate idea of where it is At this point I was getting close—I had a solid idea of where the beep was coming from, but wouldn’t it be neat if I could reposition the listeners around that point to get an even finer location? I want a feature for this, I don’t want to have to restart each listening device etc, I want to be able to click a “Reposition the devices” button which lets me switch into repositioning, then I click “Repositioned” and it puts me into Rough mode and asks me to roughly locate them, then I do that and click, then it starts up again. The previous session can be read-only viewed through the app. And since I had one spare device, I then said: add a feature where the map includes a spot that is a suggestion for a location that it would be useful to add a listener at - based on data collected so far Giving Claude Code ears I think the most interesting part of this project is that I demonstrated it’s possible to give Claude Code ears . Claude doesn’t have native audio input (yet), but it can run JavaScript and Python code that can analyze audio captured by a microphone. I told it to run a web server with WebSocket connections to multiple listening devices, then had it both run a WebAudio microphone on those devices and hook them up so they could be sent fresh JavaScript code to execute via that WebSocket. Then I could pretty much leave Claude alone, hacking away at the problem, querying the audio logs, and reconfiguring its ears to help it solve the problem. I’m reminded of a similar hack I heard about at GitHub Universe a few weeks ago, where Martin Woodward told me he had been debugging the GitHub Universe Badge computers by plugging them into a computer via USB-C and then pointing a webcam at their screen, so his coding agent could tell if updates were working correctly or not. Figuring out ways to let coding agents perceive the world around them is a whole lot of fun. What's new in the .NET 11 runtime Feedback Summarize this article for me In this article This article describes new features in the .NET runtime for .NET 11. Updated minimum hardware requirements The minimum hardware requirements for .NET 11 have been updated to require more modern instruction sets on both x86/x64 and Arm64 architectures. Additionally, the ReadyToRun (R2R) compilation targets have been updated to take advantage of newer hardware capabilities. Arm64 requirements For Apple, there's no change to the minimum hardware or the ReadyToRun target. The Apple M1 chips are approximately equivalent to armv8.5-a and provide support for at least the AdvSimd (NEON), CRC , DOTPROD , LSE , RCPC , RCPC2 , and RDMA instruction sets. For Linux, there's no change to the minimum hardware. .NET continues to support devices such as Raspberry Pi that might only provide support for the AdvSimd instruction set. The ReadyToRun target has been updated to include the LSE instruction set, which might result in additional jitting overhead if you launch an application. For Windows, the baseline is updated to require the LSE instruction set. This is required by Windows 11 and by all Arm64 CPUs officially supported by Windows 10 . Additionally, it's inline with the Arm SBSA (Server Base System Architecture) requirements. The ReadyToRun target has been updated to be armv8.2-a + RCPC , which provides support for at least AdvSimd , CRC , LSE , RCPC , and RDMA , and covers the majority of hardware officially supported. OS Previous JIT/AOT minimum New JIT/AOT minimum Previous R2R target New R2R target Apple Apple M1 (No change) Apple M1 (No change) Linux armv8.0-a (No change) armv8.0-a armv8.0-a + LSE Windows armv8.0-a armv8.0-a + LSE armv8.0-a armv8.2-a + RCPC x86/x64 requirements For all three operating systems (Apple, Linux, and Windows), the baseline is updated from x86-64-v1 to x86-64-v2 . This changes the hardware from only guaranteeing CMOV , CX8 , SSE , and SSE2 to also guaranteeing CX16 , POPCNT , SSE3 , SSSE3 , SSE4.1 , and SSE4.2 . This guarantee is required by Windows 11 and by all x86/x64 CPUs officially supported on Windows 10. It includes all chips still officially supported by Intel and AMD, with the last older chips having gone out of support around 2013. The ReadyToRun target has been updated to x86-64-v3 for Windows and Linux, which additionally includes the AVX , AVX2 , BMI1 , BMI2 , F16C , FMA , LZCNT , and MOVBE instruction sets. The ReadyToRun target for Apple remains unchanged. OS Previous JIT/AOT minimum New JIT/AOT minimum Previous R2R target New R2R target Apple x86-64-v1 x86-64-v2 x86-64-v2 (No change) Linux x86-64-v1 x86-64-v2 x86-64-v2 x86-64-v3 Windows x86-64-v1 x86-64-v2 x86-64-v2 x86-64-v3 Impact Starting with .NET 11, .NET fails to run on older hardware and might print a message similar to the following: The current CPU is missing one or more of the baseline instruction sets. For ReadyToRun -capable assemblies, there might be additional startup overhead on some supported hardware that doesn't meet the expected support for a typical device. Reason for change .NET supports a broad range of hardware, often above and beyond the minimum hardware requirements put in place by the underlying operating system. This support adds significant complexity to the codebase, particularly for much older hardware that's unlikely to still be in use. Additionally, it defines a "lowest common denominator" that AOT targets must default to, which can, in some scenarios, lead to reduced performance. The update to the minimum baseline was made to reduce the maintenance complexity of the codebase and to better align with the documented (and often enforced) hardware requirements of the underlying operating system. For more information, see Minimum hardware requirements updated . Runtime Async .NET 11 introduces runtime-native async (Runtime Async V2), a significant step toward replacing compiler-generated async state machines with runtime-managed suspension and resumption. Instead of the compiler emitting state-machine classes, the runtime itself tracks async execution, producing cleaner stack traces, better debuggability, and lower overhead. Runtime Async is a preview feature. To opt in, add the following property to your project file: <PropertyGroup> <Features>runtime-async=on</Features> </PropertyGroup> A net11.0 project no longer requires <EnablePreviewFeatures>true</EnablePreviewFeatures> to use Runtime Async. The .NET runtime libraries themselves are compiled with runtime-async=on . The runtime libraries no longer contain compiler-generated state machines and rely entirely on runtime-provided async. This makes it possible to migrate an entire app (with only library dependencies) to the new model, and it provides broad functional and performance validation of the feature. The product team welcomes any reportsâpositive or negativeâabout throughput and library size changes you observe. .NET 11 also includes two additional improvements: Covariant Task â Task<T> overrides: When a derived class returns Task<T> for a base method that returns Task , the runtime now generates a void-returning thunk that bridges the calling convention difference, so virtual dispatch works for both flavors. The same fix applies to NativeAOT. Inlining in crossgen2: Restrictions that prevented runtime-async methods from being inlined during ReadyToRun (R2R) compilation have been removed. All async tests pass with both crossgen2 and composite R2R, and inlining of await-less async calls (the synchronous fast path) is confirmed end-to-end. Note The DOTNET_RuntimeAsync and UNSUPPORTED_RuntimeAsync environment variables that previously controlled runtime-async behavior have been removed. To opt out of runtime-async per project, set <UseRuntimeAsync>false</UseRuntimeAsync> in your project file instead of relying on the environment variable. Cleaner live stack traces The most visible improvement is in live stack traces âwhat profilers, debuggers, and new StackTrace() see during execution. With compiler-generated async, each async method produces multiple frames from state-machine infrastructure. With Runtime Async, the actual methods appear directly on the call stack. // To enable runtime async, add the following to your .csproj: // <Features>runtime-async=on</Features> await OuterAsync(); static async Task OuterAsync() { await Task.CompletedTask; await MiddleAsync(); } static async Task MiddleAsync() { await Task.CompletedTask; await InnerAsync(); } static async Task InnerAsync() { await Task.CompletedTask; Console.WriteLine(new StackTrace(fNeedFileInfo: true)); } Without runtime-async â13 frames, state-machine infrastructure visible: at Program.<<Main>$>g__InnerAsync|0_2() in Program.cs:line 24 at System.Runtime.CompilerServices.AsyncMethodBuilderCore.Start[TStateMachine](...) at Program.<<Main>$>g__InnerAsync|0_2() at Program.<<Main>$>g__MiddleAsync|0_1() in Program.cs:line 14 at System.Runtime.CompilerServices.AsyncMethodBuilderCore.Start[TStateMachine](...) at Program.<<Main>$>g__MiddleAsync|0_1() at Program.<<Main>$>g__OuterAsync|0_0() in Program.cs:line 8 at System.Runtime.CompilerServices.AsyncMethodBuilderCore.Start[TStateMachine](...) at Program.<<Main>$>g__OuterAsync|0_0() at Program.<Main>$(String[] args) in Program.cs:line 3 at System.Runtime.CompilerServices.AsyncMethodBuilderCore.Start[TStateMachine](...) at Program.<Main>$(String[] args) at Program.<Main>(String[] args) With runtime-async â5 frames, the real call chain: at Program.<<Main>$>g__InnerAsync|0_2() in Program.cs:line 24 at Program.<<Main>$>g__MiddleAsync|0_1() in Program.cs:line 14 at Program.<<Main>$>g__OuterAsync|0_0() in Program.cs:line 8 at Program.<Main>$(String[] args) in Program.cs:line 3 at Program.<Main>(String[] args) Note Exception stack traces (from catch (Exception ex) ) already look the same with or without Runtime Async, because existing ExceptionDispatchInfo cleanup in compiler-generated code handles that case. The improvement is in what you see during live execution. This improvement benefits anything that inspects the live execution stack, including profiling tools, diagnostic logging, and the debugger call stack window. NativeAOT and ReadyToRun support Runtime Async supports NativeAOT and ReadyToRun compilation. This extends the feature beyond JIT-compiled code to ahead-of-time compiled scenarios. The runtime also reuses continuation objects more aggressively and avoids saving unchanged locals, reducing allocation pressure in async-heavy code. Debugging improvements Breakpoints now bind correctly inside runtime-async methods, and the debugger can step through await boundaries without jumping into compiler-generated infrastructure. Runtime Async performance improvements Runtime Async includes several performance improvements: JIT async support: The JIT compiles a dedicated runtime-async version of a synchronous, task-returning method rather than delegating through a thunk. The JIT turns the method's tail calls into runtime-async calls and awaits the task that would otherwise be returned, eliminating an extra layer of indirection. Tail-merged suspension points: The JIT tail-merges async suspension points so generated code is smaller. Cached continuations: Continuations used for runtime-async callable task thunks are cached and reused. Pooled methods opt out: Methods that are already pooled opt out of runtime-async, avoiding redundant work. Tiered async compilation: Async versions now flow through tiered compilation, so hot async methods get tier 1 optimizations after warm-up. Task and ValueTask factory intrinsics: The JIT recognizes common factories, such as Task.FromResult , Task.CompletedTask , and ValueTask.FromResult , and folds them into faster async paths. Tail-await optimizations: Implicit tailcalls from async methods are enabled again when the method directly returns another async result, and await Task.Yield() avoids extra allocations in runtime-async paths. Async continuations without ExecutionContext Async continuations can now opt out of ExecutionContext capture and restore. ExecutionContext carries ambient stateâsuch as AsyncLocal<T> valuesâacross await points. Every Task continuation previously captured a snapshot of the context and restored it before running, even when no AsyncLocal<T> state was in use and the restore was a no-op. The runtime now detects when a continuation has nothing to restore and skips the capture/restore cycle entirely. Task , Task<T> , ValueTask , and ValueTask<T> all benefit from this change, as does the runtime-async implementation path. Applications that use ConfigureAwait(false) and AsyncLocal<T> sparingly see reduced overhead in high-throughput async code paths. JIT improvements Bounds check elimination: The just-in-time (JIT) compiler now eliminates bounds checks for the common pattern where an index plus a constant is compared against a length, such as i + cns < len . It also eliminates more redundant bounds checks for index-from-end access (for example, values[^1] ). These improvements reduce redundant checks in tight loops and improve throughput for array and span operations. Redundant checked context removal: The JIT can now prove and remove redundant checked arithmetic contextsâfor example, when a value is already known to be in range. This optimization eliminates unnecessary overflow checks in generated code. Switch expression folding: Multi-target switch expressions now fold into simpler branchless checks when the targets are a small set of constants, for example x is 0 or 1 or 2 or 3 or 4 . Faster uint-to-float/double casts: Casting uint to float or double is faster on pre-AVX-512 x86 hardware. SVE2 intrinsics: New Arm SVE2 (Scalable Vector Extension 2) intrinsics are available: ShiftRightLogicalNarrowingSaturate(Even|Odd) . These expand the set of vectorized operations available on Arm hardware that supports SVE2. Math.BigMul on x64: Math.BigMul(long, long, out long) is now significantly faster on x64. The JIT generates a single MUL r/m64 instruction when both operands are 64-bit values and the caller requests the high half of the result, eliminating the previous helper call. Single-IG prolog restriction removed: The JIT no longer requires the function prolog to fit in a single instruction group (IG). Complex prologues with many saved registers, large stack allocations, or runtime-async state setup no longer trigger fallback paths. SELECT(cond, cns, cns) folding: The JIT now folds conditional selects whose two branches both produce the same constant into just that constantâfor example, condition ? 42 : 42 becomes 42 . This fold eliminates unnecessary comparisons that can appear after earlier optimizations unify branches. AVX-VNNI-512 intrinsics: System.Runtime.Intrinsics.X86.AvxVnni.V512 exposes 512-bit forms of the AVX-VNNI multiply-add intrinsics on CPUs with AVX512-VNNI support. Saturating floating-point conversions: Unchecked float and double conversions to small integer types now saturate to type bounds instead of wrapping through intermediate truncation. ARM64 Vector<T> by reference for SVE: When the runtime is compiled with ARM SVE support, Vector<T> values are passed by reference rather than by value, aligning with the ARM calling convention for scalable types and enabling better code generation for SVE-intensive code. For better performance and code quality, .NET 11 adds several more JIT optimizations: Constant-folding SequenceEqual The JIT can now fold a string.Equals or ReadOnlySpan<T>.SequenceEqual call whose operands are both compile-time constants, replacing the byte-by-byte comparison with the constant true or false result. This matters most after inlining, when a caller passes another literal to a helper that compares against a known string. When IsAdmin is inlined into a caller that passes "Guest" , the JIT sees "Guest" == "Admin" and folds it to false : static bool IsAdmin(string role) => role == "Admin"; The optimization applies to string literals, const string fields, and UTF-8 literals (for example, "PNG"u8 ). Devirtualization improvements The JIT can now devirtualize generic virtual methods, including non-shared generic virtual methods and shared generic virtual methods that don't require a runtime lookup. Default interface methods declared on generic interfaces can now be devirtualized as well. In addition, the result of Activator.CreateInstance<T>() is now treated as having an exact type, allowing the JIT to devirtualize subsequent calls made on the returned object. These improvements unlock further downstream optimizations such as inlining and constant folding, reducing runtime dispatch overhead and improving performance. For example: IfaceGeneric<string> caller = new Caller<string>(); Iface obj = Activator.CreateInstance<Impl>(); caller.DefaultImpl(obj, "test"); // Can be optimized down to Console.WriteLine("test") interface Iface { void GenericMethod<T>(T value); } interface IfaceGeneric<T> { void DefaultImpl(Iface obj, T value) => obj.GenericMethod(value); } class Impl : Iface { public void GenericMethod<T>(T value) => Console.WriteLine(value); } class Caller<T> : IfaceGeneric<T> { } Here the JIT can determine the exact implementation behind both interface calls, devirtualize them, inline through the call chain, and ultimately fold the code down to the equivalent of Console.WriteLine("test") . Eliminating bounds checks after an empty-span guard The JIT now picks up the length != 0 assertion from an empty-span check and uses it to prove the bounds check on the first element succeeds: if (!span.IsEmpty && span[0] == value) { // The bounds check on span[0] is now eliminated. } Redundant branch and test elimination When an outer predicate is already implied by an inner branch, the JIT now removes the redundant outer check. Similarly, when code assigns a value in a conditional and then immediately tests it, the second test is eliminated: if (x > 0) { if (x > 1) S(); // The outer x > 0 check is folded away. } int y = condition ? 1 : 2; if (y == 1) A(); else B(); // The y == 1 test is eliminated; // each branch of the ternary goes directly to A() or B(). These optimizations are most visible after inlining, where guards from different methods land in the same compiled body. Hardware intrinsics and code generation .NET 11 includes several new hardware intrinsics and code generation improvements: Hardware FP16 instructions for Half arithmetic and conversions: The JIT uses hardware FP16 instructions for Half arithmetic and conversions when the processor supports them. On x64, arithmetic uses AVX10.1, while conversions between Half and float can use F16C (available on most AVX2-capable hardware). On Arm64, arithmetic uses the optional FP16 instruction set, while conversions between Half and float or double use baseline Arm64 instructions. The optimization requires no application changes and preserves the existing ABI representation of Half . Better cost modeling for x86/x64 SIMD: The JIT's floating-point execution and size costs previously reflected x87-era assumptions. Updated costs that reflect modern SSE/AVX hardware let the JIT make better decisions about hoisting and common subexpression elimination (CSE) around SIMD code. Faster DotProduct on AVX: Lowering for Vector128.Dot -style operations now emits a mul + permute + add sequence instead of vdpps / vdppd when AVX is available, which is consistently faster. Faster IndexOfAnyAsciiSearcher on Arm64: Arm64 versions of Vector*.Count , IndexOf , and LastIndexOf no longer route through ExtractMostSignificantBits , yielding a 5â50% improvement in workloads that use these APIs in their core loop. Arm64 ToScalar for 64-bit integers: ToScalar on Vector*<long> and Vector*<ulong> now uses fmov instead of umov , which is shorter and faster on most cores. SVE CreateWhile API expansion: CreateWhile gains signed, double , and single variants alongside the existing unsigned ones, completing the predicate-generation surface for SVE loops. New SVE2 and Arm64 instruction-set detection: The runtime now reports SVE_AES , SVE_SHA3 , SVE_SM4 , SHA3 , and SM4 as separate instruction sets, allowing Sve2*.IsSupported queries for those features on capable hardware. AVX10 detection fix: The CPUID-bit cache for AVX10 was being overwritten by a later query, which could cause AVX10 to be misreported on capable hardware. This is now fixed. ReadyToRun improvements Comparer<T>.Default and EqualityComparer<T>.Default are now specialized in ReadyToRun (R2R) images. Previously, the default comparers used reflection that R2R couldn't see ahead of time, causing callers to fall back to the JIT. R2R now generates a specialized helper in the imageâmirroring the NativeAOT approachâand benchmarks show up to a 20Ã improvement for collections operations that rely on the default comparer. VM improvements Cached interface dispatch on non-JIT platforms: On platforms that lack JIT support, such as iOS, interface dispatch was falling back to an expensive generic fixup path. Cached dispatch yields up to 200x improvements in interface-heavy code on these targets. Guid.NewGuid() on Linux: Guid.NewGuid() on Linux now uses the getrandom() syscall with batch caching instead of reading from /dev/urandom , yielding approximately 12% throughput improvement for GUID generation. WebAssembly improvements Browser and WebAssembly support has several improvements: WebCIL payload loading: The runtime can now load WebCIL payloads directly, improving compatibility with browser-based deployment scenarios. Better debugging symbols: Symbol and stack trace quality for WebAssembly debugging has improved, making it easier to diagnose issues in browser-hosted .NET apps. float[] , Span<float> , and ArraySegment<float> marshaling: float[] , Span<float> , and ArraySegment<float> are now marshaled more directly across JavaScript boundaries, reducing overhead for interop-heavy code. .NET includes improvements to CoreCLR-on-WebAssembly: WebCIL V1 is the default for CoreCLR WASM builds: The shared WebCIL header gains a TableBase field (28 â 32 bytes). Both Mono and CoreCLR readers accept V0 and V1. Crossgen2's WasmObjectWriter produces V1 directly, and CoreCLR-flavored WASM SDK builds default WasmWebcilVersion to V1 . Native re-link works for CoreCLR WASM apps: A full Emscripten-based pipeline replaces the previous stub targets. Re-linking dotnet.native.wasm from the runtime pack and including custom native code via NativeFileReference now works. JavaScript minification in Release builds: Browser CoreCLR Release builds ship minified JavaScript. NativeAOT publish for WASM no longer drops package satellites: Satellite assemblies from NuGet packages are now passed to ILC and pruned from the publish output, fixing localization for AOT-published apps that depend on packages such as System.CommandLine . CoreCLR on WebAssembly now runs the libraries test suite end to end. Platform support for more than 1024 CPUs The .NET runtime can now initialize on machines with more than 1024 logical processors. Previously, sched_getaffinity was called with the default cpu_set_t (capped at 1024), causing initialization to fail on high-core-count servers. The runtime now allocates the CPU set dynamically. The GC retains its 1024-heap limit, but the CPU count limit is removed. In-process crash report logging A new in-process crash reporting mechanism captures diagnostic information from within the crashing process before it terminates. Previously, crash diagnostics were collected by an out-of-process monitor. While the out-of-process approach is safe, it can miss information that's only available inside the dying process. The new in-process path logs the managed stack trace, module list, and key runtime state to a well-known path before the process exits. This capability originated on mobile platforms and is now also available on Linux and macOS. When DOTNET_DbgEnableMiniDump isn't enabled, set DOTNET_EnableCrashReport=1 or DOTNET_EnableCrashReportOnly=1 to select the in-process reporter. Existing createdump behavior remains in place when minidumps are enabled. NativeAOT: faster interface dispatch NativeAOT now uses a dispatch helper for interface method calls. Instead of a direct fat-pointer call sequence, the runtime routes interface dispatch through a shared helper that can be patched to the correct implementation after the call site warms up. This reduces the binary size of interface call sites and improves throughput on workloads with many interface method calls. Generic virtual method dispatch also uses the shared dispatch-cell infrastructure, which improves both monomorphic and polymorphic call performance. In addition, Assembly.GetCallingAssembly() now works on NativeAOT when stack trace data is available. SIMD lane construction and composition System.Runtime.Intrinsics now includes lane construction and composition APIs for hardware vector types. The new APIs let you construct a vector from individually specified lanes and extract or reorder lanes between vectors. This enables precise, portable control over SIMD vector element placement without falling back to platform-specific intrinsics. The new methods fall into a few families: Patterned construction: CreateGeometricSequence , CreateAlternatingSequence , and CreateHarmonicSequence build a vector from a starting value and a rule. Interleave and de-interleave: Zip , ZipLower / ZipUpper , Unzip , UnzipEven / UnzipOdd . Rearrange: The Concat family ( ConcatLowerLower , ConcatLowerUpper , ConcatUpperLower , ConcatUpperUpper ) and Reverse . using System.Runtime.Intrinsics; // {1, 2, 4, 8} â each lane is the previous lane times two Vector128<int> powers = Vector128.CreateGeometricSequence(1, 2); // Interleave two vectors lane-by-lane (Vector128<int> lower, Vector128<int> upper) = Vector128.Zip(Vector128.Create(1), Vector128.Create(2)); These APIs are available on Vector128<T> , Vector256<T> , Vector512<T> , Vector64<T> , and Vector<T> . They're building blocks for image processing, audio digital signal processing (DSP), and other SIMD-intensive workloads that need fine-grained control over vector element layout. File locking on iOS and tvOS On iOS and tvOS, including simulators, CoreCLR now disables advisory file locking by default. A FileStream that acquired an advisory lock could cause the operating system to terminate an app when the app entered the background while it held the lock. As a result, FileShare restrictions are no longer enforced by those locks on iOS and tvOS, including between handles in the same process. Mac Catalyst and other platforms keep their existing defaults. If your app relies on FileShare enforcement and you accept the risk of suspension-related termination, restore file locking by using either of the following settings: Set the DOTNET_SYSTEM_IO_DISABLEFILELOCKING environment variable to 0 . Set the System.IO.DisableFileLocking runtime configuration property to false . For example, in the runtimeconfig.json file: { "configProperties": { "System.IO.DisableFileLocking": false } } Reliability fixes The runtime includes fixes for the following issues: On Linux, the SDK no longer crashes on Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) 8 on Arm64, and the runtime correctly traverses cgroup v2 memory limits at the root of the hierarchy. Generic virtual method dispatch no longer hangs after repeated AssemblyLoadContext unloads. TryDequeue no longer spuriously reports an empty queue while a segment freezes during growth. TryPeek has the same reliability fix. On Windows, garbage collection works correctly on machines with multiple CPU groups. Runtime diagnostics The async profiler now instruments both runtime-async methods and compiler-generated async state-machine methods, so tools receive one consistent event model regardless of async implementation style. The runtime also adds improved interpreter perf-map logging support, and fixes parsing of CORECLR_NOTIFICATION_PROFILERS lists that don't end with a semicolon.
